title: Conversation phrases
description: Getting to know someone, small talk and saying what you think, then the reactions, follow-ups and story glue that keep a chat going.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t (kotchi). Leading hyphen = attaches to a word.
conventions.register: romaji = casual form, learned first; polite = desu/masu counterpart, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.freqRank: rank in jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0); freqNote explains tokenizer-split forms. null = no usable rank.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; their examples share a base sentence.

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: 292 phrases in 68 chunks: getting to know you, likes and free time, what do you think, small talk and 8 more.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: 284 phrases in 71 chunks: getting to know you, likes and free time, what do you think, small talk and 10 more.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: 84 phrases in 21 chunks: what do you think, small talk, reacting, telling what happened and 4 more.

stages.name: Errands and service
stages.summary: 105 phrases for shops, restaurants and service: there for when you need them, not for chatting.

blocks.label: Where you're from
blocks.rationale: Ask where someone is from and say where you grew up.
blocks.interference: doko kara kita no can also mean 'where have you just come from' today.

items.polite: dochira kara irasshatta n desu ka?
items.english: where are you from?; where did you come from?
items.use: Asked when meeting a newcomer, usually meaning which country; answer with the place plus kara (kanada kara).
items.politeJa: どちらからいらっしゃったんですか？

example.romaji: nee, doko kara kita no? amerika?
example.ja: ねえ、どこから来たの？アメリカ？
example.english: Hey, where are you from? America?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, dochira kara irasshatta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、どちらからいらっしゃったんですか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, where are you from?

items.notes: Can also mean where you've just come from today; context decides.

items.english: I'm from ...; I grew up in ...
items.use: Your answer to shusshin doko?; put the country, city or prefecture first.

example.romaji: kanada no toronto shusshin da yo.
example.ja: カナダのトロント出身だよ。
example.english: I'm from Toronto, in Canada.

examplePolite.romaji: kanada no toronto shusshin desu.
examplePolite.ja: カナダのトロント出身です。
examplePolite.english: I'm from Toronto, in Canada.

items.english: where are you from?; where did you grow up?
items.use: Asks where someone was born and raised; between Japanese people it usually means which prefecture.
items.politeJa: ご出身はどちらですか？

example.romaji: shusshin doko? watashi wa oosaka.
example.ja: 出身どこ？私は大阪。
example.english: Where are you from? I'm from Osaka.

examplePolite.romaji: goshusshin wa dochira desu ka? watashi wa oosaka desu.
examplePolite.ja: ご出身はどちらですか？私は大阪です。
examplePolite.english: Where are you from? I'm from Osaka.

items.notes: Doko kara kita no? is the vaguer 'which country' version.

items.use: Casual; mostly asked between Japanese people who've moved to a city for work or study.

example.romaji: jimoto doko? natsu ni kaeru no?
example.ja: 地元どこ？夏に帰るの？
example.english: Where's home for you? Going back for the summer?

examplePolite.romaji: jimoto wa dochira desu ka? natsu ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 地元はどちらですか？夏に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Where's your hometown? Are you going back for the summer?

items.notes: Jimoto also means your local area: jimoto no tomodachi (friends from back home).

items.use: Says you've lived in one place your whole life; the place comes at the end.

example.romaji: umare mo sodachi mo oosaka da yo.
example.ja: 生まれも育ちも大阪だよ。
example.english: I was born and raised in Osaka.

examplePolite.romaji: umare mo sodachi mo oosaka desu.
examplePolite.ja: 生まれも育ちも大阪です。
examplePolite.english: I was born and raised in Osaka.

blocks.label: What you do for work
blocks.rationale: Ask about someone's job and describe your own.
blocks.interference: de hataraiteru takes de for the workplace, while sunderu takes ni.

items.english: what kind of work is it?; what do you do?
items.use: Follow-up when someone mentions their job or company; answer with a role or field.

example.romaji: kaishain na n da. donna shigoto?
example.ja: 会社員なんだ。どんな仕事？
example.english: Oh, you work for a company. What kind of work?

examplePolite.romaji: kaishain na n desu ne. donna oshigoto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 会社員なんですね。どんなお仕事ですか？
examplePolite.english: Oh, you work for a company. What kind of work do you do?

items.notes: Oshigoto adds polite o- when it's someone else's job.

items.english: I work at ...; I work in ...
items.use: The basic answer to where you work; put the place or company before de.

example.romaji: ekimae no kafe de hataraiteru yo.
example.ja: 駅前のカフェで働いてるよ。
example.english: I work at the café by the station.

examplePolite.romaji: ekimae no kafe de hataraite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅前のカフェで働いています。
examplePolite.english: I work at the café by the station.

items.notes: Hataraku takes de for the place, but sumu takes ni.

items.polite: dochira de hataraite iru n desu ka?
items.use: Asks for the company or place; people often answer with the industry instead of a company name.
items.kana: どこではたらいてるの？
items.politeJa: どちらで働いているんですか？

example.romaji: ima doko de hataraiteru no? mada ginkou?
example.ja: 今どこで働いてるの？まだ銀行？
example.english: Where are you working now? Still at the bank?

examplePolite.romaji: ima dochira de hataraite iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今どちらで働いているんですか？
examplePolite.english: Where are you working now?

items.notes: Shigoto nani shiteru no? (what do you do?) is the more common opener.

items.polite: ... kankei no shigoto o shite imasu
items.english: I work in ...; I do something to do with ...
items.use: A handy vague answer when you don't want to explain your job; put the field first (ryokou kankei, kinyuu kankei).
items.kana: 〜かんけいのしごとをしてる

example.romaji: ryokou kankei no shigoto o shiteru yo.
example.ja: 旅行関係の仕事をしてるよ。
example.english: I work in travel.

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou kankei no shigoto o shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 旅行関係の仕事をしています。
examplePolite.english: I work in travel.

items.notes: Casual speech often drops the o: ... kankei no shigoto shiteru.

items.english: I work for a company; I'm an office worker
items.use: The everyday vague answer about your job; expect donna shigoto? next.

example.romaji: futsuu no kaishain da yo. jimu no shigoto.
example.ja: 普通の会社員だよ。事務の仕事。
example.english: Just an ordinary office worker. Admin work.

examplePolite.romaji: futsuu no kaishain desu. jimu no shigoto desu.
examplePolite.ja: 普通の会社員です。事務の仕事です。
examplePolite.english: I'm just an ordinary office worker. I do admin work.

items.notes: Sarariiman is a near-synonym, used for men.

blocks.label: Where you live now
blocks.rationale: Ask where someone lives and say how and where you live.
blocks.interference: jikka is your parents' home, not just any house you live in.

items.polite: ima dochira ni osumai desu ka?
items.use: Asked once you've said where you're from, to get the current city or neighbourhood.
items.kana: いまどこにすんでるの？
items.politeJa: 今どちらにお住まいですか？

example.romaji: ima doko ni sunderu no? kono hen?
example.ja: 今どこに住んでるの？この辺？
example.english: Where do you live now? Around here?

examplePolite.romaji: ima dochira ni osumai desu ka? kono hen desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今どちらにお住まいですか？この辺ですか？
examplePolite.english: Where do you live now? Around here?

items.notes: Osumai is the set polite word for someone's home; doko ni sunde imasu ka? is fine too.

items.use: Answer to doko ni sunderu no?; name the city, area or nearest station.

example.romaji: ima wa shibuya no chikaku ni sunderu yo.
example.ja: 今は渋谷の近くに住んでるよ。
example.english: I live near Shibuya now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa shibuya no chikaku ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今は渋谷の近くに住んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I live near Shibuya now.

items.notes: Always the -te iru form (sunderu) for where you live now, and ni, not de.

items.english: do you live on your own?; living alone?
items.use: A common follow-up to where you live; answer un, hitorigurashi, or say who you live with.

example.romaji: e, hitorigurashi? ryouri toka suru no?
example.ja: え、一人暮らし？料理とかするの？
example.english: Oh, you live on your own? Do you cook and stuff?

examplePolite.romaji: hitorigurashi desu ka? ryouri toka shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一人暮らしですか？料理とかしますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you live on your own? Do you cook?

items.notes: Hitorigurashi shiteru = I live alone.

items.english: I live with my parents; I live at home
items.use: Answer to hitorigurashi? or doko ni sunderu no?; living with your parents as a young adult is common in Japan.

example.romaji: mada jikka ni sunderu n da. raku da yo.
example.ja: まだ実家に住んでるんだ。楽だよ。
example.english: I still live with my parents. It's easy.

examplePolite.romaji: mada jikka ni sunde iru n desu. raku desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: まだ実家に住んでいるんです。楽ですよ。
examplePolite.english: I still live with my parents. It's easy.

items.notes: Jikka is your parents' home; jikka ni kaeru means going home to visit them.

items.polite: tsuukin wa dono gurai desu ka?
items.use: Everyday small talk in Japanese cities, where commutes are long; answer with a time (densha de ichijikan).
items.politeJa: 通勤はどのぐらいですか？

example.romaji: tsuukin dono gurai? kekkou tooi?
example.ja: 通勤どのぐらい？結構遠い？
example.english: How long's your commute? Pretty far?

examplePolite.romaji: tsuukin wa dono gurai desu ka? kekkou tooi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 通勤はどのぐらいですか？結構遠いですか？
examplePolite.english: How long is your commute? Is it quite far?

items.notes: Add kakaru for 'how long does it take': dono gurai kakaru?

blocks.label: Why you came to Japan
blocks.rationale: Answer and ask the 'why Japan' question and what sparked it.
blocks.interference: nande asks for the reason; kikkake asks what set it off.

items.polite: doushite nihon ni kita n desu ka?
items.english: what made you come to Japan?; why did you come to Japan?
items.use: Asked of almost every foreigner; a short reason is enough (shigoto de kita, anime ga suki de).
items.kana: なんでにほんにきたの？
items.politeJa: どうして日本に来たんですか？

example.romaji: nande nihon ni kita no? anime toka?
example.ja: なんで日本に来たの？アニメとか？
example.english: What made you come to Japan? Anime or something?

examplePolite.romaji: doushite nihon ni kita n desu ka? anime toka desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どうして日本に来たんですか？アニメとかですか？
examplePolite.english: Why did you come to Japan? Was it anime or something?

items.notes: Nande and doushite both mean why; nande is more casual.

items.english: what got you started?; how did that come about?
items.use: Follow-up after someone mentions a hobby, a move or how they met someone; answer with ... ga kikkake de.

example.romaji: e, sonna ni nagaku yatteru n da. kikkake wa?
example.ja: え、そんなに長くやってるんだ。きっかけは？
example.english: Wow, you've been doing it that long? What got you into it?

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni nagaku yatte iru n desu ne. kikkake wa nan desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そんなに長くやっているんですね。きっかけは何ですか？
examplePolite.english: You've been doing it that long? What got you started?

items.notes: Kikkake is the trigger or starting point; riyuu is the reason.

items.use: De gives the reason: ryuugaku de kita (came to study), ryokou de kita (came as a tourist).

example.romaji: kyonen shigoto de kita n da. sannen no yotei.
example.ja: 去年仕事で来たんだ。3年の予定。
example.english: I came over for work last year. It's meant to be for three years.

examplePolite.romaji: kyonen shigoto de kimashita. sannen no yotei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 去年仕事で来ました。3年の予定です。
examplePolite.english: I came for work last year. I'm planning to stay three years.

items.notes: For a short work trip: shutchou de kita (here on business).

items.romaji: zutto nihon ni kitakatta n da
items.polite: zutto nihon ni kitakatta n desu
items.english: I'd always wanted to come to Japan
items.use: An easy, warm answer to why you came; add the reason after if you like.
items.ja: ずっと日本に来たかったんだ
items.kana: ずっとにほんにきたかったんだ
items.politeJa: ずっと日本に来たかったんです

example.romaji: kodomo no koro kara, zutto nihon ni kitakatta n da.
example.ja: 子供の頃から、ずっと日本に来たかったんだ。
example.english: I'd wanted to come to Japan ever since I was a kid.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no koro kara, zutto nihon ni kitakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 子供の頃から、ずっと日本に来たかったんです。
examplePolite.english: I'd wanted to come to Japan since I was a child.

items.notes: Zutto = all along; -takatta is the past of -tai (wanted to).

items.english: it started with ...; ... is what got me into it
items.use: Answer to kikkake wa?; name the trigger, then what followed.

example.romaji: anime ga kikkake de, nihongo o hajimeta n da.
example.ja: アニメがきっかけで、日本語を始めたんだ。
example.english: Anime is what got me into Japanese.

examplePolite.romaji: anime ga kikkake de, nihongo o hajimeta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: アニメがきっかけで、日本語を始めたんです。
examplePolite.english: Anime is what got me started with Japanese.

items.notes: On its own, ... ga kikkake da yo answers the question too.

blocks.label: How long you're here
blocks.rationale: Say how long you've been in Japan and how long you'll stay.
blocks.interference: dono gurai looks back (how long so far); itsu made looks ahead (until when).

items.polite: nihon ni kite dono gurai desu ka?
items.english: how long have you been in Japan?
items.use: One of the first questions you'll get; answer with a length of time plus ni naru (ninen ni naru).
items.ja: 日本に来てどのぐらい？
items.kana: にほんにきてどのぐらい？
items.politeJa: 日本に来てどのぐらいですか？

example.romaji: nihon ni kite dono gurai? nihongo umai ne.
example.ja: 日本に来てどのぐらい？日本語うまいね。
example.english: How long have you been in Japan? Your Japanese is good.

examplePolite.romaji: nihon ni kite dono gurai desu ka? nihongo ga ojouzu desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 日本に来てどのぐらいですか？日本語がお上手ですね。
examplePolite.english: How long have you been in Japan? Your Japanese is very good.

items.notes: Also said dono kurai; same thing.

items.use: Answer to how long you've lived somewhere or done something; the number goes before -nen (sannen gurai ni naru).

example.romaji: toukyou ni kite, mou gonen gurai ni naru kana.
example.ja: 東京に来て、もう5年ぐらいになるかな。
example.english: It's been about five years since I came to Tokyo, I think.

examplePolite.romaji: toukyou ni kite, mou gonen gurai ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 東京に来て、もう5年ぐらいになります。
examplePolite.english: It's been about five years since I came to Tokyo.

items.notes: Swap in other units: sankagetsu (three months), hantoshi (half a year).

items.english: I've only just got here; I just arrived
items.use: Answer to how long you've been in Japan, or for just arriving anywhere; bakkari is the casual form of bakari.

example.romaji: nihon ni wa sengetsu kita bakkari na n da.
example.ja: 日本には先月来たばっかりなんだ。
example.english: I only got to Japan last month.

examplePolite.romaji: nihon ni wa sengetsu kita bakari na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 日本には先月来たばかりなんです。
examplePolite.english: I only arrived in Japan last month.

items.notes: Works after any past verb: tabeta bakkari (I just ate).

items.polite: itsu made irassharu n desu ka?
items.english: how long are you here for?; until when are you staying?
items.use: Asked of visitors and newcomers; answer with a time plus made (rainen made), or mada kimetenai.
items.politeJa: いつまでいらっしゃるんですか？

example.romaji: nihon ni wa itsu made iru no? rainen made?
example.ja: 日本にはいつまでいるの？来年まで？
example.english: How long are you in Japan for? Till next year?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon ni wa itsu made irassharu n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本にはいつまでいらっしゃるんですか？
examplePolite.english: How long will you be in Japan?

items.notes: Irassharu is the respectful form of iru.

items.use: A safe answer to questions about plans: how long you're staying, what's next, what to order.

example.romaji: itsu kaeru ka wa mada kimetenai.
example.ja: いつ帰るかはまだ決めてない。
example.english: I haven't decided when I'm going back yet.

examplePolite.romaji: itsu kaeru ka wa mada kimete imasen.
examplePolite.ja: いつ帰るかはまだ決めていません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't decided when I'm going back yet.

items.notes: Mada + -te nai is 'not yet'; the past kimenakatta means 'I didn't decide'.

blocks.label: Speaking in Japanese
blocks.rationale: Say you're learning and steer the chat into Japanese.
blocks.interference: hanaseru? (can you speak) vs hanasou (let's speak).

items.polite: nihongo o benkyou shite iru n desu
items.use: Tells people why your Japanese is limited; the n da makes it an explanation that invites patience.
items.ja: 日本語勉強してるんだ
items.kana: にほんごべんきょうしてるんだ
items.politeJa: 日本語を勉強しているんです

example.romaji: ima, nihongo benkyou shiteru n da. yukkuri hanashite kureru?
example.ja: 今、日本語勉強してるんだ。ゆっくり話してくれる？
example.english: I'm learning Japanese at the moment. Could you speak slowly?

examplePolite.romaji: ima, nihongo o benkyou shite iru n desu. yukkuri hanashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今、日本語を勉強しているんです。ゆっくり話してください。
examplePolite.english: I'm learning Japanese at the moment. Please speak slowly.

items.use: Ask for this when someone switches to English to help you; it's how you keep getting practice.
items.politeJa: 日本語で話しましょう

example.romaji: renshuu shitai kara, nihongo de hanasou yo.
example.ja: 練習したいから、日本語で話そうよ。
example.english: I want the practice, so let's talk in Japanese.

examplePolite.romaji: renshuu shitai node, nihongo de hanashimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 練習したいので、日本語で話しましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'd like the practice, so let's speak Japanese.

items.notes: Softer: nihongo de hanashite mo ii? (is it OK if we speak Japanese?).

items.english: do you speak English?; can you speak English?
items.use: You'll hear it from people keen to switch to English; to keep practising, answer with nihongo de hanasou.

example.romaji: gomen, eigo hanaseru? nihongo mada heta de.
example.ja: ごめん、英語話せる？日本語まだ下手で。
example.english: Sorry, do you speak English? My Japanese is still bad.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, eigo hanasemasu ka? nihongo ga mada heta de.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、英語話せますか？日本語がまだ下手で。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, do you speak English? My Japanese is still bad.

items.notes: Hanaseru is the 'can' form of hanasu.

blocks.label: Compliments on your Japanese
blocks.rationale: Handle the inevitable 'your Japanese is good' and the questions that follow.
blocks.interference: dokugaku (self-taught) sounds close to daigaku (university).

items.use: Said to learners, often after only a few words; answer iie, mada mada desu (no, I've a long way to go).
items.kana: にほんごじょうずですね

example.romaji: e, nihongo jouzu desu ne! doko de benkyou shita n desu ka?
example.ja: え、日本語上手ですね！どこで勉強したんですか？
example.english: Oh, your Japanese is good! Where did you learn?

items.notes: Usually politeness, not a real assessment. Friends say nihongo umai ne.

items.english: I've still got a long way to go
items.use: Modest reply to praise, especially of your Japanese; start with iie.

example.romaji: iie, nihongo wa mada mada desu.
example.ja: いいえ、日本語はまだまだです。
example.english: Oh no, my Japanese has a long way to go.

items.notes: Casual: mada mada da yo.

items.romaji: nihongo doko de benkyou shita no?
items.polite: nihongo wa doko de benkyou shita n desu ka?
items.english: where did you learn your Japanese?
items.use: Said to you by Japanese people, usually as a compliment; answer with a place, or dokugaku (self-taught).
items.ja: 日本語どこで勉強したの？
items.kana: にほんごどこでべんきょうしたの？
items.politeJa: 日本語はどこで勉強したんですか？

example.romaji: sugoi ne! nihongo doko de benkyou shita no?
example.ja: すごいね！日本語どこで勉強したの？
example.english: Wow! Where did you learn your Japanese?

examplePolite.romaji: sugoi desu ne! nihongo wa doko de benkyou shita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すごいですね！日本語はどこで勉強したんですか？
examplePolite.english: That's impressive! Where did you learn your Japanese?

items.use: Answer to where or how you learned something, Japanese or a hobby like guitar.

example.romaji: gakkou toka wa kayotte nai. zenbu dokugaku da yo.
example.ja: 学校とかは通ってない。全部独学だよ。
example.english: I don't go to classes or anything. I've taught myself all of it.

examplePolite.romaji: gakkou ni wa kayotte imasen. zenbu dokugaku desu.
examplePolite.ja: 学校には通っていません。全部独学です。
examplePolite.english: I don't take classes. I've taught myself everything.

items.notes: Dokugaku de benkyou shita = I studied it on my own.

blocks.label: Meeting a friend's friend
blocks.rationale: Greet someone new through a mutual friend and swap contacts.
blocks.interference: rain here is the LINE app, not the weather.

items.english: so glad to meet you; great to see you
items.use: Said warmly on meeting someone you've been looking forward to meeting, or on seeing someone again.
items.politeJa: お会いできてうれしいです

example.romaji: yatto aete ureshii! zutto hanashi kiiteta yo.
example.ja: やっと会えてうれしい！ずっと話聞いてたよ。
example.english: So glad to finally meet you! I've heard so much about you.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto oai dekite ureshii desu.
examplePolite.ja: やっとお会いできてうれしいです。
examplePolite.english: I'm so glad to finally meet you.

items.notes: For a plain first meeting, hajimemashite comes first; aete ureshii adds warmth.

items.use: Explains how you know the host or the person who brought you, at a party or gathering.

example.romaji: yuki no tomodachi na n da. daigaku no toki no.
example.ja: ユキの友達なんだ。大学の時の。
example.english: I'm a friend of Yuki's. From uni.

examplePolite.romaji: yuki no tomodachi desu. daigaku no toki no.
examplePolite.ja: ユキの友達です。大学の時の。
examplePolite.english: I'm a friend of Yuki's, from university.

items.notes: Shiriai is 'an acquaintance', for someone you're not close to.

items.use: Said to someone new you want to keep in touch with; you then scan each other's QR code.
items.kana: ラインこうかんしよう

example.romaji: kyou tanoshikatta! rain koukan shiyou yo.
example.ja: 今日楽しかった！LINE交換しようよ。
example.english: Today was fun! Let's swap LINE.

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, rain koukan shimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、LINE交換しませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you like, shall we exchange LINE contacts?

items.notes: Renrakusaki koukan is the general version: swapping contact details.

items.use: The usual way to keep in touch after hitting it off; rain yatteru? asks the same about LINE.
items.politeJa: インスタやっていますか？

example.romaji: insuta yatteru? foroo shite ii?
example.ja: インスタやってる？フォローしていい？
example.english: Are you on Instagram? Can I follow you?

examplePolite.romaji: insuta yatte imasu ka? foroo shite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: インスタやっていますか？フォローしてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Are you on Instagram? Is it OK if I follow you?

items.notes: Yaru here means using an app or account.

items.english: I've heard about you from ...; ... has told me about you
items.use: Said on meeting a friend's friend, partner or new colleague, to show you were expecting them; follow with yoroshiku.

example.romaji: aa, kenta kara hanashi wa kiiteru yo. yoroshiku.
example.ja: ああ、健太から話は聞いてるよ。よろしく。
example.english: Oh, Kenta's told me about you. Nice to meet you.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou kara ohanashi wa kiite imasu. yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 部長からお話は聞いています。よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: My manager's told me about you. Nice to meet you.

items.notes: At work you'll also hear ohanashi wa ukagatte imasu, the humble version.

blocks.label: Describing your hometown
blocks.rationale: Pin down where their hometown is and say what yours is like.
blocks.interference: dono hen (whereabouts) vs donna (what kind of).

items.english: what's it like there?; what kind of place is it?
items.use: Follow-up after someone names their hometown or a place they've been.

example.romaji: sendai shusshin na n da. donna tokoro?
example.ja: 仙台出身なんだ。どんなところ？
example.english: You're from Sendai? What's it like there?

examplePolite.romaji: sendai no goshusshin na n desu ne. donna tokoro desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 仙台のご出身なんですね。どんなところですか？
examplePolite.english: So you're from Sendai. What's it like there?

items.notes: Donna + noun asks 'what kind of': donna hito? (what's he like?).

items.use: The follow-up after someone names a country or city; answer with a nearby big city or ... no chikaku (near ...).

example.romaji: igirisu no dono hen? rondon?
example.ja: イギリスのどの辺？ロンドン？
example.english: Whereabouts in England? London?

examplePolite.romaji: igirisu no dono hen desu ka? rondon desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: イギリスのどの辺ですか？ロンドンですか？
examplePolite.english: Whereabouts in England? London?

items.notes: Hen also works for vague places on its own: kono hen (around here).

items.english: there's not much there; it's the middle of nowhere
items.use: The modest stock answer about your hometown, even when it's nice; the other person will often push back.
items.kana: なにもないところだよ
items.politeJa: 何もないところですよ

example.romaji: inaka da kara, nanimo nai tokoro da yo.
example.ja: 田舎だから、何もないところだよ。
example.english: It's the countryside, so there's not much there.

examplePolite.romaji: inaka na node, nanimo nai tokoro desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 田舎なので、何もないところですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's out in the countryside, so there isn't much there.

items.notes: Nanimo + negative = nothing; inaka is the countryside, or 'back home'.

items.use: Contrasts how things were with how they are now, often followed by ima wa.

example.romaji: motomoto wa kyouto da kedo, ima wa toukyou ni sunderu.
example.ja: もともとは京都だけど、今は東京に住んでる。
example.english: I'm originally from Kyoto, but I live in Tokyo now.

examplePolite.romaji: motomoto wa kyouto desu kedo, ima wa toukyou ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: もともとは京都ですけど、今は東京に住んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I'm originally from Kyoto, but now I live in Tokyo.

items.notes: Also 'to begin with': motomoto suki ja nakatta (I never liked it in the first place).

blocks.label: Life in Japan
blocks.rationale: Answer how you're finding Japan and what you like about it.
blocks.interference: None.

items.polite: nihon no seikatsu wa dou desu ka?
items.english: how are you finding life in Japan?; how's life in Japan?
items.use: Asked once you've been here a while; answer with tanoshii, daibu nareta, or one thing you like or find hard.
items.kana: にほんのせいかつはどう？
items.politeJa: 日本の生活はどうですか？

example.romaji: nihon no seikatsu wa dou? mou nareta?
example.ja: 日本の生活はどう？もう慣れた？
example.english: How's life in Japan? Settled in yet?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon no seikatsu wa dou desu ka? mou naremashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本の生活はどうですか？もう慣れましたか？
examplePolite.english: How are you finding life in Japan? Have you settled in?

items.notes: X wa dou? works for anything: shigoto wa dou? (how's work?).

items.polite: nihon no doko ga suki desu ka?
items.english: what do you like about Japan?
items.use: Doko here means 'what part', not just places; answer with a thing plus ga suki (tabemono ga suki).
items.politeJa: 日本のどこが好きですか？

example.romaji: nihon no doko ga suki? yappari tabemono?
example.ja: 日本のどこが好き？やっぱり食べ物？
example.english: What do you like about Japan? The food, I bet?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon no doko ga suki desu ka? yappari tabemono desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本のどこが好きですか？やっぱり食べ物ですか？
examplePolite.english: What do you like about Japan? The food, I suppose?

items.notes: Works for people too: kare no doko ga suki? (what do you like about him?).

items.english: I've pretty much settled in; I'm much more used to it now
items.use: Answer to mou nareta? or how's life here; add a 'but' to keep the conversation going.

example.romaji: daibu nareta kedo, man'in densha wa mada muri.
example.ja: だいぶ慣れたけど、満員電車はまだ無理。
example.english: I've mostly settled in, but packed trains are still too much.

examplePolite.romaji: daibu naremashita kedo, man'in densha wa mada muri desu.
examplePolite.ja: だいぶ慣れましたけど、満員電車はまだ無理です。
examplePolite.english: I've mostly got used to things, but I still can't handle packed trains.

items.notes: Nareru = get used to; the thing takes ni: shigoto ni nareta.

blocks.label: Brothers sisters and family
blocks.rationale: Ask about siblings and family size and describe your own.
blocks.interference: ani is your own older brother; theirs is oniisan.

items.english: do you have any brothers or sisters?
items.use: Kyoudai covers sisters too; answer with who and how many (ani ga hitori), or hitorikko.

example.romaji: kyoudai iru? nanka suekko tte kanji suru.
example.ja: 兄弟いる？なんか末っ子って感じする。
example.english: Got any brothers or sisters? You seem like the youngest.

examplePolite.romaji: gokyoudai wa imasu ka? suekko tte kanji ga shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ご兄弟はいますか？末っ子って感じがしますね。
examplePolite.english: Do you have any brothers or sisters? You seem like the youngest.

items.notes: Go- makes it polite for someone else's family; your own is just kyoudai.

items.english: how many are there in your family?
items.use: Counts everyone in the family you grew up in, you included; answer with a number + -nin kazoku.

example.romaji: nannin kazoku? kyoudai ooi?
example.ja: 何人家族？兄弟多い？
example.english: How many in your family? Lots of brothers and sisters?

examplePolite.romaji: nannin kazoku desu ka? gokyoudai wa ooi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何人家族ですか？ご兄弟は多いですか？
examplePolite.english: How many are there in your family? Do you have many siblings?

items.use: Answer to kyoudai iru?; na n da gives it an explaining tone.

example.romaji: kyoudai inai. hitorikko na n da.
example.ja: 兄弟いない。一人っ子なんだ。
example.english: No brothers or sisters. I'm an only child.

examplePolite.romaji: kyoudai wa imasen. hitorikko na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 兄弟はいません。一人っ子なんです。
examplePolite.english: I don't have any brothers or sisters. I'm an only child.

items.use: The pattern for your siblings: family word + ga + number of people + iru (imouto ga futari iru).

example.romaji: ani ga hitori iru yo. ima amerika ni sunderu.
example.ja: 兄が一人いるよ。今アメリカに住んでる。
example.english: I've got one older brother. He lives in America now.

examplePolite.romaji: ani ga hitori imasu. ima amerika ni sunde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 兄が一人います。今アメリカに住んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I have one older brother. He lives in America now.

items.notes: Your own: ani, ane, otouto, imouto; someone else's: oniisan, oneesan.

items.english: there are four of us in my family
items.use: Answer to nannin kazoku?; count yourself in, then list who.

example.romaji: yonin kazoku da yo. ryoushin to ani to watashi.
example.ja: 4人家族だよ。両親と兄と私。
example.english: There are four of us. My parents, my brother and me.

examplePolite.romaji: yonin kazoku desu. ryoushin to ani to watashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 4人家族です。両親と兄と私です。
examplePolite.english: There are four of us: my parents, my older brother and me.

items.notes: Counting people: hitori, futari, sannin, yonin (not yon-nin or shinin).

blocks.label: Hobbies and what you like
blocks.rationale: Ask about hobbies and say what you're into.
blocks.interference: no ga suki follows a verb (taberu no ga suki); a noun takes ga suki directly.

items.english: what are your hobbies?; what do you do for fun?
items.use: A standard getting-to-know-you question; answer with ... ga shumi or ... ga suki.

example.romaji: shumi wa? nanka hamatteru mono aru?
example.ja: 趣味は？なんかハマってるものある？
example.english: What are your hobbies? Anything you're into?

examplePolite.romaji: goshumi wa nan desu ka? nanika suki na koto wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ご趣味は何ですか？何か好きなことはありますか？
examplePolite.english: What are your hobbies? Is there anything you enjoy?

items.notes: Shumi wa? can sound like an interview question, so friends often ask yasumi no hi nani shiteru? instead.

items.use: Put the hobby first; for an activity use a verb plus koto (ryouri suru koto ga shumi).

example.romaji: shashin ga shumi na n da. kamera mo motteru yo.
example.ja: 写真が趣味なんだ。カメラも持ってるよ。
example.english: Photography's my hobby. I've got a proper camera too.

examplePolite.romaji: shumi wa shashin desu. kamera mo motte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 趣味は写真です。カメラも持っています。
examplePolite.english: My hobby is photography. I have a camera too.

items.use: The casual way to ask about a food, band or activity; tte marks the topic, like wa.

example.romaji: nattou tte suki? nihonjin demo kirai na hito ooi yo.
example.ja: 納豆って好き？日本人でも嫌いな人多いよ。
example.english: Do you like natto? Lots of Japanese people hate it too.

examplePolite.romaji: nattou wa suki desu ka? nihonjin demo kirai na hito ga ooi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 納豆は好きですか？日本人でも嫌いな人が多いですよ。
examplePolite.english: Do you like natto? Plenty of Japanese people don't.

items.notes: Answer suki, daisuki, or amari suki ja nai (not really).

items.use: Turns a verb into a like: plain verb + no ga suki (oyogu no ga suki).

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa eiga miru no ga suki.
example.ja: 休みの日は映画見るのが好き。
example.english: On days off I like watching films.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi no hi wa eiga o miru no ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 休みの日は映画を見るのが好きです。
examplePolite.english: On my days off I like watching films.

items.notes: With a noun, drop the no (neko ga suki); suki takes ga, not o.

items.romaji: shumi tte iu hodo ja nai kedo
items.polite: shumi to iu hodo ja nai n desu kedo
items.english: it's not really a hobby, but ...
items.use: A modest lead-in before naming something you do; Japanese speakers often play their hobbies down like this.
items.ja: 趣味っていうほどじゃないけど
items.kana: しゅみっていうほどじゃないけど
items.politeJa: 趣味というほどじゃないんですけど

example.romaji: shumi tte iu hodo ja nai kedo, tama ni e o kaku.
example.ja: 趣味っていうほどじゃないけど、たまに絵を描く。
example.english: It's not really a hobby, but I draw sometimes.

examplePolite.romaji: shumi to iu hodo ja nai n desu kedo, tama ni e o kakimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 趣味というほどじゃないんですけど、たまに絵を描きます。
examplePolite.english: It's not really a hobby, but I draw now and then.

items.notes: ... tte iu hodo ja nai works for anything: 'not enough to call it ...'.

blocks.label: Weekends and free time
blocks.rationale: Say what you usually do when you're off.
blocks.interference: daitai (usually) vs zettai (definitely).

items.use: Answers shumi wa? or yasumi no hi nani shiteru?; finish with what you do, often in the -te iru form.
items.kana: しゅうまつはだいたい〜

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa daitai ie de hiru made neteru.
example.ja: 週末はだいたい家で昼まで寝てる。
example.english: On weekends I mostly sleep in till noon.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa daitai jimu ni itte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 週末はだいたいジムに行っています。
examplePolite.english: On weekends I usually go to the gym.

items.notes: Daitai means 'mostly, roughly'; with numbers it's 'about': daitai sanzen en (about 3,000 yen).

items.use: Lead-in for what you do in your free time; finish with a plain or -masu verb.

example.romaji: jikan ga aru toki wa, yoku eiga miru yo.
example.ja: 時間がある時は、よく映画見るよ。
example.english: When I've got time, I watch a lot of films.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga aru toki wa, yoku eiga o mimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 時間がある時は、よく映画を見ます。
examplePolite.english: When I have time, I often watch films.

items.notes: Hima na toki wa ... says the same with hima (free).

items.english: I just laze around at home
items.use: A self-mocking answer to what you do on days off; everyone says it and nobody judges.
items.kana: いえでごろごろしてる
items.politeJa: 家でゴロゴロしています

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa daitai ie de gorogoro shiteru.
example.ja: 休みの日はだいたい家でゴロゴロしてる。
example.english: On days off I mostly just laze around at home.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi no hi wa daitai ie de gorogoro shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 休みの日はだいたい家でゴロゴロしています。
examplePolite.english: On my days off I mostly just relax at home.

items.notes: Uchi de is just as common as ie de.

blocks.label: Do you do this
blocks.rationale: Ask about everyday pastimes with a simple yes-no question.
blocks.interference: jimu ni kayotteru (go regularly) vs jimu ni itta (went once).

items.english: do you watch films much?; do you watch movies and stuff?
items.use: Toka softens it to 'films or that kind of thing', keeping the question light.

example.romaji: eiga toka miru? saikin nanka yokatta?
example.ja: 映画とか見る？最近なんかよかった？
example.english: Do you watch films? Seen anything good lately?

examplePolite.romaji: eiga toka mimasu ka? saikin yokatta no wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 映画とか見ますか？最近よかったのはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you watch films? Have you seen anything good lately?

items.notes: Eiga o miru is watching at home or anywhere; eiga ni iku is going to the cinema.

items.use: A common follow-up to living alone; answer suru yo, tama ni (sometimes) or zenzen shinai.

example.romaji: hitorigurashi da yo ne? ryouri suru?
example.ja: 一人暮らしだよね？料理する？
example.english: You live on your own, right? Do you cook?

examplePolite.romaji: hitorigurashi desu yo ne? ryouri shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一人暮らしですよね？料理しますか？
examplePolite.english: You live on your own, don't you? Do you cook?

items.notes: Jisui suru is cooking for yourself instead of eating out.

items.polite: nanika supootsu o yatte imasu ka?
items.use: Yaru covers playing any sport; answer with the sport + yatteru (sakkaa yatteru).
items.ja: 何かスポーツやってる？
items.kana: なにかスポーツやってる？
items.politeJa: 何かスポーツをやっていますか？

example.romaji: nanika supootsu yatteru? se takai ne.
example.ja: 何かスポーツやってる？背高いね。
example.english: Do you play any sport? You're tall.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika supootsu o yatte imasu ka? se ga takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かスポーツをやっていますか？背が高いですね。
examplePolite.english: Do you play any sport? You're very tall.

items.notes: Often asked about school days too: bukatsu wa nani yatteta? (what club were you in?).

items.use: Geemu means video games by default; board games are boodo geemu.

example.romaji: geemu suru? kondo issho ni yarou yo.
example.ja: ゲームする？今度一緒にやろうよ。
example.english: Do you play games? Let's play together sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: geemu shimasu ka? kondo issho ni yarimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: ゲームしますか？今度一緒にやりませんか？
examplePolite.english: Do you play video games? Want to play together sometime?

items.notes: Yaru works too: geemu yaru?

items.use: Kayou means going somewhere regularly; use it for gyms, schools and classes.

example.romaji: shuu ni sankai, jimu ni kayotteru yo.
example.ja: 週に3回、ジムに通ってるよ。
example.english: I go to the gym three times a week.

examplePolite.romaji: shuu ni sankai, jimu ni kayotte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 週に3回、ジムに通っています。
examplePolite.english: I go to the gym three times a week.

items.notes: Iku is a single trip; kayou is a habit (eikaiwa ni kayou).

blocks.label: Food you like
blocks.rationale: Trade favourite foods and say how adventurous you are.
blocks.interference: tabeta koto aru? (ever eaten it) vs tabeta? (did you eat).

items.polite: suki na tabemono wa nan desu ka?
items.use: A small-talk staple; answer with the food plus ka na (raamen ka na) to sound relaxed.
items.politeJa: 好きな食べ物は何ですか？

example.romaji: suki na tabemono wa? nihon ryouri da to?
example.ja: 好きな食べ物は？日本料理だと？
example.english: What's your favourite food? Out of Japanese food?

examplePolite.romaji: suki na tabemono wa nan desu ka? nihon ryouri de wa?
examplePolite.ja: 好きな食べ物は何ですか？日本料理では？
examplePolite.english: What's your favourite food? Among Japanese dishes?

items.notes: Suki na + noun works for any favourite: suki na eiga wa? (favourite film?).

items.english: have you ever tried it?; have you ever eaten ...?
items.use: Asked when offering or talking about a food; answer aru, or mada nai (not yet).
items.politeJa: 食べたことありますか？

example.romaji: monjayaki tabeta koto aru? oishii yo.
example.ja: もんじゃ焼き食べたことある？おいしいよ。
example.english: Have you ever had monjayaki? It's good.

examplePolite.romaji: monjayaki, tabeta koto arimasu ka? oishii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: もんじゃ焼き、食べたことありますか？おいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Have you ever had monjayaki? It's delicious.

items.notes: Past verb + koto aru = have ever done; works with any verb (itta koto aru).

items.english: I'll eat anything; I'm not fussy
items.use: Answer when asked what you'd like or whether you can eat something; add ... igai wa for the exception.

example.romaji: nandemo taberu yo. nattou igai wa.
example.ja: なんでも食べるよ。納豆以外は。
example.english: I'll eat anything. Except natto.

examplePolite.romaji: nandemo tabemasu yo. nattou igai wa.
examplePolite.ja: なんでも食べますよ。納豆以外は。
examplePolite.english: I eat anything. Except natto.

items.notes: Nandemo = anything at all; nanimo with a negative means nothing.

items.english: anything you don't eat?; are you picky?
items.use: A host or friend asks before cooking or ordering; answer tokuni nai (nothing really) or name the food.
items.politeJa: 好き嫌いはありますか

example.romaji: kyou wa uchi de tsukuru kedo, suki kirai aru?
example.ja: 今日はうちで作るけど、好き嫌いある？
example.english: I'm cooking tonight. Anything you don't eat?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika suki kirai wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か好き嫌いはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Is there anything you don't eat?

items.notes: For allergies say arerugii ga arimasu.

blocks.label: Places you've been
blocks.rationale: Ask where someone has travelled and say where you want to go.
blocks.interference: itta koto aru? (ever been) vs itta? (did you go).

items.english: have you been to ...?; have you ever been to ...?
items.use: Asks about experience, not one trip; answer aru, or mada nai (not yet).

example.romaji: okinawa itta koto aru? umi ga kirei da yo.
example.ja: 沖縄行ったことある？海がきれいだよ。
example.english: Have you ever been to Okinawa? The sea's beautiful.

examplePolite.romaji: okinawa ni itta koto arimasu ka? umi ga kirei desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 沖縄に行ったことありますか？海がきれいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Have you ever been to Okinawa? The sea is beautiful.

items.notes: Itta? alone asks about one trip; itta koto aru? asks 'ever'.

items.english: I haven't been there yet; I've never been
items.use: Answer to ... itta koto aru?; mada makes it sound like you'd like to go.
items.politeJa: まだ行ったことがありません

example.romaji: hokkaidou wa mada itta koto nai n da.
example.ja: 北海道はまだ行ったことないんだ。
example.english: I haven't been to Hokkaido yet.

examplePolite.romaji: hokkaidou wa mada itta koto ga arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 北海道はまだ行ったことがありません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't been to Hokkaido yet.

items.notes: Without mada, itta koto nai is a flat 'never been'.

items.english: I'd love to go someday; I want to go one day
items.use: Natural follow-up to mada itta koto nai, or when someone mentions a place they love.
items.politeJa: いつか行ってみたいです

example.romaji: kyuushuu, itsuka itte mitai na.
example.ja: 九州、いつか行ってみたいな。
example.english: I'd love to go to Kyushu someday.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuushuu ni wa itsuka itte mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 九州にはいつか行ってみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to go to Kyushu someday.

items.notes: -te mitai = want to try doing; itsuka = someday.

items.polite: nihon de wa doko ni ikimashita ka?
items.english: where have you been in Japan?
items.use: Asked of visitors and newcomers; answer with a few places joined by toka (kyouto toka nara toka).
items.politeJa: 日本ではどこに行きましたか？

example.romaji: nihon de doko itta? kyouto wa?
example.ja: 日本でどこ行った？京都は？
example.english: Where have you been in Japan? Kyoto?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon de wa doko ni ikimashita ka? kyouto wa ikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本ではどこに行きましたか？京都は行きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Where have you been in Japan? Have you been to Kyoto?

items.notes: Casual speech drops the ni: doko (ni) itta?

items.english: do you travel much?; do you travel a lot?
items.use: General small talk about travel; answer with how often (nen ni nikai gurai) or where you last went.

example.romaji: yoku ryokou suru? kaigai mo?
example.ja: よく旅行する？海外も？
example.english: Do you travel much? Abroad too?

examplePolite.romaji: yoku ryokou shimasu ka? kaigai ni mo ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: よく旅行しますか？海外にも行きますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you travel much? Do you go abroad too?

items.notes: Yoku here means 'often', not 'well'.

blocks.label: Shows and favourites
blocks.rationale: Swap what you've been watching and who you're a fan of.
blocks.interference: oshi is the person you're a fan of, not a crush.

items.polite: saikin nanika omoshiroi no mimashita ka?
items.use: An easy conversation starter about films, shows or videos; answer with a title and a quick verdict.
items.ja: 最近何か面白いの見た？
items.kana: さいきんなにかおもしろいのみた？
items.politeJa: 最近何か面白いの見ましたか？

example.romaji: nee, saikin nanika omoshiroi no mita? osusume aru?
example.ja: ねえ、最近何か面白いの見た？おすすめある？
example.english: Hey, seen anything good lately? Any recommendations?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin nanika omoshiroi no mimashita ka? osusume wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近何か面白いの見ましたか？おすすめはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Seen anything good lately? Any recommendations?

items.notes: Omoshiroi covers both 'funny' and 'interesting'; the no stands in for 'thing'.

items.polite: ima nanika dorama mite imasu ka?
items.english: are you watching any shows at the moment?
items.use: Small-talk opener; dorama covers any TV series, Japanese or foreign.
items.kana: いまなにかドラマみてる？
items.politeJa: 今何かドラマ見ていますか？

example.romaji: ima nanika dorama miteru? omoshiroi no oshiete.
example.ja: 今何かドラマ見てる？面白いの教えて。
example.english: Watching any shows right now? Tell me a good one.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, nanika dorama o mite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近、何かドラマを見ていますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you watching any shows lately?

items.notes: Miteru is the spoken form of mite iru; the same works for reading: ima nanika yonderu?

items.english: who's your fave? (idol, band member, character)
items.use: Asked among fans of a group, show or anime; answer with a name plus ga oshi.

example.romaji: kono guruupu, oshi wa dare? watashi wa kono hito.
example.ja: このグループ、推しは誰？私はこの人。
example.english: Who's your fave in this group? Mine's this one.

examplePolite.romaji: kono guruupu de, oshi wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: このグループで、推しは誰ですか？
examplePolite.english: Who's your favourite in this group?

items.notes: From osu (to push, back); oshikatsu is fan activity like buying merch and going to shows.

blocks.label: Music and gigs
blocks.rationale: Ask about someone's music taste, gigs and karaoke songs.
blocks.interference: raibu is a live gig or concert, not 'live' as in living.

items.english: what kind of music do you listen to?
items.use: Answer with a genre or artist, often with toka (rokku toka).
items.kana: どんなおんがくきくの？
items.politeJa: どんな音楽を聴きますか？

example.romaji: donna ongaku kiku no? rokku toka?
example.ja: どんな音楽聴くの？ロックとか？
example.english: What kind of music do you listen to? Rock?

examplePolite.romaji: donna ongaku o kikimasu ka? rokku toka desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どんな音楽を聴きますか？ロックとかですか？
examplePolite.english: What kind of music do you listen to? Rock?

items.notes: Kiku means both 'listen' and 'ask'; context tells them apart.

items.polite: suki na aatisuto wa imasu ka?
items.english: any artists you like?; got a favourite artist?
items.use: Aatisuto mostly means a singer or band, not a painter.
items.ja: 好きなアーティストいる？
items.kana: すきなアーティストいる？
items.politeJa: 好きなアーティストはいますか？

example.romaji: suki na aatisuto iru? saikin nani kiiteru?
example.ja: 好きなアーティストいる？最近何聴いてる？
example.english: Any artists you like? What are you listening to lately?

examplePolite.romaji: suki na aatisuto wa imasu ka? saikin nani o kiite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 好きなアーティストはいますか？最近何を聴いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have a favourite artist? What are you listening to these days?

items.notes: Iru, not aru, because artists are people.

items.english: do you go to gigs?; do you go to concerts?
items.use: Raibu is any live music show, from a small bar gig to a stadium concert.
items.politeJa: ライブとか行きますか？

example.romaji: raibu toka iku? raigetsu issho ni ikanai?
example.ja: ライブとか行く？来月一緒に行かない？
example.english: Do you go to gigs? Want to come with me next month?

examplePolite.romaji: raibu toka ikimasu ka? raigetsu issho ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: ライブとか行きますか？来月一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Do you go to concerts? Would you like to go together next month?

items.notes: Konsaato sounds more formal or classical; raibu is the everyday word.

items.polite: karaoke de wa nani o utaimasu ka?
items.english: what do you sing at karaoke?
items.use: Asked when planning a karaoke night or getting to know someone's music taste.
items.kana: カラオケでなにうたう？
items.politeJa: カラオケでは何を歌いますか？

example.romaji: karaoke de itsumo nani utau? kondo issho ni ikou yo.
example.ja: カラオケでいつも何歌う？今度一緒に行こうよ。
example.english: What do you usually sing at karaoke? Let's go together sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: karaoke de wa itsumo nani o utaimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: カラオケではいつも何を歌いますか？
examplePolite.english: What do you usually sing at karaoke?

items.notes: Your go-to song is your juuhachiban.

blocks.label: How long and how good
blocks.rationale: Follow up on a hobby by asking how long, and say how new or rusty you are.
blocks.interference: mukashi yatteta (used to do) vs yatteru (do now).

items.polite: dono gurai yatte iru n desu ka?
items.english: how long have you been doing it?
items.use: Follow-up when someone mentions a hobby or sport; answer with a length of time (sannen gurai).
items.ja: どのぐらいやってるの？
items.kana: どのぐらいやってるの？
items.politeJa: どのぐらいやっているんですか？

example.romaji: sugoi umai ne. dono gurai yatteru no?
example.ja: すごいうまいね。どのぐらいやってるの？
example.english: You're really good. How long have you been doing it?

examplePolite.romaji: sugoku jouzu desu ne. dono gurai yatte iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すごく上手ですね。どのぐらいやっているんですか？
examplePolite.english: You're really good. How long have you been doing it?

items.notes: Japanese uses the present -te iru where English says 'have been doing'.

items.english: I only took it up recently; I just started
items.use: Said about a new hobby, often to excuse being bad at it.
items.kana: さいきんはじめたんだ

example.romaji: gitaa wa saikin hajimeta n da. mada heta da yo.
example.ja: ギターは最近始めたんだ。まだ下手だよ。
example.english: I only took up guitar recently. I'm still bad.

examplePolite.romaji: gitaa wa saikin hajimeta n desu. mada heta desu.
examplePolite.ja: ギターは最近始めたんです。まだ下手です。
examplePolite.english: I only took up guitar recently. I'm still bad.

items.notes: Put the hobby first with wa: yoga wa saikin hajimeta n da.

items.english: I used to do ...; I used to play ...
items.use: For past hobbies, sports or instruments; the activity goes in the middle (mukashi tenisu yatteta).

example.romaji: mukashi piano yatteta kedo, mou zenzen hikenai.
example.ja: 昔ピアノやってたけど、もう全然弾けない。
example.english: I used to play piano, but I can't play at all now.

examplePolite.romaji: mukashi piano o yatte imashita kedo, mou zenzen hikemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 昔ピアノをやっていましたけど、もう全然弾けません。
examplePolite.english: I used to play the piano, but I can't play at all any more.

items.notes: -te ita (yatteta) is the usual way to say 'used to'.

items.english: I'm not any good at it, though
items.use: A modest add-on after saying you do something; expected even when you're decent.

example.romaji: gitaa hiku yo. zenzen heta da kedo.
example.ja: ギター弾くよ。全然下手だけど。
example.english: I play guitar. I'm not any good, though.

examplePolite.romaji: gitaa o hikimasu. zenzen heta desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ギターを弾きます。全然下手ですけど。
examplePolite.english: I play the guitar. Not very well, though.

items.notes: Heta = bad at; jouzu = good at, said of others, not yourself.

blocks.label: Asking their view
blocks.rationale: Invite someone's opinion or reaction on a topic.
blocks.interference: sou omowanai? fishes for agreement; dou omou? is open.

items.use: Ask someone's opinion; answer X to omou (I think X) or sou omou.

example.romaji: kono fuku, dou omou? chotto hade kana.
example.ja: この服、どう思う？ちょっと派手かな。
example.english: What do you think of this outfit? Too loud?

examplePolite.romaji: kono fuku, dou omoimasu ka? chotto hade deshou ka.
examplePolite.ja: この服、どう思いますか？ちょっと派手でしょうか。
examplePolite.english: What do you think of this outfit? Is it a bit loud?

items.notes: Use dou (how), not nani (what): nani o omou? sounds wrong.

items.english: don't you think?; don't you agree?
items.use: Tags your opinion and invites agreement; answer sou da ne to agree or uun, dou kana to hedge.

example.romaji: ano eiga, nagasugita yo. sou omowanai?
example.ja: あの映画、長すぎたよ。そう思わない？
example.english: That film was way too long. Don't you think?

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga, chotto nagakatta desu yo ne. sou omoimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの映画、ちょっと長かったですよね。そう思いませんか？
examplePolite.english: That film was a bit long. Don't you think?

items.notes: Asked in the negative but means 'you agree, right?', so un means you agree.

items.polite: jissai dou na n desu ka?
items.english: what's it really like?; how is it, honestly?
items.use: Asks for the real story behind a reputation: a job, a city, a relationship.

example.romaji: toukyou no seikatsu tte, jissai dou na no?
example.ja: 東京の生活って、実際どうなの？
example.english: So what's life in Tokyo really like?

examplePolite.romaji: toukyou no seikatsu tte, jissai dou na n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 東京の生活って、実際どうなんですか？
examplePolite.english: So what's life in Tokyo really like?

items.notes: Jissai means 'in reality'; jissai wa ... (actually, ...) introduces the truth.

items.english: so what did you think?; your thoughts?
items.use: Asked right after someone has seen, read, tried or done something; answer with a one-line verdict.

example.romaji: ano hon, yomiowatta? de, kansou wa?
example.ja: あの本、読み終わった？で、感想は？
example.english: Did you finish that book? So, what did you think?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hon, yomiowarimashita ka? kansou wa dou deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの本、読み終わりましたか？感想はどうでしたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you finish that book? What did you think?

items.notes: Kansou means 'impressions' of an experience; a view on an issue is iken.

items.english: did you see that news?; did you hear about that?
items.use: Opens a chat about a current story you both probably know about.
items.politeJa: あのニュース見ましたか？

example.romaji: ne, kesa no ano nyuusu mita? bikkuri shita.
example.ja: ね、今朝のあのニュース見た？びっくりした。
example.english: Hey, did you see that news this morning? I was shocked.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa no ano nyuusu, mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今朝のあのニュース、見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you see that news this morning?

items.notes: Ano points to something you both know; use kono nyuusu when showing it on your phone.

blocks.label: Saying it's good
blocks.rationale: Give a quick positive verdict on something.
blocks.interference: omoshirokatta means fun or interesting, not only funny.

items.polite: ii n ja nai desu ka?
items.english: sounds good to me; why not?; I think it's fine
items.use: Approves a friend's plan, outfit or choice; a flat tone can sound like 'whatever'.
items.politeJa: いいんじゃないですか？

example.romaji: sono fuku, ii n ja nai? niau yo.
example.ja: その服、いいんじゃない？似合うよ。
example.english: That outfit's nice, I think. It suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: sono an, ii n ja nai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: その案、いいんじゃないですか？
examplePolite.english: That idea sounds good to me.

items.notes: Not a negative: ja nai? here means 'isn't it?'.

items.english: that was interesting; that was fun; that was funny
items.use: For films, books, talks or anything that held your interest or made you laugh.

example.romaji: ano eiga, sugoku omoshirokatta yo.
example.ja: あの映画、すごく面白かったよ。
example.english: That movie was really good.

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga, sugoku omoshirokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの映画、すごく面白かったです。
examplePolite.english: That movie was really good.

items.notes: omoshiroi is 'interesting' as much as 'funny'; for a fun event, tanoshikatta fits better.

items.use: Approves of how something looks, feels, or is coming along.

example.romaji: un, ii kanji! sono mama tsuzukete.
example.ja: うん、いい感じ！そのまま続けて。
example.english: Yeah, looks good! Keep going like that.

examplePolite.romaji: ii kanji desu ne. sono mama tsuzukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いい感じですね。そのまま続けてください。
examplePolite.english: That's looking good. Please keep going.

items.notes: About a person it means likable: ii kanji no hito (a nice person).

items.english: that works; that's an option; I'm into that
items.use: Says an idea or combination is acceptable or even good; the opposite is nashi (no way).

example.romaji: piza ni painappuru? un, ari da ne.
example.ja: ピザにパイナップル？うん、アリだね。
example.english: Pineapple on pizza? Yeah, that works.

examplePolite.romaji: sono kangae, ari desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その考え、アリですね。
examplePolite.english: That idea could work.

items.notes: Ari ka nashi ka? (yes or no?) asks whether something's acceptable.

items.polite: mite son wa nai desu yo
items.english: it's worth a watch; you won't regret seeing it
items.use: Recommends a film, show or sight to a friend.

example.romaji: ano eiga, ichido mite son wa nai yo.
example.ja: あの映画、一度見て損はないよ。
example.english: That film's worth seeing at least once.

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga, ichido mite son wa nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの映画、一度見て損はないですよ。
examplePolite.english: That film's worth seeing at least once.

items.notes: Works with other verbs: itte son wa nai (worth going), yonde son wa nai (worth reading).

blocks.label: Saying it's not great
blocks.rationale: Give a mild negative verdict without sounding harsh.
blocks.interference: awanakatta (didn't suit me) vs aenakatta (couldn't meet).

items.english: not quite there; a bit lacking; so-so
items.use: Says food, a film or an idea falls a bit short; softer than mazui or tsumaranai.

example.romaji: kono raamen, aji ga imaichi da na.
example.ja: このラーメン、味がいまいちだな。
example.english: This ramen's a bit meh.

examplePolite.romaji: kono raamen, aji ga imaichi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このラーメン、味がいまいちですね。
examplePolite.english: The flavour of this ramen is a bit lacking.

items.notes: Before a verb it means 'not quite': imaichi wakaranai (I don't quite get it).

items.english: I'm not that keen on it; I don't really like it
items.use: The everyday soft way to say you dislike something; kirai is much stronger.
items.ja: あんまり好きじゃない
items.kana: あんまりすきじゃない
items.politeJa: あまり好きじゃないです

example.romaji: horaa eiga wa anmari suki ja nai n da.
example.ja: ホラー映画はあんまり好きじゃないんだ。
example.english: I'm not really into horror films.

examplePolite.romaji: horaa eiga wa amari suki ja nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: ホラー映画はあまり好きじゃないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm not really into horror films.

items.notes: Anmari is the spoken form of amari; it needs a negative after it.

items.use: Said when something isn't what you wanted but you can't say why: a haircut, a recipe, a word.

example.romaji: kono iro, nanka chigau na. betsu no ni shiyou.
example.ja: この色、なんか違うな。別のにしよう。
example.english: This colour's not quite right. Let's go with another.

examplePolite.romaji: kono iro, nanka chigaimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この色、なんか違いますね。
examplePolite.english: This colour isn't quite right.

items.notes: Nanka means 'somehow, kind of'; chigau alone means 'that's wrong' or 'that's different'.

items.polite: kitai shite ita hodo ja nakatta desu
items.english: it wasn't as good as I'd hoped
items.use: Mild disappointment about a film, restaurant or trip that had been hyped.
items.ja: 期待してたほどじゃなかった
items.kana: きたいしてたほどじゃなかった
items.politeJa: 期待していたほどじゃなかったです

example.romaji: hyouban ii kedo, kitai shiteta hodo ja nakatta.
example.ja: 評判いいけど、期待してたほどじゃなかった。
example.english: It's got great reviews, but it wasn't as good as I'd hoped.

examplePolite.romaji: hyouban wa ii desu kedo, kitai shite ita hodo ja nakatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 評判はいいですけど、期待していたほどじゃなかったです。
examplePolite.english: It's got great reviews, but it wasn't as good as I'd hoped.

items.notes: Hodo ja nai means 'not as much as'; omotta hodo ja nakatta (not as ... as I thought) is the same idea.

items.english: it wasn't for me; it didn't suit me
items.use: A polite way to dislike something without calling it bad; it puts the problem on your taste.
items.kana: わたしにはあわなかった
items.politeJa: 私には合わなかったです

example.romaji: ano manga, watashi ni wa awanakatta na.
example.ja: あの漫画、私には合わなかったな。
example.english: That manga wasn't really for me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano manga wa, watashi ni wa awanakatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの漫画は、私には合わなかったです。
examplePolite.english: That manga wasn't for me.

items.notes: Also for food or medicine that disagrees with you. Present tense: watashi ni wa awanai.

blocks.label: Liking it your way
blocks.rationale: Say you like something in a low-key way and say what you like about it.
blocks.interference: warukunai and kirai ja nai sound negative but mean you like it.

items.use: Mild praise that often means 'actually quite good'; tone decides how warm it is.

example.romaji: kono mise, warukunai ne. mata koyou.
example.ja: この店、悪くないね。また来よう。
example.english: This place isn't bad. Let's come again.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, warukunai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、悪くないですね。
examplePolite.english: This place isn't bad.

items.notes: Also 'it's not your fault': kimi wa warukunai yo.

items.english: I don't mind it; I kind of like it
items.use: A shy or understated way to say you like something; it usually means more than it says.

example.romaji: kou iu ongaku, kirai ja nai yo.
example.ja: こういう音楽、嫌いじゃないよ。
example.english: I kind of like this kind of music.

examplePolite.romaji: kou iu ongaku, kirai ja nai desu.
examplePolite.ja: こういう音楽、嫌いじゃないです。
examplePolite.english: I kind of like this kind of music.

items.notes: Said about a person it can be a coy confession of liking them.

items.english: I like how ...; what I like is ...
items.use: Names the specific thing you like about a person, place or work.

example.romaji: kare no yasashii tokoro ga suki.
example.ja: 彼の優しいところが好き。
example.english: I love how kind he is.

examplePolite.romaji: kono machi no shizuka na tokoro ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: この町の静かなところが好きです。
examplePolite.english: What I like about this town is how quiet it is.

items.notes: Tokoro here means 'side, aspect', not 'place'; it also works for dislikes: ... tokoro ga iya.

items.english: well, I like it (even if others don't)
items.use: Defends your taste after someone criticises something, without starting an argument.

example.romaji: e, sonna ni dame? watashi wa suki da kedo.
example.ja: え、そんなにダメ？私は好きだけど。
example.english: Huh, is it that bad? I like it, though.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ka? watashi wa suki desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: そうですか？私は好きですけど。
examplePolite.english: Really? I like it, though.

items.notes: Wa sets you against the others; the trailing kedo leaves the rest unsaid.

blocks.label: Framing your own view
blocks.rationale: Open your opinion so it lands as personal, not as fact.
blocks.interference: watashi dattara (if it were me) vs watashi datta (it was me).

items.english: I'm not really sure, but ...; I don't know much, but ...
items.use: Hedges an opinion or guess on a topic you don't know well.
items.politeJa: よくわからないですけど

example.romaji: yoku wakannai kedo, sore tabun daijoubu da yo.
example.ja: よくわかんないけど、それたぶん大丈夫だよ。
example.english: I'm not totally sure, but that's probably fine.

examplePolite.romaji: yoku wakaranai desu kedo, tabun daijoubu da to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: よくわからないですけど、たぶん大丈夫だと思います。
examplePolite.english: I'm not really sure, but I think it's probably fine.

items.notes: Wakannai is the spoken form of wakaranai.

items.english: if it were me, I'd ...; if I were you, ...
items.use: Gives advice by saying what you'd do, which is softer than telling someone what to do.

example.romaji: watashi dattara, sugu yamechau kana.
example.ja: 私だったら、すぐ辞めちゃうかな。
example.english: If it were me, I'd quit right away.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi dattara, mou ichido hanashite mimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私だったら、もう一度話してみますね。
examplePolite.english: If it were me, I'd try talking to them once more.

items.notes: Men often say ore dattara or boku dattara; the line usually ends in kana or to omou.

items.use: Opens your own view and marks it as just your opinion; safe in any register.

example.romaji: kojinteki ni wa, mae no hou ga suki datta.
example.ja: 個人的には、前の方が好きだった。
example.english: Personally, I liked the old one better.

examplePolite.romaji: kojinteki ni wa, kono an ni sansei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 個人的には、この案に賛成です。
examplePolite.english: Personally, I'm in favour of this plan.

items.english: for me; as far as I'm concerned
items.use: A casual, youthful way to give your own view.

example.romaji: watashiteki ni wa, kore de zenzen ii yo.
example.ja: 私的には、これで全然いいよ。
example.english: As far as I'm concerned, this is totally fine.

items.notes: Don't confuse it with shiteki (private), written the same; in polite talk use kojinteki ni wa.

items.english: honestly; to be blunt; let's be real
items.use: Opens a frank admission among friends, often something people don't usually say out loud.

example.romaji: butchake, ano eiga tsumaranakatta yo ne.
example.ja: ぶっちゃけ、あの映画つまらなかったよね。
example.english: Honestly, that film was boring, wasn't it?

items.notes: Avoid with bosses or customers; shoujiki (honestly) is the neutral word.

blocks.label: Comparing here and there
blocks.rationale: Compare Japan with home, or one thing with another.
blocks.interference: sumiyasui is easy (yasui) to live in, not cheap.

items.use: Asks someone who knows both things, such as two cities, jobs or versions, to compare them.

example.romaji: nihon no seikatsu, kuni to kurabete dou?
example.ja: 日本の生活、国と比べてどう？
example.english: How does life in Japan compare with back home?

examplePolite.romaji: mae no shigoto to kurabete dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 前の仕事と比べてどうですか？
examplePolite.english: How does it compare with your last job?

items.notes: The answer usually uses yori (than): nihon yori takai (pricier than Japan).

items.english: it's not that different; about the same
items.use: Plays down a difference in price, taste or quality when someone asks which is better.
items.politeJa: そんなに変わらないです

example.romaji: dotchi mo nedan wa sonna ni kawaranai yo.
example.ja: どっちも値段はそんなに変わらないよ。
example.english: They're not that different in price.

examplePolite.romaji: nedan wa sonna ni kawaranai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 値段はそんなに変わらないですよ。
examplePolite.english: The price isn't that different.

items.notes: Kawaranai also means 'you haven't changed': zenzen kawaranai ne.

items.use: Asks someone who has lived or worked in two places to name the main difference.
items.kana: なにがいちばんちがう？

example.romaji: nihon to igirisu de, nani ga ichiban chigau?
example.ja: 日本とイギリスで、何が一番違う？
example.english: What's the biggest difference between Japan and the UK?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon to oosutoraria de, nani ga ichiban chigaimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本とオーストラリアで、何が一番違いますか？
examplePolite.english: What's the biggest difference between Japan and Australia?

items.notes: Set up the pair with ... to ... de (between ... and ...).

items.english: you can't beat ...; ... is the best after all
items.use: Said after comparing, or on coming back to something familiar like home, mum's cooking or a hot bath.
items.politeJa: やっぱり〜が一番ですね

example.romaji: ryokou mo ii kedo, yappari ie ga ichiban da ne.
example.ja: 旅行もいいけど、やっぱり家が一番だね。
example.english: Travel's nice, but there's no place like home.

examplePolite.romaji: natsu wa yappari tsumetai biiru ga ichiban desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 夏はやっぱり冷たいビールが一番ですね。
examplePolite.english: In summer, you can't beat a cold beer.

items.notes: Yappari (yappa in fast speech) means 'as expected, after all'.

items.english: is it a nice place to live?; is it easy to live there?
items.use: Asked of someone who lives in a city, area or country you're curious about.

example.romaji: oosaka tte sumiyasui? bukka wa dou?
example.ja: 大阪って住みやすい？物価はどう？
example.english: Is Osaka a nice place to live? What are prices like?

examplePolite.romaji: oosaka wa sumiyasui desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大阪は住みやすいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is Osaka a nice place to live?

items.notes: -yasui after a verb stem means 'easy to': tsukaiyasui (easy to use), wakariyasui (easy to understand).

blocks.label: It depends
blocks.rationale: Avoid a flat answer when the honest view is 'it depends'.
blocks.interference: ichigai ni wa ienai (can't generalise) vs nantomo ienai (can't say).

items.english: it depends on the situation; it depends
items.use: A non-committal answer to a yes-or-no question about habits or rules.

example.romaji: zangyou? maa, toki to baai ni yoru kana.
example.ja: 残業？まあ、時と場合によるかな。
example.english: Overtime? Well, it depends.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa toki to baai ni yorimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは時と場合によりますね。
examplePolite.english: That depends on the situation.

items.notes: Shorter: ... ni yoru (it depends on ...): hito ni yoru (depends on the person).

items.english: hard to say; I can't really say
items.use: When you can't judge yet or won't commit; also for a feeling that's hard to put into words.

example.romaji: mada hajimatta bakari da kara, nantomo ienai na.
example.ja: まだ始まったばかりだから、なんとも言えないな。
example.english: It's only just started, so it's hard to say.

examplePolite.romaji: mada hajimatta bakari na node, nantomo iemasen.
examplePolite.ja: まだ始まったばかりなので、なんとも言えません。
examplePolite.english: It's only just started, so I can't really say.

items.notes: nantomo ienai aji, 'a taste you can't describe', is praise.

items.english: that's a tough one; it's a tricky question
items.use: Buys time or avoids taking sides on a hard choice; also a soft no to a request.
items.kana: むずかしいところだね

example.romaji: dotchi mo ii kara, muzukashii tokoro da ne.
example.ja: どっちもいいから、難しいところだね。
example.english: They're both good, so that's a tough one.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa muzukashii tokoro desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは難しいところですね。
examplePolite.english: That's a tough one.

items.notes: At work, muzukashii (it's difficult) often means no.

items.english: you can't really generalise; it's hard to say
items.use: Gently pushes back on a sweeping claim about a group or place.
items.kana: いちがいにはいえない

example.romaji: nihonjin wa tsumetai? sore wa ichigai ni wa ienai yo.
example.ja: 日本人は冷たい？それは一概には言えないよ。
example.english: Japanese people are cold? You can't really generalise like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa ichigai ni wa iemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは一概には言えませんね。
examplePolite.english: You can't really generalise about that.

items.notes: Often after ... to wa: warui to wa ichigai ni wa ienai (you can't just call it bad).

items.romaji: kuni ni yotte chigau yo ne
items.polite: kuni ni yotte chigaimasu yo ne
items.english: it differs from country to country, doesn't it
items.use: Common in cross-cultural chat when comparing customs like tipping or table manners.
items.kana: くにによってちがうよね
items.politeJa: 国によって違いますよね

example.romaji: chippu no shuukan tte, kuni ni yotte chigau yo ne.
example.ja: チップの習慣って、国によって違うよね。
example.english: Tipping customs differ from country to country, don't they?

examplePolite.romaji: aisatsu no shikata mo, kuni ni yotte chigaimasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 挨拶の仕方も、国によって違いますよね。
examplePolite.english: Even greetings differ from country to country, don't they?

items.notes: Swap the noun: hito ni yotte (depending on the person), mise ni yotte (depending on the shop).

blocks.label: How have you been
blocks.rationale: Open a catch-up by asking how someone's doing.
blocks.interference: genki datta? (been well since we last met) vs genki? (are you well).

items.use: Opens a catch-up with a friend or coworker; answer with a bit of news, or maa maa (so-so).

example.romaji: saikin dou? shigoto isogashii?
example.ja: 最近どう？仕事忙しい？
example.english: How's it going? Busy with work?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin dou desu ka? oshigoto wa isogashii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近どうですか？お仕事は忙しいですか？
examplePolite.english: How have things been? Is work busy?

items.notes: The closest thing to English 'how are you?' for people you see often.

items.english: how are you doing?; how's it going?
items.use: A casual greeting between friends or coworkers; answer with bochibochi, aikawarazu da yo or genki da yo.

example.romaji: oo, saikin choushi dou? isogashii?
example.ja: おー、最近調子どう？忙しい？
example.english: Hey, how's it going lately? Busy?

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. saikin choushi wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。最近調子はどうですか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. How have you been lately?

items.notes: Also asks about one specific thing: ashi no choushi dou? (how's your leg?).

items.use: An easy opener when you run into someone; a vague answer is fine.

example.romaji: saikin isogashii? zenzen aenai ne.
example.ja: 最近忙しい？全然会えないね。
example.english: Been busy lately? We never get to see each other.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin isogashii desu ka? shibaraku aemasen deshita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 最近忙しいですか？しばらく会えませんでしたね。
examplePolite.english: Have you been busy? We haven't seen each other in a while.

items.notes: Typical answers: maa ne ('yeah, kind of') or sou demo nai ('not really').

items.use: To someone you haven't seen for a while; answer un, genki datta yo, or with your news.

example.romaji: uwa, hisashiburi! genki datta?
example.ja: うわ、久しぶり！元気だった？
example.english: Wow, long time no see! How've you been?

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. ogenki deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気でしたか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time. How have you been?

items.notes: Only after a gap; for someone you saw last week, use saikin dou?

items.use: Asked when you catch up after time apart; if nothing's new, answer toku ni nai yo or aikawarazu da yo.
items.ja: 何か変わったことあった？
items.kana: なにかかわったことあった？
items.politeJa: 何か変わったことありましたか？

example.romaji: hisashiburi da ne. nanika kawatta koto atta?
example.ja: 久しぶりだね。何か変わったことあった？
example.english: It's been a while. Anything new with you?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, nanika kawatta koto arimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近、何か変わったことありましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has anything new happened lately?

items.notes: Kawatta koto means 'anything different'; kawatta hito means 'an odd person'.

blocks.label: Nothing much new
blocks.rationale: Answer 'how are you' when life is just ticking along.
blocks.interference: kawari nai (nothing's changed) vs kawaranai (won't change).

items.english: nothing much, really; nothing in particular
items.use: The usual answer to 'anything new?' or 'any plans?' when nothing is going on.

example.romaji: saikin? toku ni nanimo nai yo. itsumo doori.
example.ja: 最近？特に何もないよ。いつも通り。
example.english: Lately? Nothing much. Same as usual.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin desu ka? toku ni nanimo nai desu. itsumo doori desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近ですか？特に何もないです。いつも通りです。
examplePolite.english: Lately? Nothing much. Same as always.

items.notes: Can be cut to toku ni; betsu ni on its own can sound curt.

items.english: same as ever; nothing much new
items.use: Answer to choushi dou? or saikin dou? when nothing has changed.

example.romaji: un, aikawarazu da yo. shigoto bakkari.
example.ja: うん、相変わらずだよ。仕事ばっかり。
example.english: Yeah, same as ever. All work.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, aikawarazu desu. shigoto bakari de.
examplePolite.ja: はい、相変わらずです。仕事ばかりで。
examplePolite.english: Yes, same as ever. Just work.

items.notes: Also says someone hasn't changed, often teasing: aikawarazu da ne (you haven't changed a bit).

items.use: Modest answer to how's it going or how's business; strongly Kansai but understood everywhere.

example.romaji: shigoto? maa, bochibochi da ne.
example.ja: 仕事？まあ、ぼちぼちだね。
example.english: Work? Oh, getting by.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto desu ka? maa, bochibochi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 仕事ですか？まあ、ぼちぼちです。
examplePolite.english: Work? Oh, getting by.

items.notes: Also means 'about time, little by little': bochibochi kaerou ka (shall we head home soon?).

items.english: no change; all well, same as ever
items.use: As a question it asks if all is well since you last met; as an answer it means nothing new, all fine.
items.politeJa: お変わりありませんか

example.romaji: hisashiburi da ne. kawari nai?
example.ja: 久しぶりだね。変わりない？
example.english: Long time no see. All good?

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. okawari arimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お変わりありませんか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. Is everything well with you?

items.notes: A common answer is un, aikawarazu (yeah, same as ever).

items.use: Answer to how's it going when things are tough but okay; sounds modest and a bit tired.
items.politeJa: なんとかやっています

example.romaji: shigoto wa taihen da kedo, nantoka yatteru yo.
example.ja: 仕事は大変だけど、なんとかやってるよ。
example.english: Work's tough, but I'm getting by.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto wa taihen desu kedo, nantoka yatte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 仕事は大変ですけど、なんとかやっています。
examplePolite.english: Work's tough, but I'm getting by.

items.notes: Nantoka means 'somehow'; nantoka naru (it'll work out somehow) is a common pair.

blocks.label: Busy tired or rested
blocks.rationale: Say how busy or worn out you've been.
blocks.interference: nebusoku (short on sleep) vs nemui (sleepy right now).

items.english: things have been hectic; I've been rushed off my feet
items.use: Explains why you've been out of touch or slow to reply, often after gomen.
items.politeJa: バタバタしていました

example.romaji: gomen, kongetsu zutto batabata shiteta.
example.ja: ごめん、今月ずっとバタバタしてた。
example.english: Sorry, it's been hectic all month.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kongetsu zutto batabata shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今月ずっとバタバタしていました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, it's been hectic all month.

items.notes: Batabata is the sound of rushing around; for right now say ima batabata shiteru (I'm swamped).

items.english: I've been a bit worn out lately
items.use: An honest answer to 'how are you?' that admits you're tired without complaining.
items.ja: 最近ちょっと疲れ気味
items.kana: さいきんちょっとつかれぎみ
items.politeJa: 最近ちょっと疲れ気味です

example.romaji: saikin chotto tsukaregimi. shigoto ga isogashikute.
example.ja: 最近ちょっと疲れ気味。仕事が忙しくて。
example.english: I've been a bit worn out lately. Work's been busy.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin chotto tsukaregimi desu. shigoto ga isogashikute.
examplePolite.ja: 最近ちょっと疲れ気味です。仕事が忙しくて。
examplePolite.english: I've been a little tired lately. Work has been busy.

items.notes: -gimi means 'a touch of': kazegimi is 'a bit of a cold'.

items.english: I haven't been sleeping enough; a bit short on sleep
items.use: Said when someone asks if you're okay or says you look tired.

example.romaji: un, daijoubu. chotto nebusoku na n da.
example.ja: うん、大丈夫。ちょっと寝不足なんだ。
example.english: Yeah, I'm fine. Just a bit short on sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu. chotto nebusoku na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です。ちょっと寝不足なんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm fine. Just a bit short on sleep.

items.notes: Nebusoku is a noun: nebusoku de atama ga itai (my head hurts from lack of sleep).

items.use: Said after a busy stretch such as a move, a project or a new baby, to say you're free again.
items.politeJa: やっと落ち着きました

example.romaji: hikkoshi mo owatte, yatto ochitsuita yo.
example.ja: 引っ越しも終わって、やっと落ち着いたよ。
example.english: The move's done, so things have finally settled down.

examplePolite.romaji: hikkoshi mo owatte, yatto ochitsukimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 引っ越しも終わって、やっと落ち着きました。
examplePolite.english: The move's done, so things have finally settled down.

items.notes: Ochitsuku also means 'to calm down': ochitsuite! (calm down!).

items.use: Said on waking with a stretch, or as the answer to yoku neta? (did you sleep well?).

example.romaji: un, yuube wa yoku neta yo. arigatou.
example.ja: うん、ゆうべはよく寝たよ。ありがとう。
example.english: Yeah, I slept well last night, thanks.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, okagesama de yuube wa yoku nemashita.
examplePolite.ja: はい、おかげさまでゆうべはよく寝ました。
examplePolite.english: Yes, thanks, I slept well last night.

items.notes: Politely, people also ask and answer with yoku nemuremashita (were able to sleep well).

blocks.label: Last weekend
