blocks.rationale: Ask about and sum up a weekend or holiday.
blocks.interference: yukkuri dekita (got to relax) vs yukkuri (slowly).

items.polite: shuumatsu wa nani o shimashita ka?
items.english: what did you do on the weekend?
items.use: A Monday catch-up question for friends or coworkers; a short answer is fine.
items.politeJa: 週末は何をしましたか？

example.romaji: shuumatsu nani shita? dokka itta?
example.ja: 週末何した？どっか行った？
example.english: What'd you do on the weekend? Go anywhere?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa nani o shimashita ka? dokoka ikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末は何をしましたか？どこか行きましたか？
examplePolite.english: What did you do on the weekend? Did you go anywhere?

items.notes: A common answer is ie de gorogoro shiteta, 'I lazed around at home'.

items.english: that was fun; I had a great time
items.use: Say after a trip, party or day out; the usual answer to dou datta?

example.romaji: kyou wa honto ni tanoshikatta! mata ikou ne.
example.ja: 今日はほんとに楽しかった！また行こうね。
example.english: Today was so much fun! Let's go again.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni tanoshikatta desu. mata ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に楽しかったです。また行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: I really enjoyed today. Let's go again.

items.notes: For a funny or interesting film or book, omoshirokatta fits better.

items.english: did you get to relax on the weekend?
items.use: A kind Monday question, often to a coworker after a busy week.
items.kana: しゅうまつゆっくりできた？
items.politeJa: 週末はゆっくりできましたか？

example.romaji: ohayou. shuumatsu yukkuri dekita?
example.ja: おはよう。週末ゆっくりできた？
example.english: Morning. Did you get to relax on the weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: ohayou gozaimasu. shuumatsu wa yukkuri dekimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: おはようございます。週末はゆっくりできましたか？
examplePolite.english: Good morning. Did you get some rest on the weekend?

items.notes: Yukkuri suru is to take it easy; yukkuri shite ne means 'take your time' or 'rest up'.

items.english: go anywhere over the long weekend?
items.use: Asked after a holiday break such as Golden Week or Obon.
items.kana: れんきゅうどこかいった？
items.politeJa: 連休はどこか行きましたか？

example.romaji: renkyuu dokoka itta? zutto ie ni ita?
example.ja: 連休どこか行った？ずっと家にいた？
example.english: Go anywhere over the long weekend? Or stay home the whole time?

examplePolite.romaji: renkyuu wa dokoka ikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 連休はどこか行きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you go anywhere over the long weekend?

items.notes: Casual speech often shortens dokoka to dokka.

blocks.label: How work is going
blocks.rationale: Check in on someone's job, the default catch-up topic.
blocks.interference: shigoto nani shiteru no asks what job; shigoto dou asks how it's going.

items.use: A standard catch-up question for a friend or colleague you haven't seen in a while.

example.romaji: hisashiburi! shigoto dou? isogashii?
example.ja: 久しぶり！仕事どう？忙しい？
example.english: Long time no see! How's work? Busy?

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. oshigoto wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お仕事はどうですか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. How's work?

items.notes: Typical answers are maa maa ('so-so') or bochibochi ('getting by').

items.polite: oshigoto wa nani o sarete imasu ka?
items.english: what do you do for work?
items.use: Asked when getting to know someone; people often answer by field, like kyouiku kankei (something in education).
items.politeJa: お仕事は何をされていますか？

example.romaji: hee, toukyou ni sunderu n da. shigoto nani shiteru no?
example.ja: へえ、東京に住んでるんだ。仕事何してるの？
example.english: Oh, you live in Tokyo? What do you do for work?

examplePolite.romaji: shitsurei desu kedo, oshigoto wa nani o sarete imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 失礼ですけど、お仕事は何をされていますか？
examplePolite.english: If you don't mind me asking, what do you do for work?

items.english: do you do a lot of overtime?
items.use: Common work small talk; long hours are a normal thing to grumble about.

example.romaji: ima no kaisha, zangyou ooi?
example.ja: 今の会社、残業多い？
example.english: Do you do a lot of overtime at your company?

examplePolite.romaji: ima no kaisha wa zangyou ga ooi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今の会社は残業が多いですか？
examplePolite.english: Is there a lot of overtime at your company?

items.notes: Zangyou suru is to work overtime; kyou mo zangyou is 'overtime again today'.

blocks.label: Your news
blocks.rationale: Share what's new with you and follow up on their news.
blocks.interference: hamatteru (hooked on) vs haitteru (is inside).

items.english: I'm really into ...; I'm hooked on ...
items.use: Says what you're obsessed with right now; ask back with saikin nani ni hamatteru?

example.romaji: saikin, kankoku dorama ni hamatteru n da.
example.ja: 最近、韓国ドラマにハマってるんだ。
example.english: I'm really into Korean dramas lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, kankoku dorama ni hamatte iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、韓国ドラマにハマっているんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm really into Korean dramas lately.

items.notes: Hamaru literally means 'to get stuck in'; it implies a recent, strong craze rather than a lasting like (suki).

items.polite: mae ni itte ita ..., dou narimashita ka?
items.english: how did that ... you mentioned turn out?
items.use: Follows up on something a friend told you last time: an interview, a date, a trip.
items.ja: 前に言ってた〜、どうなった？
items.kana: まえにいってた〜、どうなった？
items.politeJa: 前に言っていた〜、どうなりましたか？

example.romaji: mae ni itteta mensetsu, dou natta? ukatta?
example.ja: 前に言ってた面接、どうなった？受かった？
example.english: How did that interview you mentioned go? Did you get it?

examplePolite.romaji: mae ni itte ita mensetsu, dou narimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 前に言っていた面接、どうなりましたか？
examplePolite.english: How did that interview you mentioned go?

items.notes: Itteta is short for itte ita (was saying); ano ken (that thing) can fill the gap.

items.use: Shares news when catching up; say where with ni: yokohama ni hikkoshita n da.

example.romaji: jitsu wa, sengetsu yokohama ni hikkoshita n da.
example.ja: 実は、先月横浜に引っ越したんだ。
example.english: Actually, I moved to Yokohama last month.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa, sengetsu yokohama ni hikkoshita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 実は、先月横浜に引っ越したんです。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I moved to Yokohama last month.

items.notes: Hikkosu is the verb; hikkoshi is the move itself.

items.use: Shares job news when catching up; expect the follow-up doko ni? (where to?).

example.romaji: sou sou, haru ni tenshoku shita n da yo.
example.ja: そうそう、春に転職したんだよ。
example.english: Oh yeah, I changed jobs in the spring.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa, haru ni tenshoku shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 実は、春に転職したんです。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I changed jobs in the spring.

items.notes: Tenshoku means moving to a new employer; a transfer inside your company is idou or tenkin.

items.english: I ... for the first time in ages
items.use: Tells someone about doing something you hadn't done for a long time; any past verb fits the gap.

example.romaji: kinou, hisashiburi ni eigakan de eiga mita.
example.ja: 昨日、久しぶりに映画館で映画見た。
example.english: Yesterday I saw a film at the cinema for the first time in ages.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, hisashiburi ni eigakan ni ikimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、久しぶりに映画館に行きました。
examplePolite.english: Yesterday I went to the cinema for the first time in ages.

items.notes: Hisashiburi alone is 'long time no see'; with ni it goes before the verb.

blocks.label: Weather and seasons
blocks.rationale: Make the easy seasonal small talk Japanese conversations open with.
blocks.interference: mushiatsui (humid) vs atsui (hot).

items.use: Seasonal small talk in early autumn with neighbours, coworkers, anyone; just agree with sou da ne.
items.kana: すずしくなってきたね
items.politeJa: 涼しくなってきましたね

example.romaji: asaban, daibu suzushiku natte kita ne.
example.ja: 朝晩、だいぶ涼しくなってきたね。
example.english: It's really getting cooler in the mornings and evenings.

examplePolite.romaji: asaban, daibu suzushiku natte kimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 朝晩、だいぶ涼しくなってきましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's really getting cooler in the mornings and evenings.

items.notes: Swap the adjective for other seasons: atsuku natte kita ne (getting hot), samuku natte kita ne (getting cold).

items.english: it's been nothing but rain, huh
items.use: Weather small talk in the June rainy season or any wet week; answer hontou ni ne.

example.romaji: saikin ame bakkari da ne. sentakumono ga kawakanai.
example.ja: 最近雨ばっかりだね。洗濯物が乾かない。
example.english: It's been nothing but rain lately. The laundry won't dry.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin ame bakari desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 最近雨ばかりですね。
examplePolite.english: It's been raining a lot lately, hasn't it.

items.notes: Bakkari works with any noun: shigoto bakkari, 'nothing but work'.

items.use: A go-to summer opener with neighbours, coworkers or anyone; just agree with it.

example.romaji: kyou mo mushiatsui ne. ase ga tomaranai.
example.ja: 今日も蒸し暑いね。汗が止まらない。
example.english: Muggy again today, huh. I can't stop sweating.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou mo mushiatsui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日も蒸し暑いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's humid again today, isn't it.

items.notes: Plain atsui is just hot; mushiatsui is hot and sticky, the normal Japanese summer.

items.english: the temperature's all over the place, huh
items.use: Small talk in spring or autumn, when days are warm and mornings cold.
items.politeJa: 寒暖差がすごいですね

example.romaji: kandansa sugoi ne. asa samukute hiru atsui.
example.ja: 寒暖差すごいね。朝寒くて昼暑い。
example.english: The temperature's all over the place. Cold mornings, hot afternoons.

examplePolite.romaji: kandansa ga sugoi desu ne. kaze ni ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 寒暖差がすごいですね。風邪に気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: The temperature's swinging a lot. Take care not to catch a cold.

items.notes: Often followed by kaze hikanai you ni ne, 'don't catch a cold'.

items.use: Common spring small talk, since many people in Japan suffer from cedar pollen.

example.romaji: kafunshou aru? kotoshi hidoi rashii yo.
example.ja: 花粉症ある？今年ひどいらしいよ。
example.english: Do you get hay fever? They say it's bad this year.

examplePolite.romaji: kafunshou wa arimasu ka? kotoshi wa hidoi rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 花粉症はありますか？今年はひどいらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Do you get hay fever? Apparently it's bad this year.

items.notes: To say you have it: kafunshou nan da, or politely kafunshou desu.

blocks.label: Uh-huh I'm listening
blocks.rationale: Shows you're following while your friend talks.
blocks.interference: fuun can sound bored if overused, and hai-hai can sound dismissive.

items.use: Said softly and often while a friend talks, to show you're following.

example.romaji: un un, sore de dou natta no?
example.ja: うんうん、それでどうなったの？
example.english: Uh-huh, and then what happened?

items.notes: In polite talk use hai or ee; hai hai can sound impatient.

items.use: A listener's 'I see', but it can sound unimpressed or doubtful.

example.romaji: fuun, sou nan da.
example.ja: ふーん、そうなんだ。
example.english: Hmm, is that right.

items.notes: To elders say naruhodo or sou nan desu ne; fuun can sound rude.

items.use: A quick double yes; drawn out, it brushes someone off.

example.romaji: hai hai, wakatta yo.
example.ja: はいはい、わかったよ。
example.english: Yeah, yeah, I get it.

items.notes: Said quick and bright it's a friendly 'yes, yes', even on the phone; never drawn out to a superior.

blocks.label: Really seriously
blocks.rationale: Reacts with surprise to news so the teller keeps going.
blocks.interference: ee needs a rising pitch or it sounds like a polite 'yes'; uso desho isn't calling them a liar.

items.use: A drawn-out reaction to surprising news, or a mild protest when asked to do something.

example.romaji: ee! mou kaeru no?
example.ja: えー！もう帰るの？
example.english: What? You're leaving already?

examplePolite.romaji: ee! mou kaeru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: えー！もう帰るんですか？
examplePolite.english: What? You're leaving already?

items.notes: A short, flat ee means 'yes' in polite speech; surprise is long and rising.

items.use: Said with a rising tone while someone tells you news, to show interest and invite more.

example.romaji: e, sou na no? zenzen shiranakatta.
example.ja: え、そうなの？全然知らなかった。
example.english: Oh, really? I had no idea.

examplePolite.romaji: e, sou na n desu ka? zenzen shirimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: え、そうなんですか？全然知りませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Oh, really? I had no idea.

items.notes: Said flat and falling, sou na n da means 'oh, I see' rather than asking.

items.use: Casual reaction to surprising news, often muttered to yourself.

example.romaji: maji ka, mou urikire?
example.ja: マジか、もう売り切れ？
example.english: Seriously? Sold out already?

items.notes: maji de? asks 'for real?'; politely say hontou desu ka.

items.use: Disbelief at news you don't want to be true.

example.romaji: uso desho? mou owari?
example.ja: うそでしょ？もう終わり？
example.english: You're kidding. It's over already?

items.notes: It doesn't call anyone a liar; politely, say hontou desu ka.

blocks.label: Oh I didn't know
blocks.rationale: Acknowledges new information or a sudden understanding.
blocks.interference: sou datta n da takes in news; sou iu koto ka means it finally clicked.

items.english: oh, so that's what it was; I had no idea
items.use: Said when someone's explanation clears up something you'd wondered about.

example.romaji: sou datta n da. dakara kinou inakatta n da ne.
example.ja: そうだったんだ。だから昨日いなかったんだね。
example.english: Oh, I see. So that's why you weren't there yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: sou datta n desu ne. dakara kinou inakatta n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうだったんですね。だから昨日いなかったんですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I see. So that's why you weren't there yesterday.

items.notes: Sou na n da reacts to plain new info; datta adds 'that explains it'.

items.english: I didn't know (that); I had no idea
items.use: React to news or a fact that surprises you, often after e, honto?

example.romaji: e, kekkon shita no? zenzen shiranakatta!
example.ja: え、結婚したの？全然知らなかった！
example.english: What, you got married? I had no idea!

examplePolite.romaji: e, kekkon sareta n desu ka? zenzen shirimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: え、結婚されたんですか？全然知りませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Oh, you got married? I had no idea.

items.notes: shiranai (present) is 'I don't know'; use the past for news you've just heard.

items.english: oh, so that's it; now I get it
items.use: Said when something finally makes sense, often half to yourself.

example.romaji: aa, sou iu koto ka! yatto wakatta.
example.ja: ああ、そういうことか！やっと分かった。
example.english: Oh, so that's it! I finally get it.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, sou iu koto desu ne. yatto wakarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、そういうことですね。やっと分かりました。
examplePolite.english: Ah, so that's what it is. Now I understand.

items.notes: Close to naruhodo; the ka falls, so it isn't a question.

items.use: Said when you check and see that what someone told you is true.

example.romaji: a, honto da. ame futteru.
example.ja: あ、ほんとだ。雨降ってる。
example.english: Oh, you're right. It's raining.

examplePolite.romaji: a, hontou desu ne. ame ga futte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、本当ですね。雨が降っています。
examplePolite.english: Oh, so it is. It's raining.

items.notes: hontou? (really?) asks; honto da confirms.

items.english: I didn't notice; I didn't realize
items.use: When you missed something right in front of you; also an apology for an oversight.

example.romaji: gomen, kiteta no? zenzen kizukanakatta.
example.ja: ごめん、来てたの？全然気づかなかった。
example.english: Sorry, you were here? I didn't notice at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, irasshatta n desu ka. zenzen kizukimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、いらっしゃったんですか。全然気づきませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, you were here? I didn't notice at all.

items.notes: shiranakatta is for facts you didn't know; kizukanakatta is for things you failed to see.

blocks.label: So true so relatable
blocks.rationale: Signals you share the feeling or experience they describe.
blocks.interference: aru aru means 'that happens', wakaru wakaru means 'I feel that'.

items.english: I know, I know; I totally get it
items.use: Sympathy when a friend describes a feeling or situation you've had too.

example.romaji: wakaru wakaru, getsuyoubi tte honto ni darui yo ne.
example.ja: わかるわかる、月曜日ってほんとにだるいよね。
example.english: I know, right? Mondays are such a drag.

items.notes: It means 'I feel the same', not 'I understand your words'.

items.use: Young people's reply when a friend says exactly what you were thinking.

example.romaji: sore na. ano eiga, maji de nagakatta.
example.ja: それな。あの映画、マジで長かった。
example.english: So true. That movie was seriously long.

items.notes: Sounds young and online; sou da yo ne is the safe everyday version.

items.use: Said when someone describes a familiar everyday mishap that happens to everyone.

example.romaji: eki norisugosu no, aru aru da yo ne.
example.ja: 駅乗り過ごすの、あるあるだよね。
example.english: Missing your stop is such a classic.

items.notes: Also a noun: X aru aru means typical X moments, like ryuugakusei aru aru.

blocks.label: Sounds fun looks good
blocks.rationale: Comments on what someone describes, shows or serves you.
blocks.interference: -sou guesses from outside; oishisou is before eating, oishikatta after.

items.use: Reacting to someone's plans or photos.

example.romaji: kyanpu iku no? tanoshisou!
example.ja: キャンプ行くの？楽しそう！
example.english: You're going camping? Sounds fun!

examplePolite.romaji: kyanpu ni iku n desu ka? tanoshisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: キャンプに行くんですか？楽しそうですね。
examplePolite.english: You're going camping? That sounds fun.

items.notes: Don't confuse with tanoshii sou da, 'I hear it's fun'.

items.use: Reacting to a film, book, idea or plan you'd like to try.

example.romaji: sono eiga, omoshirosou. kondo mite miyou.
example.ja: その映画、面白そう。今度見てみよう。
example.english: That movie looks good. I'll check it out sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: sono eiga, omoshirosou desu ne. kondo mite mimasu.
examplePolite.ja: その映画、面白そうですね。今度見てみます。
examplePolite.english: That movie looks good. I'll watch it sometime.

items.notes: Omoshiroi covers both funny and interesting; context decides.

items.english: sounds rough; that must be hard
items.use: Sympathizing when someone describes a busy or difficult situation.

example.romaji: maiban shuuden made? taihensou da ne.
example.ja: 毎晩終電まで？大変そうだね。
example.english: Until the last train every night? That sounds rough.

examplePolite.romaji: maiban shuuden made desu ka? taihensou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 毎晩終電までですか？大変そうですね。
examplePolite.english: Until the last train every night? That sounds hard.

items.notes: For something already over, taihen datta ne ('that must have been hard') fits better.

items.use: Said when food arrives or you see it, before eating; after eating say oishii or oishikatta.

example.romaji: uwa, oishisou! itadakimasu.
example.ja: うわ、おいしそう！いただきます。
example.english: Wow, that looks so good! Let's eat.

examplePolite.romaji: oishisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: おいしそうですね。
examplePolite.english: That looks delicious.

items.notes: -sou on an adjective means looks: takasou (looks expensive). Ii becomes yosasou (looks good).

items.use: Judges by looks or description, before you've tried it.

example.romaji: kono mise, yosasou da ne.
example.ja: この店、よさそうだね。
example.english: This place looks good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, yosasou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、よさそうですね。
examplePolite.english: This place looks nice.

items.notes: Not ii sou: the 'looks' form of ii is irregular.

items.use: Said after finishing a meal; to a host or staff, follow with gochisousama deshita.

example.romaji: aa, oishikatta. gochisousama!
example.ja: あー、おいしかった。ごちそうさま！
example.english: Mm, that was delicious. Thanks for the meal!

examplePolite.romaji: totemo oishikatta desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: とてもおいしかったです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: That was really delicious. Thank you for the meal.

blocks.label: Good for you
blocks.rationale: Responds warmly when a friend shares good news.
blocks.interference: ii naa is envy for them, ii jan is approval; yokatta ne is for them, yokatta alone is your own relief.

items.use: Approves of something; with a shrug it pushes 'why not, go for it'.

example.romaji: ii jan, sono fuku. niau yo.
example.ja: いいじゃん、その服。似合うよ。
example.english: Nice outfit. It suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: ii ja nai desu ka, sono fuku. niaimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いいじゃないですか、その服。似合いますよ。
examplePolite.english: That outfit's nice. It suits you.

items.notes: The 'why not' use: ii jan, ikou yo (come on, let's go).

items.english: good for you; I'm glad for you
items.use: Said when someone shares good news or a worry turns out fine.

example.romaji: goukaku shita no? yokatta ne!
example.ja: 合格したの？よかったね！
example.english: You passed? I'm so happy for you!

examplePolite.romaji: goukaku shita n desu ka? yokatta desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: 合格したんですか？よかったですね！
examplePolite.english: You passed? That's wonderful!

items.notes: Yokatta without ne is relief about your own situation: 'phew, thank goodness'.

items.english: lucky you; I'm jealous; that's nice
items.use: Wistful reaction to someone's good news or to something you wish you had.

example.romaji: ii naa, hawai iku no?
example.ja: いいなあ、ハワイ行くの？
example.english: Lucky you, you're going to Hawaii?

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne, hawai ni iku n desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: いいですね、ハワイに行くんですか。
examplePolite.english: How nice, you're going to Hawaii?

items.notes: The polite ii desu ne loses the hint of envy.

items.use: Quick praise for a good move, shot, or idea, often in sports and games.

example.romaji: naisu! ima no shuuto, sugoi yo.
example.ja: ナイス！今のシュート、すごいよ。
example.english: Nice! That shot was amazing.

examplePolite.romaji: naisu desu! ima no shuuto, sugokatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: ナイスです！今のシュート、すごかったです。
examplePolite.english: Nice! That shot was great.

items.notes: Often joined to a noun: naisu aidia (nice idea), naisu shotto.

blocks.label: And then what
blocks.rationale: Pushes a story forward to the next part.
blocks.interference: A flat sore de? sounds impatient; nani nani is eager, not suspicious.

items.use: Prompts the speaker to go on; said flat and falling, it can sound like an impatient 'so what?'.

example.romaji: sore de? kanojo wa nante itta no?
example.ja: それで？彼女は何て言ったの？
example.english: And then? What did she say?

examplePolite.romaji: sore de, kanojo wa nante itta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それで、彼女は何て言ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: And then what did she say?

items.notes: Also starts your own next step in a story: sore de, kaetta, 'so I went home'.

items.polite: nani ga atta n desu ka?
items.use: Asking with concern when someone looks upset or something is clearly wrong.

example.romaji: kaoiro warui yo. nani ga atta no?
example.ja: 顔色悪いよ。何があったの？
example.english: You look pale. What happened?

examplePolite.romaji: kaoiro ga warui desu yo. nani ga atta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔色が悪いですよ。何があったんですか？
examplePolite.english: You look pale. What happened?

items.notes: Dou shita no? ('what's wrong?') is the softer near-twin.

items.english: how did it turn out?; so what happened?
items.use: Asking for the outcome of something you heard about earlier, like an interview or a fight.

example.romaji: kinou no mensetsu, dou natta no?
example.ja: 昨日の面接、どうなったの？
example.english: How did yesterday's interview go?

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no mensetsu wa dou natta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の面接はどうなったんですか？
examplePolite.english: How did yesterday's interview go?

items.notes: Nani ga atta no? asks what happened; dou natta no? asks how it ended.

items.use: Eager reaction when you overhear something interesting and want in.

example.romaji: nani nani? nan no hanashi?
example.ja: なになに？何の話？
example.english: What, what? What are you talking about?

items.use: Asking for more items or details after someone has listed a few.

example.romaji: pan to gyuunyuu ne. hoka ni wa?
example.ja: パンと牛乳ね。他には？
example.english: Bread and milk, got it. What else?

examplePolite.romaji: pan to gyuunyuu desu ne. hoka ni wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: パンと牛乳ですね。他にはありますか？
examplePolite.english: Bread and milk. Anything else?

items.notes: Staff check you've finished ordering with ijou de yoroshii desu ka? ('will that be all?').

blocks.label: How was it
blocks.rationale: Gets someone talking about an event, trip or weekend.
blocks.interference: dou datta asks about the past; dou is about now.

items.use: Ask about a trip, test, date or meal that's over; answer tanoshikatta, yokatta, or maa maa (so-so).

example.romaji: ryokou dou datta? tanoshikatta?
example.ja: 旅行どうだった？楽しかった？
example.english: How was the trip? Was it fun?

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou wa dou deshita ka? tanoshikatta desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 旅行はどうでしたか？楽しかったですか？
examplePolite.english: How was your trip? Did you enjoy it?

items.notes: dou desu ka asks about now; dou datta asks about something finished.

items.polite: nani ga ichiban yokatta desu ka?
items.use: A follow-up after someone tells you about a trip, a concert or a meal.
items.kana: なにがいちばんよかった？
items.politeJa: 何が一番よかったですか？

example.romaji: kyouto dou datta? nani ga ichiban yokatta?
example.ja: 京都どうだった？何が一番よかった？
example.english: How was Kyoto? What was the best part?

examplePolite.romaji: kyouto wa dou deshita ka? nani ga ichiban yokatta desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 京都はどうでしたか？何が一番よかったですか？
examplePolite.english: How was Kyoto? What did you like best?

items.notes: Doko ga ichiban yokatta? asks for the best place rather than the best thing.

items.polite: dare to itta n desu ka?
items.use: Following up when someone says they went somewhere, often from curiosity about who they're seeing.

example.romaji: umi itta no? dare to itta no?
example.ja: 海行ったの？誰と行ったの？
example.english: You went to the beach? Who'd you go with?

examplePolite.romaji: umi ni itta n desu ka? dare to itta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 海に行ったんですか？誰と行ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: You went to the beach? Who did you go with?

items.notes: Hitori de ('on my own') is a common, unremarkable answer.

items.english: were you okay?; did it go all right?
items.use: Checking on someone after an event: a storm, an exam, a late train, a talk with the boss.

example.romaji: kinou no jishin, daijoubu datta?
example.ja: 昨日の地震、大丈夫だった？
example.english: Were you okay in yesterday's earthquake?

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no jishin, daijoubu deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の地震、大丈夫でしたか？
examplePolite.english: Were you all right in yesterday's earthquake?

items.notes: Daijoubu? asks about now; daijoubu datta? asks about something that's over.

blocks.label: And you your take
blocks.rationale: Turns the question back and draws out their preferences and views.
blocks.interference: sotchi wa is the casual 'you'; anata wa sounds cold.

items.use: Turns the question back to a friend after you've answered.

example.romaji: un, genki da yo. sotchi wa?
example.ja: うん、元気だよ。そっちは？
example.english: Yeah, I'm good. And you?

items.notes: Politely, use the person's name: tanaka-san wa? Anata wa? sounds stiff.

items.polite: saikin nani ni hamatte imasu ka?
items.use: A friendly way to ask about current hobbies, shows or foods.
items.kana: さいきんなににはまってる？
items.politeJa: 最近何にハマっていますか？

example.romaji: saikin nani ni hamatteru? nanka osusume aru?
example.ja: 最近何にハマってる？なんかおすすめある？
example.english: What are you into lately? Any recommendations?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin nani ni hamatte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近何にハマっていますか？
examplePolite.english: What have you been into lately?

items.notes: Hamaru means to get hooked; answer with X ni hamatteru.

items.english: which do you prefer?; which do you like better?
items.use: Asking someone to pick between two things, like dogs or cats, or summer or winter.

example.romaji: inu to neko, dotchi ga suki?
example.ja: 犬と猫、どっちが好き？
example.english: Dogs or cats, which do you like better?

examplePolite.romaji: inu to neko, dochira ga suki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 犬と猫、どちらが好きですか？
examplePolite.english: Dogs or cats, which do you prefer?

items.notes: Answer X no hou ga suki ('I prefer X'); for three or more choices, ask dore ga ichiban suki?

items.polite: doushite sou omou n desu ka?
items.use: Asking for someone's reasons, out of curiosity or to challenge them.
items.politeJa: どうしてそう思うんですか？

example.romaji: e, nande sou omou no? setsumei shite.
example.ja: え、なんでそう思うの？説明して。
example.english: Huh, why do you think so? Explain.

examplePolite.romaji: doushite sou omou n desu ka? oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どうしてそう思うんですか？教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Why do you think so? Please tell me.

items.notes: Doushite is softer than nande, so use it when politeness matters.

blocks.label: What's it like
blocks.rationale: Asks how a job, place or new situation is going.
blocks.interference: tte dou attaches to a noun ('shigoto tte dou?'); donna kanji stands alone.

items.use: Put any topic before tte to ask someone's impression of it: a new job, a place, a person.

example.romaji: atarashii apaato tte dou? hiroi?
example.ja: 新しいアパートってどう？広い？
example.english: How's the new apartment? Is it big?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii apaato wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しいアパートはどうですか？
examplePolite.english: How's the new apartment?

items.notes: Also used to suggest something: ashita tte dou? 'how about tomorrow?'

items.english: what's it like?; how's it going?
items.use: Ask for a quick impression of a place or thing, or how something is going; answer ii kanji (going well).

example.romaji: atarashii shigoto, donna kanji?
example.ja: 新しい仕事、どんな感じ？
example.english: How's the new job going?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii oshigoto, donna kanji desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しいお仕事、どんな感じですか？
examplePolite.english: How's your new job going?

items.notes: kanji here is 'feel', not the Chinese characters.

items.english: getting used to it?; settled in?
items.use: Asked of someone a few weeks into a new job, school, town or country; as a newcomer you'll hear it a lot.

example.romaji: atarashii shokuba, mou nareta?
example.ja: 新しい職場、もう慣れた？
example.english: Getting used to the new workplace?

examplePolite.romaji: nihon no seikatsu ni wa mou naremashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 日本の生活にはもう慣れましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you got used to life in Japan yet?

items.notes: Answer daibu naremashita ('pretty much') or mada desu ('not yet'). The thing goes before ni: shigoto ni nareta.

blocks.label: Asking about people
blocks.rationale: Finds out about the people in someone's life and story.
blocks.interference: nante itteta asks what they said; nante iu asks what something is called.

items.english: what's he like?; what's she like?
items.use: Asking about someone's personality or looks when they come up, like a new boss or a date.

example.romaji: atarashii joushi, donna hito?
example.ja: 新しい上司、どんな人？
example.english: What's your new boss like?

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii joushi wa donna hito desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 新しい上司はどんな人ですか？
examplePolite.english: What's your new boss like?

items.notes: When asking about someone's elder or superior, kata replaces hito: donna kata desu ka?

items.polite: dou yatte shiriatta n desu ka?
items.use: Asking a couple or a pair of friends how they met; a staple at weddings and parties.
items.ja: どうやって知り合ったの？
items.kana: どうやってしりあったの？
items.politeJa: どうやって知り合ったんですか？

example.romaji: kareshi to dou yatte shiriatta no?
example.ja: 彼氏とどうやって知り合ったの？
example.english: How did you meet your boyfriend?

examplePolite.romaji: goshujin to wa dou yatte shiriatta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ご主人とはどうやって知り合ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: How did you meet your husband?

items.notes: Common answers: shigoto de ('through work'), tomodachi no shoukai de ('through a friend'), apuri de ('on an app').

items.use: Asking what someone else said, like a boss, a doctor or a friend you're both waiting on.
items.politeJa: 何て言っていましたか？

example.romaji: kanojo, nante itteta? okotteta?
example.ja: 彼女、何て言ってた？怒ってた？
example.english: What did she say? Was she mad?

examplePolite.romaji: isha wa nante itte imashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 医者は何て言っていましたか？
examplePolite.english: What did the doctor say?

items.notes: Nante is the casual form of nan to; nante itta? asks about one remark at one moment.

blocks.label: Yes exactly
blocks.rationale: Agrees warmly with what your friend just said.
blocks.interference: sou sou confirms their point; da yo ne echoes a shared feeling.

items.use: Eager agreement when someone says what you were thinking; also opens something you just remembered.

example.romaji: sou sou, sore ga iitakatta no!
example.ja: そうそう、それが言いたかったの！
example.english: Yes, exactly, that's what I was trying to say!

examplePolite.romaji: sou sou, sore ga iitakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: そうそう、それが言いたかったんです。
examplePolite.english: Yes, exactly, that's what I was trying to say.

items.notes: A single sou desu ne is calmer agreement.

items.use: Agreeing warmly, as if you'd been thinking the same thing.

example.romaji: da yo ne, watashi mo sou omotta.
example.ja: だよね、私もそう思った。
example.english: Right? I thought so too.

examplePolite.romaji: desu yo ne, watashi mo sou omoimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ですよね、私もそう思いました。
examplePolite.english: Right? I thought so too.

items.notes: Often said as sou da yo ne; with a rising tone it asks for agreement.

items.use: A strong, slangy yes to an opinion, mostly among younger friends.

example.romaji: honto sore. watashi mo zutto sou omotteta.
example.ja: ほんとそれ。私もずっとそう思ってた。
example.english: So true. I've always thought that too.

items.notes: Often cut to just sore! with the same meaning.

items.use: Agree that something is obvious; sorya is a squeezed sore wa.

example.romaji: sorya sou da yo, juu jikan mo aruita n da kara.
example.ja: そりゃそうだよ、十時間も歩いたんだから。
example.english: Well, of course, we walked for ten hours.

items.notes: Close to sore wa sou, but means 'obviously' more than 'fair point'.

items.use: Said in frustration when someone repeats your point as their own or hasn't been listening.

example.romaji: dakara, sou itteru jan! kiite nakatta no?
example.ja: だから、そう言ってるじゃん！聞いてなかったの？
example.english: That's what I'm saying! Weren't you listening?

items.notes: Jan is a casual 'isn't it'; here it sounds pushy, so keep it for friends.

blocks.label: Me too I agree
blocks.rationale: Says you share their view or experience.
blocks.interference: 'me neither' is watashi mo + a negative verb, not watashi mo alone; sono toori is a bit formal.

items.use: Saying the same goes for you; men often say boku mo or ore mo instead.

example.romaji: watashi mo kinou sore mita yo.
example.ja: 私も昨日それ見たよ。
example.english: I watched that yesterday too.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi mo kinou sore o mimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 私も昨日それを見ました。
examplePolite.english: I watched that yesterday too.

items.notes: It also covers 'me neither' after a negative statement.

items.use: Agree with an opinion; sou omowanai is 'I don't think so'.

example.romaji: un, watashi mo sou omou.
example.ja: うん、私もそう思う。
example.english: Yeah, I think so too.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, watashi mo sou omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: はい、私もそう思います。
examplePolite.english: Yes, I think so too.

items.notes: Usually with mo: watashi mo sou omou, 'I think so too'.

items.use: A short, slightly firm way to back someone's opinion.

example.romaji: doukan. ano eiga wa nagasugita yo ne.
example.ja: 同感。あの映画は長すぎたよね。
example.english: Agreed. That movie was way too long.

examplePolite.romaji: doukan desu. ano eiga wa nagasugimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 同感です。あの映画は長すぎましたね。
examplePolite.english: I agree. That movie was far too long.

items.notes: It agrees with an opinion; for a shared fact or experience, say watashi mo.

items.use: Confirms that someone's guess or statement is correct.

example.romaji: sou, sono toori. yoku wakatta ne.
example.ja: そう、そのとおり。よくわかったね。
example.english: Yes, exactly. Good, you got it.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, sono toori desu.
examplePolite.ja: はい、そのとおりです。
examplePolite.english: Yes, that's exactly right.

items.notes: Sounds a bit firm, like a teacher; in chat sou sou or sou da yo is more common.

blocks.label: OK got it
blocks.rationale: Accepts a suggestion or confirms you understood.
blocks.interference: wakarimashita is polite; ryoukai can sound curt to elders.

items.use: Casual yes to a plan or request; with a rising tone it asks 'okay?'.

example.romaji: okkee, ja ashita kuji ne.
example.ja: オッケー、じゃ明日九時ね。
example.english: OK, nine tomorrow then.

examplePolite.romaji: okkee desu. ja, ashita kuji ni onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: オッケーです。じゃ、明日九時にお願いします。
examplePolite.english: OK. Nine tomorrow, then.

items.notes: okkee desu is fine with coworkers; to a boss or client say wakarimashita.

items.use: Quick okay to a plan or instruction, very common in texts between friends and coworkers.

example.romaji: ryoukai, ja eki de matteru ne.
example.ja: 了解、じゃ駅で待ってるね。
example.english: Got it, I'll wait at the station then.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoukai shimashita. eki de matte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 了解しました。駅で待っています。
examplePolite.english: Understood. I'll wait at the station.

items.notes: Some people find ryoukai shimashita too blunt for a boss; shouchi shimashita is safer upward.

items.use: A cheerful drawn-out yes, called back when someone calls your name or asks you to do something; shop staff use it too.

example.romaji: haai, ima iku kara chotto matte!
example.ja: はーい、今行くからちょっと待って！
example.english: Coming! Just a sec!

examplePolite.romaji: haai, ima sugu ikimasu!
examplePolite.ja: はーい、今すぐ行きます！
examplePolite.english: Coming, right away!

items.notes: A short hai is the plain yes; haai sounds friendly, or childish if overused.

items.use: Reassures someone that something is fine or will work.

example.romaji: mondai nai yo, ashita de ii.
example.ja: 問題ないよ、明日でいい。
example.english: No problem, tomorrow's fine.

examplePolite.romaji: mondai arimasen. ashita de daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 問題ありません。明日で大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: No problem. Tomorrow is fine.

items.notes: Not used for 'you're welcome'; for that say iie or ii yo.

items.use: Polite reply when someone explains something or asks you to do something; with friends, say wakatta.

example.romaji: hai, wakarimashita. ashita made ni yarimasu.
example.ja: はい、わかりました。明日までにやります。
example.english: Okay, understood. I'll have it done by tomorrow.

items.notes: To a boss or customer, shouchi shimashita or kashikomarimashita sounds more formal.

blocks.label: Hmm I'm not sure
blocks.rationale: Hedges instead of fully agreeing.
blocks.interference: uun can mean 'no' or just 'hmm' depending on pitch; maa ne is half agreement, not a yes.

items.use: Fills the pause while you think, or softens a no; a long, falling uun often means the answer is no.

example.romaji: uun, dou shiyou kana. mada kimete nai.
example.ja: うーん、どうしようかな。まだ決めてない。
example.english: Hmm, what should I do? I haven't decided yet.

examplePolite.romaji: uun, dou shimashou ka ne. mada kimete imasen.
examplePolite.ja: うーん、どうしましょうかね。まだ決めていません。
examplePolite.english: Hmm, what to do. I haven't decided yet.

items.notes: Said short with a drop (ううん, also uun), it means no; un alone is yeah.

items.use: A low-key yes to a compliment or a question like 'busy?', without boasting or making a fuss.

example.romaji: maa ne. chotto isogashii kedo, daijoubu.
example.ja: まあね。ちょっと忙しいけど、大丈夫。
example.english: Yeah, sort of. A bit busy, but I'm fine.

items.notes: With a smug smile it means 'of course'; politely, say maa, sou desu ne.

items.english: hmm, I'm not sure; I wonder
items.use: A gentle way to doubt something or avoid a firm answer.

example.romaji: dou darou. kare, saikin isogashii mitai da yo.
example.ja: どうだろう。彼、最近忙しいみたいだよ。
example.english: Hmm, not sure. He seems busy lately.

examplePolite.romaji: dou deshou ne. kare wa saikin isogashii mitai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: どうでしょうね。彼は最近忙しいみたいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Hard to say. He seems to be busy lately.

items.notes: Often said as dou darou ne with a tilt of the head; it usually leans toward 'probably not'.

items.use: Answering a sweeping question, like 'are Japanese people shy?', without a yes or no.

example.romaji: sore wa hito ni yoru yo. suki na hito mo iru shi.
example.ja: それは人によるよ。好きな人もいるし。
example.english: That depends on the person. Some people love it.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa hito ni yorimasu ne. suki na hito mo imasu shi.
examplePolite.ja: それは人によりますね。好きな人もいますし。
examplePolite.english: That depends on the person. Some people like it.

items.notes: Swap in any noun: basho ni yoru, 'depends on the place'; toki ni yoru, 'depends on the time'.

blocks.label: Not really
blocks.rationale: Disagrees gently by playing the claim down.
blocks.interference: sou demo nai means 'not really'; sou ja nai means 'that's wrong'.

items.use: A soft no to a question or a compliment, like 'is it hard?' or 'you must be busy'.

example.romaji: muzukashii? iya, sou demo nai yo.
example.ja: 難しい？いや、そうでもないよ。
example.english: Is it hard? Nah, not really.

examplePolite.romaji: muzukashii desu ka? iie, sou demo nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 難しいですか？いいえ、そうでもないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Is it difficult? No, not really.

items.notes: Much softer than chigau; also a modest way to brush off praise.

items.english: it's not that bad; not that much
items.use: Toning down what someone said, whether it was too gloomy or too glowing.
items.politeJa: そこまでじゃないです

example.romaji: taihen? iya, soko made ja nai yo.
example.ja: 大変？いや、そこまでじゃないよ。
example.english: Rough? Nah, it's not that bad.

examplePolite.romaji: taihen desu ka? iie, soko made ja nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大変ですか？いいえ、そこまでじゃないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Is it hard? No, it's not that bad.

items.notes: Close to sou demo nai, but it disputes how much, not whether.

items.use: Pushing back on a general claim without flatly calling it wrong.

example.romaji: takai kara oishii? sou to mo kagiranai yo.
example.ja: 高いからおいしい？そうとも限らないよ。
example.english: Pricey means tasty? Not necessarily.

examplePolite.romaji: sou to mo kagirimasen yo. yasukute oishii mise mo arimasu kara.
examplePolite.ja: そうとも限りませんよ。安くておいしい店もありますから。
examplePolite.english: Not necessarily. There are cheap places that are good too.

items.notes: The wider pattern X to wa kagiranai means 'X isn't always so'.

blocks.label: True but
blocks.rationale: Grants their point before pushing back.
blocks.interference: The trailing kedo does the disagreeing; there's no need to add demo.

items.use: Granting someone's point before giving your own view.

example.romaji: sore wa sou da kedo, ima wa okane nai yo.
example.ja: それはそうだけど、今はお金ないよ。
example.english: That's true, but I don't have the money right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa sou desu kedo, ima wa okane ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: それはそうですけど、今はお金がないんです。
examplePolite.english: That's true, but I don't have the money at the moment.

items.notes: Often trails off after kedo, letting the tone carry the 'but'.

items.english: I get how you feel, but...
items.use: Showing sympathy before disagreeing or giving advice.
items.politeJa: 気持ちはわかりますけど

example.romaji: kimochi wa wakaru kedo, ima yameru no wa mottainai yo.
example.ja: 気持ちはわかるけど、今辞めるのはもったいないよ。
example.english: I get how you feel, but quitting now would be a waste.

examplePolite.romaji: kimochi wa wakarimasu kedo, ima yameru no wa mottainai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 気持ちはわかりますけど、今辞めるのはもったいないですよ。
examplePolite.english: I understand how you feel, but it'd be a shame to quit now.

items.notes: The wa matters: you understand the feeling, not that you agree with the plan.

items.english: it's not that simple; not so fast
items.use: Push back when someone suggests an easy way out or tries to get away with something.

example.romaji: yasumitai kedo, sou wa ikanai n da yo.
example.ja: 休みたいけど、そうはいかないんだよ。
example.english: I'd love a day off, but it's not that simple.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumitai n desu kedo, sou wa ikanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 休みたいんですけど、そうはいかないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'd love a day off, but it's not that simple.

items.notes: iku here means 'go smoothly', as in umaku ikanai (it isn't going well).

blocks.label: Moving the story along
blocks.rationale: Lets you carry a story forward and signal a twist is coming.
blocks.interference: sore de sa just moves on, while sore ga sa warns that a twist is coming.

items.use: Keeps your story rolling and holds the floor between events; also brings the talk back to your point.

example.romaji: sore de sa, kare ga kyuu ni nakidashita n da yo.
example.ja: それでさ、彼が急に泣き出したんだよ。
example.english: And so, he suddenly burst into tears.

items.notes: Sa is a casual filler like 'you know' and can follow almost any phrase; 'de sa' is the short version.

items.use: Used mid-story to lead into the surprising next event; the sa holds the listener's attention.

example.romaji: soshitara sa, kyuu ni ame ga futte kita no.
example.ja: そしたらさ、急に雨が降ってきたの。
example.english: And then, out of nowhere, it started pouring.

items.notes: Soshitara also means 'in that case': soshitara, ashita ni shiyou.

items.english: well, here's the thing... (a twist is coming)
items.use: Signals that things didn't go as expected; often the answer to 'dou datta?' (how did it go?).

example.romaji: shiken? sore ga sa, zenzen dame datta.
example.ja: 試験？それがさ、全然ダメだった。
example.english: The exam? Well, here's the thing: it went terribly.

examplePolite.romaji: sore ga desu ne, mada henji ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: それがですね、まだ返事がないんです。
examplePolite.english: Well, the thing is, there's still no reply.

items.notes: Don't confuse it with 'sore de sa', which just moves on; 'sore ga' warns of a surprise.

items.english: before I knew it; next thing I knew
items.use: In a story, jumps to a result you didn't notice happening, like falling asleep or time flying.

example.romaji: ki ga tsuitara, mou asa datta.
example.ja: 気がついたら、もう朝だった。
example.english: Next thing I knew, it was already morning.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga tsuitara, sanjikan mo tatte imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 気がついたら、3時間も経っていました。
examplePolite.english: Before I knew it, three hours had gone by.

items.notes: Also said as 'ki ga tsuku to'. 'Ki ga tsuku' on its own means 'to notice'.

blocks.label: Sympathy for a hard time
blocks.rationale: Lets you show you understand when someone tells you something rough.
blocks.interference: taihen datta ne is for something over, taihen da ne for something still going; kawaisou ni can sound condescending.

items.english: that must have been hard; what an ordeal
items.use: Sympathy after someone tells you about a rough time; often followed by daijoubu?

example.romaji: sore wa taihen datta ne. mou daijoubu?
example.ja: それは大変だったね。もう大丈夫？
example.english: That must have been rough. Are you okay now?

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa taihen deshita ne. mou daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それは大変でしたね。もう大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: That must have been hard. Are you all right now?

items.notes: For something still going on, say taihen da ne (that's tough).

items.use: Said to show you understand someone's frustration or sadness, often with yo.

example.romaji: sore wa kuyashii yo ne. kimochi wakaru.
example.ja: それは悔しいよね。気持ちわかる。
example.english: That's so frustrating. I know how you feel.

examplePolite.romaji: sono kimochi, yoku wakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: その気持ち、よくわかります。
examplePolite.english: I really understand how you feel.

items.notes: Wakaru wakaru is a quick, casual I get it.

items.english: that sounds really hard; that must hurt
items.use: Sympathy for emotional pain: a breakup, a loss, a painful situation.

example.romaji: wakareta no? sore wa tsurai ne.
example.ja: 別れたの？それはつらいね。
example.english: You broke up? That must really hurt.

examplePolite.romaji: wakareta n desu ka. sore wa tsurai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 別れたんですか。それはつらいですね。
examplePolite.english: You broke up? That must be hard.

items.notes: taihen is about hassle and effort; tsurai is about pain.

items.use: Said about a person or animal in a sad situation; to someone's face it can sound pitying.

example.romaji: sono neko, kega shiteru. kawaisou ni.
example.ja: その猫、ケガしてる。かわいそうに。
example.english: That cat's hurt. Poor thing.

items.notes: Kawaisou means pitiful; don't mix it up with kawaii (cute).

blocks.label: Telling them not to worry
blocks.rationale: Lets you wave off an apology or settle someone's worry.
blocks.interference: ki ni shinaide (never mind it) and shinpai shinaide (don't worry) overlap, while zenzen daijoubu is about yourself.

items.english: don't worry about it; never mind
items.use: Said when someone apologizes or thanks you a lot, or feels bad about a mistake.
items.politeJa: 気にしないでください

example.romaji: ii yo, ki ni shinaide. dare demo machigaeru yo.
example.ja: いいよ、気にしないで。誰でも間違えるよ。
example.english: It's fine, don't worry about it. Everyone makes mistakes.

examplePolite.romaji: iie, ki ni shinaide kudasai. daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: いいえ、気にしないでください。大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: No, please don't worry about it. It's fine.

items.notes: Ki ni suru means mind or be bothered by; shinpai shinaide is about being anxious, not about minding.

items.english: totally fine; no problem at all
items.use: Reassure someone who apologizes or asks if you're okay.
items.kana: ぜんぜんだいじょうぶ

example.romaji: un, zenzen daijoubu da yo. ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: うん、全然大丈夫だよ。気にしないで。
example.english: Yeah, totally fine. Don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: hai, zenzen daijoubu desu. ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: はい、全然大丈夫です。気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Yes, totally fine. Please don't worry about it.

items.notes: Textbooks say zenzen needs a negative, but zenzen daijoubu is normal everyday speech.

items.use: Said to reassure someone about you or about a situation.
items.politeJa: 心配しないでください

example.romaji: daijoubu, shinpai shinaide. sugu kaeru kara.
example.ja: 大丈夫、心配しないで。すぐ帰るから。
example.english: I'm fine, don't worry. I'll be home soon.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai shinaide kudasai. mou genki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 心配しないでください。もう元気です。
examplePolite.english: Please don't worry. I'm fine now.

items.notes: Shinpai kakete gomen means sorry I made you worry.

items.english: it'll work out; it'll be fine somehow
items.use: Said to calm someone stressed about a problem, or to yourself.

example.romaji: sonna ni shinpai shinakute mo, nantoka naru yo.
example.ja: そんなに心配しなくても、なんとかなるよ。
example.english: No need to worry so much. It'll work out.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo. kitto nantoka narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ。きっとなんとかなりますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's okay. I'm sure it'll work out.

items.notes: Nantoka suru means manage somehow: nantoka shite! (do something!).

blocks.label: Saying you are worn out
blocks.rationale: Lets you say how tired you are when someone asks how you are.
blocks.interference: nemurenakatta (couldn't sleep) is not nemui (sleepy).

items.use: Past tense because it describes how you feel now; often a sigh at the end of the day.

example.romaji: aa, tsukareta. kyou wa hayaku neyou.
example.ja: ああ、疲れた。今日は早く寝よう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm tired. I'm going to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto tsukaremashita. hayaku nemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと疲れました。早く寝ます。
examplePolite.english: I'm a bit tired today. I'll go to bed early.

items.notes: Related: otsukare, the 'good work' greeting at the end of a job or day.

items.use: Explains why you're tired or out of it today.

example.romaji: kinou zenzen nemurenakatta. ima sugoku nemui.
example.ja: 昨日全然眠れなかった。今すごく眠い。
example.english: I couldn't sleep at all last night. I'm so sleepy now.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa amari nemuremasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はあまり眠れませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't sleep very well last night.

items.notes: nerarenakatta means the same and is just as common.

items.use: Said when tiredness, stress or patience has run out; heavier than mou muri.

example.romaji: nemukute mou genkai. saki ni neru ne.
example.ja: 眠くてもう限界。先に寝るね。
example.english: I'm too sleepy to keep going. I'm heading to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: nemukute mou genkai desu. saki ni yasumimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 眠くてもう限界です。先に休みます。
examplePolite.english: I'm too sleepy to go on. I'll turn in first.

items.notes: genkai is 'limit'; you'll hear it about overtime and deadlines too.

blocks.label: Hungry and thirsty
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you need food or a drink.
blocks.interference: hara hetta is rough and masculine; onaka suita is the neutral one.

items.use: Everyday way to say you're hungry; Japanese says it in the past form.

example.romaji: aa, onaka suita. nanika tabeyou.
example.ja: あー、お腹すいた。何か食べよう。
example.english: Ugh, I'm hungry. Let's eat something.

examplePolite.romaji: onaka sukimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: お腹すきましたね。
examplePolite.english: I'm getting hungry, aren't you?

items.notes: Ask others with onaka suiteru? (are you hungry?). Men may say hara hetta.

items.use: Soft, cute way to say you're very hungry; fine for anyone, common with kids.

example.romaji: mou onaka pekopeko, hayaku tabeyou!
example.ja: もうお腹ペコペコ、早く食べよう！
example.english: I'm starving, let's eat already!

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka pekopeko desu. hayaku tabemashou.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹ペコペコです。早く食べましょう。
examplePolite.english: I'm starving. Let's eat soon.

items.notes: Gentler than hara hetta; pekopeko is the sound-word for an empty stomach.

items.use: Literally 'my throat has dried'; the everyday way to say you want a drink.

example.romaji: nodo kawaita, nanka nomou yo.
example.ja: 喉渇いた、なんか飲もうよ。
example.english: I'm thirsty, let's get a drink.

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita ne. nanika nomimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 喉が渇きましたね。何か飲みませんか？
examplePolite.english: I'm thirsty. Shall we get something to drink?

items.notes: Past tense because it describes the state now, like tsukareta.

items.use: Blunt everyday way to say you're hungry, mostly among male friends and family.

example.romaji: aa, hara hetta. nanka tabe ni ikou.
example.ja: ああ、腹減った。なんか食べに行こう。
example.english: Man, I'm starving. Let's go grab something.

items.notes: Neutral: onaka suita. Polite: onaka ga sukimashita.

blocks.label: Didn't catch that
blocks.rationale: Asks for a repeat or slower speech when you're lost.
blocks.interference: The kudasai and onegai shimasu forms are polite; wakarimasen can mean 'I don't know'.

items.english: once more, please; could you say that again?
items.use: Ask someone to repeat what they said; staff and teachers hear it from learners all the time.
items.ja: もう一度お願いします
items.kana: もういちどおねがいします

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou ichido onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、もう一度お願いします。
example.english: Sorry, could you say that again?

items.notes: Casual: mou ikkai itte. Add yukkuri (slowly) if speed is the problem.

items.english: I didn't catch that; I couldn't hear
items.use: When noise or a quiet voice is the problem; usually followed by a request to repeat.

example.romaji: gomen, kikoenakatta. mou ikkai itte?
example.ja: ごめん、聞こえなかった。もう一回言って？
example.english: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Say it again?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kikoemasen deshita. mou ichido onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、聞こえませんでした。もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I couldn't hear. Once more, please.

items.notes: kikoeru is 'can be heard'; kiku is 'listen' or 'ask'.

items.use: Ask a fast speaker to slow down; mou sukoshi (a bit more) makes it softer.
items.ja: ゆっくり話してください
items.kana: ゆっくりはなしてください

example.romaji: sumimasen, mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、もう少しゆっくり話してください。
example.english: Sorry, could you speak a little more slowly?

items.notes: With friends, just yukkuri itte.

items.use: Own up when you zoned out, then ask them to repeat with 'mou ikkai itte'.
items.ja: ごめん、聞いてなかった
items.kana: ごめん、きいてなかった
items.politeJa: すみません、聞いていませんでした

example.romaji: gomen, kiitenakatta. mou ikkai itte?
example.ja: ごめん、聞いてなかった。もう一回言って？
example.english: Sorry, I wasn't listening. Say that again?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kiite imasen deshita. mou ichido onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、聞いていませんでした。もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I wasn't listening. Could you say it once more?

items.notes: Kiitenakatta can also mean 'nobody told me': 'sonna no kiitenakatta' is 'I wasn't told that'.

items.english: I don't understand; I don't know
items.use: Polite way to say you don't follow or can't answer; with friends, say wakannai.

example.romaji: sumimasen, nihongo ga yoku wakarimasen.
example.ja: すみません、日本語がよくわかりません。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really understand Japanese.

items.notes: For facts, shirimasen also means 'I don't know' but can sound cold; wakarimasen is softer.

blocks.label: What do you mean
blocks.rationale: Asks what or who they are referring to.
blocks.interference: nan no hanashi? can sound like denial if said sharply.

items.english: what do you mean?; what's going on?
items.use: Ask someone to explain something confusing or surprising; said sharply, it demands an explanation.

example.romaji: e, chuushi? dou iu koto?
example.ja: え、中止？どういうこと？
example.english: Wait, cancelled? What do you mean?

examplePolite.romaji: e, chuushi desu ka? dou iu koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、中止ですか？どういうことですか？
examplePolite.english: Wait, it's cancelled? What do you mean?

items.notes: dou iu imi? asks only what a word or sentence means.

items.english: what do you mean?; what are you talking about?
items.use: Asks what someone is referring to; often feigned innocence when accused of something.

example.romaji: nan no koto? watashi, nani mo shiranai yo.
example.ja: 何のこと？私、何も知らないよ。
example.english: What are you talking about? I don't know anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nan no koto desu ka? watashi wa nani mo shirimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 何のことですか？私は何も知りません。
examplePolite.english: What do you mean? I don't know anything.

items.notes: Close to nan no hanashi; nan no koto points at one thing someone mentioned.

items.use: Asked when someone mentions a person you can't place.

example.romaji: e, 'senpai' tte dare no koto?
example.ja: え、「先輩」って誰のこと？
example.english: Wait, who do you mean by 'senpai'?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sore wa dare no koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、それは誰のことですか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, who do you mean?

items.notes: 'Nan no koto?' is the same question for things: 'what do you mean?'.

items.use: Ask when you've lost the thread, or play dumb about something you'd rather not discuss.

example.romaji: e, nan no hanashi? zenzen shiranai kedo.
example.ja: え、何の話？全然知らないけど。
example.english: Huh, what are you talking about? I've no idea.

examplePolite.romaji: e, nan no hanashi desu ka? zenzen shiranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: え、何の話ですか？全然知らないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Huh, what are you talking about? I've no idea.

items.notes: Joining a group, ask nan no hanashi shiteru no? (what are you all talking about?).

blocks.label: What's the word
blocks.rationale: Buys time when a word escapes you.
blocks.interference: nan dakke recalls a thing, nante iu n dakke recalls a word; both are half to yourself.

items.use: Muttered while you try to recall something you knew, or asked so the listener reminds you.

example.romaji: ano mise no namae, nan dakke?
example.ja: あの店の名前、何だっけ？
example.english: What was that shop called again?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, onamae wa nan deshitakke?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お名前は何でしたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, what was your name again?

items.notes: -kke turns a question into 'remind me': 'itsu dakke?' (when was it again?).

items.english: what's the word for it again?
items.use: Say it out loud while you hunt for a word; people will often jump in and supply it.
items.politeJa: 何て言うんでしたっけ

example.romaji: are, nante iu n dakke? kasa no chiisai yatsu.
example.ja: あれ、何て言うんだっけ？傘の小さいやつ。
example.english: What's it called again? The little umbrella thing.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, nihongo de nante iu n deshitakke?
examplePolite.ja: これ、日本語で何て言うんでしたっけ？
examplePolite.english: What's this called in Japanese again?

items.notes: Without -kke, 'nihongo de nante iu?' simply asks how to say something in Japanese.

items.use: Fills the gap while a word escapes you and invites the listener to guess; often repeated: 'hora, are, are!'.

example.romaji: hora, are da yo, are! ano akai yatsu.
example.ja: ほら、あれだよ、あれ！あの赤いやつ。
example.english: You know, that thing! The red one.

examplePolite.romaji: hora, are desu yo. ano yuumei na mise.
examplePolite.ja: ほら、あれですよ。あの有名な店。
examplePolite.english: You know, that one. That famous shop.

items.notes: 'Are da yo, are' is the same move. Hora alone also means 'look!' or 'see?'.

items.english: in English it's...; in English you'd say...
items.use: Falls back on English when you can't find the Japanese; people will often teach you the word.

example.romaji: eigo de iu to 'deadline' na n da kedo...
example.ja: 英語で言うと「deadline」なんだけど…
example.english: In English it's 'deadline', but...

examplePolite.romaji: eigo de iu to 'deadline' desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 英語で言うと「deadline」ですね。
examplePolite.english: In English you'd say 'deadline'.

items.notes: 'Eigo de nante iu?' asks the reverse: 'what's that in English?'.

blocks.label: Hey guess what
blocks.rationale: Grabs attention to start a story or share news.
blocks.interference: ano ne and ano sa open a topic; a drawn-out ano... is just hesitation.

items.use: Soft opener before you tell someone something; common with kids and partners.

example.romaji: ano ne, kyou gakkou de omoshiroi koto atta no.
example.ja: あのね、今日学校で面白いことあったの。
example.english: You know what? Something funny happened at school today.

items.notes: ano alone is a hesitant 'um'; ano ne and ano sa announce you have something to say.

items.use: Casual opener before a question or news among friends; more direct than ano ne.

example.romaji: ano sa, ashita hima? eiga ikanai?
example.ja: あのさ、明日暇？映画行かない？
example.english: Hey, are you free tomorrow? Want to see a movie?

items.notes: With people you'd speak politely to, open with ano, sumimasen instead.

items.english: listen to this; hear me out
items.use: Grab a friend's attention before news or a rant; chotto kiite yo is more insistent.
items.politeJa: ちょっと聞いてください

example.romaji: chotto kiite! kinou sugoi koto ga atta no.
example.ja: ちょっと聞いて！昨日すごいことがあったの。
example.english: Listen to this! Something crazy happened yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kiite kudasai. kinou sugoi koto ga atta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと聞いてください。昨日すごいことがあったんです。
examplePolite.english: Listen to this. Something amazing happened yesterday.

items.notes: kiku also means 'ask': chotto kiite ii? is 'can I ask you something?'

items.use: Opens gossip or news, often as 'nee, kiita?'; say 'e, nani?' to get the rest.

example.romaji: nee, kiita? tanaka-san, kekkon suru n da tte.
example.ja: ねえ、聞いた？田中さん、結婚するんだって。
example.english: Hey, did you hear? Tanaka's getting married.

examplePolite.romaji: ano nyuusu, mou kikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: あのニュース、もう聞きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you heard the news yet?

items.notes: Kiku also means 'to ask': 'sensei ni kiita?' is 'did you ask the teacher?'.

items.use: Shares a surprising fact or bit of trivia; the reply is 'shiranakatta!' (I had no idea) or 'shitteta' (I knew).

example.romaji: shitteta? ano mise, raigetsu shimaru n da yo.
example.ja: 知ってた？あの店、来月閉まるんだよ。
example.english: Did you know? That shop's closing next month.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, shitte imashita ka? kekkou yuumei desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: これ、知っていましたか？けっこう有名ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Did you know about this? It's pretty well known.

items.notes: Past shitteta is 'did you know (before I told you)'; 'shitteru?' asks 'do you know it?'.

blocks.label: By the way
blocks.rationale: Shifts to a new topic or back to an old one.
blocks.interference: hanashi kawaru changes the topic; hanashi modoru goes back.

items.english: to change the subject; by the way
items.use: Signals a new topic; tokorode is the textbook 'by the way'.

example.romaji: hanashi kawaru kedo, raishuu no nomikai iku?
example.ja: 話変わるけど、来週の飲み会行く？
example.english: Changing the subject, are you going to next week's drinks?

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi wa kawarimasu ga, raishuu no nomikai ni ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 話は変わりますが、来週の飲み会に行きますか？
examplePolite.english: To change the subject, are you going to next week's drinks?

items.english: oh, right; oh, I just remembered
items.use: Said when something suddenly comes to mind, just before you bring it up.

example.romaji: a, sou da. kore, omiyage.
example.ja: あ、そうだ。これ、お土産。
example.english: Oh, right. This is a souvenir for you.

examplePolite.romaji: a, sou da. kore, omiyage desu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、そうだ。これ、お土産です。
examplePolite.english: Oh, right. Here's a souvenir for you.

items.notes: Not agreement: for 'that's right' say sou da ne or sou desu.

items.polite: sore de omoidashita n desu kedo
items.use: Switches to a related topic that something just said brought to mind.
items.ja: それで思い出したけど
items.kana: それでおもいだしたけど
items.politeJa: それで思い出したんですけど

example.romaji: a, sore de omoidashita kedo, kagi kaeshite.
example.ja: あ、それで思い出したけど、鍵返して。
example.english: Oh, that reminds me, give me back my key.

examplePolite.romaji: sore de omoidashita n desu kedo, raishuu no kaigi wa nanji kara desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それで思い出したんですけど、来週の会議は何時からですか？
examplePolite.english: That reminds me, what time does next week's meeting start?

items.notes: Omoidasu = to recall; 'a, omoidashita!' is 'oh, now I remember!'.

items.english: going back to what we were saying
items.use: Steers the talk back to an earlier topic after a tangent.

example.romaji: hanashi modoru kedo, ryokou itsu ni suru?
example.ja: 話戻るけど、旅行いつにする？
example.english: Going back to what we said, when shall we do the trip?

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi ga modorimasu kedo, sakki no ken wa dou narimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 話が戻りますけど、さっきの件はどうなりましたか？
examplePolite.english: Going back a bit, what happened with that earlier matter?

items.notes: The opposite move is 'hanashi kawaru kedo' (changing the subject).

blocks.label: Wrapping up
blocks.rationale: Ends a chat or call smoothly.
blocks.interference: jaa sou iu koto de settles a plan rather than just saying goodbye.

items.use: Signals you're about to leave a visit, a cafe or a party; the 'go home' part is left unsaid.

example.romaji: jaa sorosoro. ashita hayai shi.
example.ja: じゃあそろそろ。明日早いし。
example.english: Well, I should go. I've got an early start.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa sorosoro shitsurei shimasu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: ではそろそろ失礼します。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: Well, I'll be going. Thank you for the meal.

items.notes: Sorosoro alone means 'about time' or 'soon'.

items.english: I'll be in touch; I'll get back to you
items.use: Said when ending a chat or call without a fixed plan; it can also be a soft no to an invitation.

example.romaji: jaa, yotei ga wakattara mata renraku suru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、予定がわかったらまた連絡するね。
example.english: Okay, I'll get back to you once I know my plans.

examplePolite.romaji: kakunin shite, mata renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 確認して、また連絡します。
examplePolite.english: I'll check and get back to you.

items.notes: Renraku means contact; renraku shite means get in touch with me.

items.english: okay, so that's settled; right, let's go with that
items.use: Wraps up a plan or a call once things are decided, right before saying bye.
items.ja: じゃあ、そういうことで
items.kana: じゃあ、そういうことで

example.romaji: jaa, sou iu koto de. mata ashita ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、そういうことで。また明日ね。
example.english: Okay, that's settled. See you tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, sou iu koto de yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: では、そういうことでよろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Right, let's go with that, then. Thank you.

items.use: Said to warn that a call or chat may cut off soon.

example.romaji: yabai, juuden kiresou. ato de kakenaosu ne.
example.ja: やばい、充電切れそう。後でかけ直すね。
example.english: Ugh, my battery's about to die. I'll call you back.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, juuden ga kiresou desu. ato de renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、充電が切れそうです。後で連絡します。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my battery's almost dead. I'll get in touch later.

items.notes: Juuden kireta means it died; a charger is juudenki.

blocks.label: Bye for now
blocks.rationale: Lets you say goodbye to a friend you will see again soon.
blocks.interference: sayounara sounds final; mata ne is the friendly default.

items.use: The everyday goodbye between friends and family; answer with mata ne or jaa ne.

example.romaji: jaa, mata ne. kaettara renraku suru.
example.ja: じゃあ、またね。帰ったら連絡する。
example.english: Okay, see you. I'll message you when I get home.

items.notes: Jaa ne is just as common. With people you speak desu/masu to, say shitsurei shimasu instead.

items.english: see you then; bye for now
items.use: Said as you split up, often right after making plans, to someone you'll see again.

example.romaji: jaa mata, raishuu no kin'youbi ni ne.
example.ja: じゃあまた、来週の金曜日にね。
example.english: See you then, next Friday.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa mata, kin'youbi ni oai shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ではまた、金曜日にお会いしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Until Friday, then.

items.notes: With a boss or client, shitsurei shimasu is safer than dewa mata.

items.use: Said when you'll meet again the next day: classmates, coworkers, friends.

example.romaji: ja, mata ashita. chikoku shinaide ne.
example.ja: じゃ、また明日。遅刻しないでね。
example.english: See you tomorrow. Don't be late.

examplePolite.romaji: mata ashita mo yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: また明日もよろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: See you tomorrow, and thanks in advance.

items.notes: Swap in other times: mata raishuu (next week), mata ato de (later today).

items.use: When you'll meet or talk again the same day.

example.romaji: ima isogashii kara, mata ato de ne.
example.ja: 今忙しいから、また後でね。
example.english: I'm busy right now, so later, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: mata nochihodo renraku shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: また後ほど連絡します。
examplePolite.english: I'll get back to you later.

items.notes: Not for 'see you someday'; that's mata kondo or mata ne.

items.use: Light, cute goodbye among friends and to kids, usually with a wave.

example.romaji: baibai! mata asobou ne.
example.ja: バイバイ！また遊ぼうね。
example.english: Bye! Let's hang out again.

items.notes: Adults say it too, women more than men; never to a boss or customer.

blocks.label: Saying hi
blocks.rationale: Lets you greet a friend or someone you run into.
blocks.interference: doumo means both hi and thanks.

items.use: A bright, playful hello to a close friend, often with a wave across a room or at the start of a call or message.

example.romaji: yahhoo! gomen ne, chotto okureta.
example.ja: やっほー！ごめんね、ちょっと遅れた。
example.english: Hiya! Sorry, I'm a bit late.

items.notes: Sounds cheerful and a little cute; more common from women and young people. Also the shout people give from a mountaintop.

items.english: I missed you; I wanted to see you
items.use: Said on meeting a friend, partner or family member after time apart; the usual answer is 'watashi mo!' (me too).
items.politeJa: お会いしたかったです

example.romaji: hisashiburi! zutto aitakatta yo.
example.ja: 久しぶり！ずっと会いたかったよ。
example.english: Long time no see! I've really missed you.

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. zutto oai shitakatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。ずっとお会いしたかったです。
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. I've been wanting to see you.

items.notes: Japanese has no direct 'I miss you': past aitakatta covers the reunion, while 'aitai' (I want to see you) is for while you're still apart.

items.use: A quick thanks to staff or someone holding a door; also a nod-like hi to someone you half know.

example.romaji: doumo, hontou ni tasukatta yo.
example.ja: どうも、本当に助かったよ。
example.english: Thanks, that really helped.

examplePolite.romaji: doumo, hontou ni tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: どうも、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you, that really helped.

items.notes: Alone it can sound curt; doumo arigatou or doumo sumimasen is fuller.

items.use: Hello from about sunset on, to neighbours, shop staff or people you don't know well.

example.romaji: konbanwa! mada mise aiteru?
example.ja: こんばんは！まだ店開いてる？
example.english: Evening! Is the shop still open?

examplePolite.romaji: konbanwa. mada aite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こんばんは。まだ開いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Good evening. Are you still open?

items.notes: Close friends and family don't say it to each other.

items.use: A neighbour's greeting when they see you leaving; it isn't really asking where, so answer vaguely.

example.romaji: a, ohayou gozaimasu. odekake desu ka?
example.ja: あ、おはようございます。お出かけですか？
example.english: Oh, good morning. Off out?

items.notes: The stock answer is ee, chotto soko made (just up the road).

blocks.label: Thanking a friend
blocks.rationale: Lets you thank someone casually for a favour.
blocks.interference: warui ne here means thanks, I owe you, not "that's bad".

items.use: Jokey, light thanks among friends, from the English.

example.romaji: sankyuu! ato de okane kaesu ne.
example.ja: サンキュー！後でお金返すね。
example.english: Thanks! I'll pay you back later.

items.notes: Never to superiors or strangers.

items.english: thanks a lot; thank you very much
items.use: Warmer than plain arigatou, to friends, family or someone younger.
items.politeJa: どうもありがとうございます

example.romaji: purezento, doumo arigatou. sugoku ureshii.
example.ja: プレゼント、どうもありがとう。すごく嬉しい。
example.english: Thanks so much for the present. I love it.

examplePolite.romaji: purezento, doumo arigatou gozaimasu. taisetsu ni shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: プレゼント、どうもありがとうございます。大切にします。
examplePolite.english: Thank you so much for the present. I'll treasure it.

items.english: that really helped; you saved me
items.use: Thanks that stresses the relief someone gave you, like lending you something or covering for you.

example.romaji: kasa kashite kurete, hontou ni tasukatta yo.
example.ja: 傘貸してくれて、本当に助かったよ。
example.english: Thanks for lending me the umbrella, it really saved me.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o kashite kudasatte, hontou ni tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 傘を貸してくださって、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for lending me the umbrella, it really helped.

items.notes: Also 'phew, saved' after a close call. Tasukaru (present) accepts an offer: sou shite kureru to tasukaru.

items.english: sorry for the trouble; thanks, I owe you
items.use: Said to a friend who does you a favour or goes out of their way, mixing thanks with apology; they answer 'ii yo, ii yo'.

example.romaji: ogotte moratte warui ne.
example.ja: おごってもらって悪いね。
example.english: Thanks for treating me. I owe you.

examplePolite.romaji: iroiro tetsudatte moratte, sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: いろいろ手伝ってもらって、すみません。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for all your help, and sorry for the trouble.

items.notes: More common from men and older speakers; 'gomen ne, arigatou' does the same job.

items.use: Thanks for something now finished, like a meal, a lesson or a favour; shop staff say it as you leave.
items.ja: ありがとうございました
items.kana: ありがとうございました

example.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni arigatou gozaimashita.
example.ja: 今日は本当にありがとうございました。
example.english: Thank you so much for today.

items.notes: Arigatou gozaimasu is for help now or still going on; with friends, just arigatou.

blocks.label: Saying sorry
blocks.rationale: Lets you apologise to a friend, lightly or properly.
blocks.interference: gomen gomen is light, and suman is masculine.

items.use: Quick, breezy apology to a friend for something small, like being a bit late.

example.romaji: gomen gomen, densha okureta.
example.ja: ごめんごめん、電車遅れた。
example.english: Sorry, sorry, my train was late.

items.notes: Too light for anything serious; it can sound like you don't care.

items.use: A sincere personal apology to family, friends or a partner; children use it with anyone.

example.romaji: gomen nasai, kinou no yakusoku wasureteta.
example.ja: ごめんなさい、昨日の約束忘れてた。
example.english: I'm sorry, I forgot our plans yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: gomen nasai, kinou no yakusoku o wasurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: ごめんなさい、昨日の約束を忘れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I forgot about yesterday's appointment.

items.notes: Gomen alone is the casual short form. At work or with strangers, sumimasen fits better.

items.english: it was my fault; my bad
items.use: A sincere apology that takes the blame, usually after an argument; often paired with 'gomen'.

example.romaji: gomen, watashi ga warukatta. mou shinai.
example.ja: ごめん、私が悪かった。もうしない。
example.english: Sorry, it was my fault. I won't do it again.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ken wa watashi ga warukatta desu. sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: この件は私が悪かったです。すみません。
examplePolite.english: This was my fault. I'm sorry.

items.notes: Men often say 'ore ga warukatta'. Stronger than plain 'gomen' because it admits fault.

items.use: Quick apology from men to friends or juniors; also a gruff thanks.

example.romaji: suman, okureta. densha ga tomatteta.
example.ja: すまん、遅れた。電車が止まってた。
example.english: Sorry I'm late. The train had stopped.

items.notes: Never to a superior. Sumanai is an older, stiffer version.

blocks.label: Ending a hangout
blocks.rationale: Lets you wrap up time together warmly and stay in touch.
blocks.interference: tsuitara rain shite (text me when you get home) and rain shite (message me) differ only by the first word.

items.use: Said when parting after time together, and often again by text that night; reply 'kochira koso' (likewise).
items.politeJa: 今日はありがとうございました

example.romaji: kyou wa arigatou. sugoku tanoshikatta.
example.ja: 今日はありがとう。すごく楽しかった。
example.english: Thanks for today. I had a great time.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当にありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you so much for today.

items.notes: The polite form uses past gozaimashita because the event is over.

items.use: A warm goodbye between friends after spending time together.

example.romaji: kyou tanoshikatta! mata asobou ne.
example.ja: 今日楽しかった！また遊ぼうね。
example.english: Today was fun! Let's hang out again.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tanoshikatta desu. mata asobimashou ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は楽しかったです。また遊びましょうね。
examplePolite.english: Today was fun. Let's get together again.

items.notes: Asobu covers adults hanging out, not just kids playing.

items.use: Said to someone heading home, especially at night or in bad weather; answer un, arigatou.
items.kana: きをつけてかえってね
items.politeJa: 気をつけてお帰りください

example.romaji: mou kurai kara, ki o tsukete kaette ne.
example.ja: もう暗いから、気をつけて帰ってね。
example.english: It's dark now, so get home safe.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga tsuyoi node, ki o tsukete okaeri kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 雨が強いので、気をつけてお帰りください。
examplePolite.english: It's raining hard, so get home safely.

items.notes: Ki o tsukete alone means take care, or watch out.

items.english: text me when you get home
items.use: Said when parting at night so you know they got home safe; answer 'un, suru ne'.
items.politeJa: 着いたらLINEしてください

example.romaji: ki o tsukete ne. tsuitara rain shite.
example.ja: 気をつけてね。着いたらLINEして。
example.english: Get home safe. Text me when you're back.

examplePolite.romaji: otsukaresama deshita. tsuitara rain shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: お疲れさまでした。着いたらLINEしてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for today. Please message me when you get home.

items.notes: LINE is Japan's main messaging app, so 'rain suru' means 'to text'; 'renraku shite' (get in touch) works for any app.

items.use: LINE is Japan's main messaging app; said at a goodbye or when you want an update.

example.romaji: tsuitara rain shite ne.
example.ja: 着いたらLINEしてね。
