example.english: Message me when you get there.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara rain kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったらLINEください。
examplePolite.english: Message me if anything comes up.

items.notes: LINE works as a suru verb: rain suru, rain shita. Meeru shite is the older email version.

blocks.label: Replying to thanks
blocks.rationale: Lets you brush off thanks or praise.
blocks.interference: douitashimashite sounds stiff between friends; ie ie is the natural reply.

items.use: The everyday reply to thanks, an apology or praise; friendly and fits almost anyone.

example.romaji: ie ie, ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: いえいえ、気にしないで。
example.english: No, no, don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: ie ie, ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いえいえ、気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Not at all, please don't worry about it.

items.notes: Far more common in real life than douitashimashite.

items.english: we're in the same boat; no need to thank me
items.use: Your reply when someone thanks you or apologizes for a favour: we all help each other, so don't worry.

example.romaji: ki ni shinaide. otagaisama da yo.
example.ja: 気にしないで。お互い様だよ。
example.english: Don't worry about it. We all help each other out.

examplePolite.romaji: iie, komatta toki wa otagaisama desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いいえ、困った時はお互い様ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Not at all, we all need help sometimes.

items.notes: Also said when both sides share the blame or the hardship: 'it's the same for both of us'.

items.english: not at all (reply to thanks or praise); outrageous
items.use: A humble brush-off of thanks or praise, stronger than ie ie.

example.romaji: tondemonai, tasukerareta no wa kotchi da yo.
example.ja: とんでもない、助けられたのはこっちだよ。
example.english: Not at all, you're the one who helped me.

examplePolite.romaji: tondemonai desu. kochira koso tasukarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: とんでもないです。こちらこそ助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Not at all. You helped me more.

items.notes: Before a noun it means outrageous or terrible: tondemonai koto ni natta (things got crazy).

items.use: The textbook reply to thanks; real speakers often prefer ie ie, which sounds less stiff.

example.romaji: douitashimashite. mata nanka attara itte ne.
example.ja: どういたしまして。またなんかあったら言ってね。
example.english: You're welcome. Let me know if you need anything else.

examplePolite.romaji: douitashimashite. mata nanika attara itsu demo itte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どういたしまして。また何かあったらいつでも言ってください。
examplePolite.english: You're welcome. Just ask anytime you need something.

items.notes: Can sound as if you agree you did a big favour.

blocks.label: What to call each other
blocks.rationale: Lets you settle names and casual speech when you first meet.
blocks.interference: ... tte yonde (call me ...) is not yonde (read it).

items.polite: nan to oyobi sureba ii desu ka?
items.use: Asked on first meeting to settle a name or nickname; answer with '... tte yonde'.
items.politeJa: 何とお呼びすればいいですか？

example.romaji: kore kara yoroshiku. nante yobeba ii?
example.ja: これからよろしく。なんて呼べばいい？
example.english: Nice to meet you. What should I call you?

examplePolite.romaji: hajimemashite. nan to oyobi sureba ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: はじめまして。何とお呼びすればいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Nice to meet you. How should I address you?

items.notes: The polite version uses humble o-yobi suru, which suits anyone senior to you.

items.use: Tells someone the name or nickname you want; the answer to 'nante yobeba ii?'.

example.romaji: tomo tte yonde. minna sou yonderu kara.
example.ja: トモって呼んで。みんなそう呼んでるから。
example.english: Call me Tomo. Everyone does.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no koto wa mai tte yonde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 私のことはマイって呼んでください。
examplePolite.english: Please call me Mai.

items.notes: Whether to add -san, -chan or -kun is usually left to the other person.

items.english: you can talk casually with me
items.use: Invites someone to drop desu/masu; often said on finding out you're the same age.

example.romaji: onaidoshi da shi, tameguchi de ii yo.
example.ja: 同い年だし、タメ口でいいよ。
example.english: We're the same age, so you can talk casually.

examplePolite.romaji: onaidoshi desu kara, tameguchi de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 同い年ですから、タメ口でいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: We're the same age, so feel free to talk casually.

items.notes: Tameguchi = casual talk between equals. With someone older, wait for this cue before dropping desu/masu.

blocks.label: Studies and job hunting
blocks.rationale: Talk about what you study or that you're between jobs.
blocks.interference: ryuugaku (study abroad) vs ryokou (travel).

items.english: what's your major?; what are you studying?
items.use: Asked of university students; answer with the subject (keizai, nihon bungaku).

example.romaji: daigakusei na n da. senkou wa?
example.ja: 大学生なんだ。専攻は？
example.english: Oh, you're at uni. What are you studying?

examplePolite.romaji: daigakusei na n desu ne. senkou wa nan desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大学生なんですね。専攻は何ですか？
examplePolite.english: So you're a university student. What's your major?

items.notes: Nani benkyou shiteru no? asks the same more casually.

items.polite: daigaku de ... o benkyou shite imasu
items.use: Answer to senkou wa?; ... o senkou shiteru (I major in ...) is a bit more formal.
items.kana: だいがくで〜をべんきょうしてる
items.politeJa: 大学で〜を勉強しています

example.romaji: daigaku de keizai o benkyou shiteru yo.
example.ja: 大学で経済を勉強してるよ。
example.english: I'm studying economics at uni.

examplePolite.romaji: daigaku de keizai o benkyou shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 大学で経済を勉強しています。
examplePolite.english: I'm studying economics at university.

items.notes: Casual speech often drops the o: keizai benkyou shiteru.

items.english: I'm here studying abroad; I'm an exchange student
items.use: Says you're in Japan to study; the school or country takes ni (... ni ryuugaku shiteru).

example.romaji: ima toukyou no daigaku ni ryuugaku shiteru n da.
example.ja: 今東京の大学に留学してるんだ。
example.english: I'm on exchange at a university in Tokyo.

examplePolite.romaji: ima toukyou no daigaku ni ryuugaku shite iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今東京の大学に留学しているんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm studying abroad at a university in Tokyo.

items.notes: Ryuugakusei is the person: an international student.

items.english: I'm job hunting at the moment; I'm between jobs
items.use: A light way to say you're not working right now; ima wa marks it as temporary.
items.kana: いまはしごとさがしちゅう

example.romaji: kaisha yamete, ima wa shigoto sagashichuu.
example.ja: 会社辞めて、今は仕事探し中。
example.english: I quit my job, and now I'm looking for work.

examplePolite.romaji: kaisha o yamete, ima wa shigoto sagashichuu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 会社を辞めて、今は仕事探し中です。
examplePolite.english: I left my company, and I'm looking for work now.

items.notes: -chuu means 'in the middle of': kaigichuu (in a meeting).

blocks.label: Age and birth year
blocks.rationale: Work out ages, which Japanese friends often check early.
blocks.interference: nannen umare (what year born) vs nannen (how many years).

items.use: Asked among people of about the same age to work out who's older; with an older adult use oikutsu desu ka?, or don't ask.

example.romaji: toshi ikutsu? onaji gurai da yo ne?
example.ja: 年いくつ？同じぐらいだよね？
example.english: How old are you? We're about the same, right?

examplePolite.romaji: shitsurei desu kedo, oikutsu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 失礼ですけど、おいくつですか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry to ask, but how old are you?

items.notes: Nansai? asks the same and is just as common among friends; ikutsu? alone works too.

items.use: Said happily on finding out you're the same age, which often means you can drop polite speech.

example.romaji: e, kyuujuuhachinen? onaidoshi da!
example.ja: え、98年？同い年だ！
example.english: Wait, '98? We're the same age!

examplePolite.romaji: e, kyuujuuhachinen desu ka? onaidoshi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: え、98年ですか？同い年ですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, '98? We're the same age.

items.notes: Next you'll often hear tamego de ii yo (let's drop the polite speech).

items.use: A softer way to ask someone's age; answer with the year (kyuujuuhachinen umare).

example.romaji: nannen umare? watashi kyuujuuhachinen.
example.ja: 何年生まれ？私98年。
example.english: What year were you born? I'm '98.

examplePolite.romaji: nannen umare desu ka? watashi wa kyuujuuhachinen desu.
examplePolite.ja: 何年生まれですか？私は98年です。
examplePolite.english: What year were you born? I was born in '98.

items.notes: Japanese also count in era years (heisei juunen) and by zodiac animal.

items.use: A classic small-talk question; many Japanese link blood type to personality, so expect comments on your answer.

example.romaji: nee, ketsuekigata wa? ee gata desho?
example.ja: ねえ、血液型は？A型でしょ？
example.english: Hey, what's your blood type? You're type A, right?

examplePolite.romaji: ketsuekigata wa nan desu ka? watashi wa oo gata desu.
examplePolite.ja: 血液型は何ですか？私はO型です。
examplePolite.english: What's your blood type? I'm type O.

items.notes: Answer with the letter + gata (ee gata, bii gata, oo gata, eebii gata); not knowing is fine.

blocks.label: Partner kids and pets
blocks.rationale: Ask about someone's household beyond their parents and siblings.
blocks.interference: katteru here means keeping a pet (飼う), not buying (買う).

items.use: Asked fairly freely in Japan; answer shiteru, shitenai, or mada (not yet).

example.romaji: kekkon shiteru? yubiwa shiteru kara.
example.ja: 結婚してる？指輪してるから。
example.english: Are you married? I noticed the ring.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon shite imasu ka? yubiwa o shite iru node.
examplePolite.ja: 結婚していますか？指輪をしているので。
examplePolite.english: Are you married? I noticed your ring.

items.notes: Use -te iru for being married now; kekkon shita means 'got married'.

items.use: Usually follows kekkon shiteru?; answer with the number (futari iru) or inai.

example.romaji: kodomo iru? nansai gurai?
example.ja: 子供いる？何歳ぐらい？
example.english: Do you have kids? How old are they?

examplePolite.romaji: okosan wa imasu ka? nansai gurai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お子さんはいますか？何歳ぐらいですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have children? How old are they?

items.notes: Okosan is someone else's child; for your own say kodomo.

items.use: Small-talk question; answer with the animal + katteru (neko katteru).
items.politeJa: ペットを飼っていますか？

example.romaji: petto katteru? inu toka neko toka.
example.ja: ペット飼ってる？犬とか猫とか。
example.english: Got any pets? A dog or a cat or something?

examplePolite.romaji: petto o katte imasu ka? inu toka neko toka.
examplePolite.ja: ペットを飼っていますか？犬とか猫とか。
examplePolite.english: Do you have any pets? A dog or a cat?

items.notes: Kau here is 'keep' (an animal), which sounds the same as kau 'buy'.

blocks.label: Polite first-meeting questions
blocks.rationale: Recognise the formal versions people use with a stranger.
blocks.interference: These are polite forms; among friends doko kara kita no replaces dochira kara desu ka.

items.use: Short way to ask a name, e.g. at a reception or to a child; answer with your name plus desu.

example.romaji: kawaii ne. onamae wa?
example.ja: かわいいね。お名前は？
example.english: So cute. What's your name?

examplePolite.romaji: shitsurei desu ga, onamae wa nan desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 失礼ですが、お名前は何ですか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, but may I ask your name?

items.notes: The o- is only for other people's names; your own is just namae.

items.use: Polite question to someone new about their country or town; answer with the place plus kara desu.

example.romaji: nihongo ojouzu desu ne. dochira kara desu ka?
example.ja: 日本語お上手ですね。どちらからですか？
example.english: Your Japanese is great. Where are you from?

items.notes: Casually: doko kara kita no? It can also mean where have you come from today.

items.use: Opens a personal or awkward question to someone you don't know well, like their name, age or company.

example.romaji: shitsurei desu ga, otoshi wa oikutsu desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼ですが、お年はおいくつですか？
example.english: Excuse me for asking, but how old are you?

items.notes: Not for getting someone's attention; use sumimasen for that.

blocks.label: Getting into their hobby
blocks.rationale: Show interest in trying their hobby or pull them into yours.
blocks.interference: yatte mitai means want to try, not want to see.

items.english: I'd like to give it a try too
items.use: Shows interest when someone describes their hobby; often followed by kondo oshiete.
items.kana: わたしもやってみたい
items.politeJa: 私もやってみたいです

example.romaji: e, tanoshisou! watashi mo yatte mitai.
example.ja: え、楽しそう！私もやってみたい。
example.english: Oh, that sounds fun! I'd like to try it too.

examplePolite.romaji: tanoshisou desu ne! watashi mo yatte mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 楽しそうですね！私もやってみたいです。
examplePolite.english: That sounds fun! I'd like to try it too.

items.notes: Swap in the verb: watashi mo tabete mitai (I want to try it too).

items.english: you'll have to show me sometime; tell me sometime
items.use: A friendly reply when someone mentions a skill, a place or a recipe; a light request, not a firm plan.

example.romaji: sono omise ii ne! kondo oshiete.
example.ja: そのお店いいね！今度教えて。
example.english: That place sounds great! Tell me where it is sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: sono omise ii desu ne! kondo oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: そのお店いいですね！今度教えてください。
examplePolite.english: That place sounds lovely! Please tell me about it sometime.

items.notes: Kondo = next time or sometime soon; oshieru is both 'teach' and 'tell'.

items.english: you'll love it, trust me; you'll get hooked
items.use: Said when recommending a show, food or hobby; hamaru is to get hooked on something.

example.romaji: kono anime mite mite! zettai hamaru yo.
example.ja: このアニメ見て見て！絶対ハマるよ。
example.english: Watch this anime! You'll be hooked, I promise.

examplePolite.romaji: kono anime, zehi mite kudasai. zettai hamarimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このアニメ、ぜひ見てください。絶対ハマりますよ。
examplePolite.english: Do watch this anime. I'm sure you'll love it.

items.notes: ... ni hamatteru = I'm really into ... right now.

blocks.label: Eating and drinking out
blocks.rationale: Sort out food and drink limits when you go out together.
blocks.interference: osake yowai means you get drunk easily, not that you dislike drinking.

items.use: Osake means alcohol in general; often asked before inviting you out. Answer nomu yo, or amari nomenai (I can't drink much).

example.romaji: osake nomu? kondo nomi ni ikou yo.
example.ja: お酒飲む？今度飲みに行こうよ。
example.english: Do you drink? Let's go for drinks sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: osake wa nomimasu ka? kondo nomi ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: お酒は飲みますか？今度飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Do you drink? Would you like to go for a drink sometime?

items.notes: The rice wine English calls sake is nihonshu.

items.polite: karai no wa daijoubu desu ka?
items.english: are you okay with spicy food?
items.use: Asked before ordering or cooking; answer daijoubu (fine) or chotto nigate (not great with it).
items.kana: からいのだいじょうぶ？
items.politeJa: 辛いのは大丈夫ですか？

example.romaji: kimuchi nabe ni shiyou ka. karai no daijoubu?
example.ja: キムチ鍋にしようか。辛いの大丈夫？
example.english: Shall we get kimchi hotpot? Are you okay with spicy?

examplePolite.romaji: karai no wa daijoubu desu ka? kekkou karai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 辛いのは大丈夫ですか？結構辛いですよ。
examplePolite.english: Are you okay with spicy food? It's pretty hot.

items.notes: Swap in any food: sakana daijoubu? (are you okay with fish?).

items.english: I can't hold my drink; I'm a lightweight
items.use: Explains why you're drinking slowly or turning down a refill; the opposite is osake tsuyoi.

example.romaji: gomen, osake yowai n da. uuroncha ni suru.
example.ja: ごめん、お酒弱いんだ。ウーロン茶にする。
example.english: Sorry, I'm a lightweight. I'll have oolong tea.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, osake yowai n desu. uuroncha de.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お酒弱いんです。ウーロン茶で。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I can't hold my drink. Oolong tea for me.

items.notes: Osake means any alcohol, not just sake; osake wa nigate (not good with alcohol) also works.

items.polite: okiniiri no omise wa arimasu ka?
items.english: got a favourite place to eat or hang out?
items.use: Asks for a local recommendation or about someone's regular spots.
items.ja: お気に入りのお店ある？
items.kana: おきにいりのおみせある？
items.politeJa: お気に入りのお店はありますか？

example.romaji: kono hen de okiniiri no omise aru? oshiete.
example.ja: この辺でお気に入りのお店ある？教えて。
example.english: Got a favourite place around here? Tell me.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hen de okiniiri no omise wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この辺でお気に入りのお店はありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have a favourite place around here?

items.notes: Okiniiri means 'favourite'; ikitsuke no mise is 'my regular place'.

items.use: A classic question to foreigners about the sticky fermented beans; a yes usually gets a surprised reaction.

example.romaji: e, nattou taberareru no? sugoi ne.
example.ja: え、納豆食べられるの？すごいね。
example.english: Wait, you can eat natto? Impressive.

examplePolite.romaji: nattou wa taberaremasu ka? nigate na hito mo ooi desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 納豆は食べられますか？苦手な人も多いですけど。
examplePolite.english: Can you eat natto? Lots of people can't stand it.

items.notes: Taberareru means 'can eat'; it works for any food: sashimi taberareru?

blocks.label: Which type are you
blocks.rationale: Play the 'this or that' game about what kind of person you are.
blocks.interference: ha here means side or camp (派), not the topic particle wa.

items.polite: inu ha desu ka, neko ha desu ka?
items.use: A classic icebreaker; the same frame works for any pair: koohii ha? koucha ha?
items.politeJa: 犬派ですか、猫派ですか？

example.romaji: nee, inu ha? neko ha? watashi wa zettai neko.
example.ja: ねえ、犬派？猫派？私は絶対猫。
example.english: Hey, dog person or cat person? I'm totally cats.

examplePolite.romaji: tokoro de, inu ha desu ka, neko ha desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ところで、犬派ですか、猫派ですか？
examplePolite.english: By the way, are you a dog person or a cat person?

items.notes: Answer inu ha, neko ha, or ryouhou suki (I like both).

items.english: I'm more of a homebody; I like staying in
items.use: Describes how you spend free time; the opposite is autodoa ha (outdoorsy).

example.romaji: watashi, kanzen ni indoa ha da yo. yasumi wa ie.
example.ja: 私、完全にインドア派だよ。休みは家。
example.english: I'm a total homebody. Days off, I'm at home.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa indoa ha desu. yasumi wa daitai ie ni imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 私はインドア派です。休みはだいたい家にいます。
examplePolite.english: I'm a homebody. On days off I'm usually at home.

items.notes: Light and friendly; hikikomori (shut-in) is a much stronger, negative word.

items.polite: yougaku to hougaku, dochira o kikimasu ka?
items.english: do you listen to Western or Japanese music?
items.use: A common question in Japan, where music is split into yougaku (foreign) and hougaku (Japanese).
items.ja: 洋楽と邦楽どっち聴く？
items.kana: ようがくとほうがくどっちきく？
items.politeJa: 洋楽と邦楽、どちらを聴きますか？

example.romaji: yougaku to hougaku dotchi kiku? watashi wa hougaku bakkari.
example.ja: 洋楽と邦楽どっち聴く？私は邦楽ばっかり。
example.english: Western or Japanese music? I only listen to Japanese stuff.

examplePolite.romaji: yougaku to hougaku, dochira o kikimasu ka? watashi wa hougaku bakari desu.
examplePolite.ja: 洋楽と邦楽、どちらを聴きますか？私は邦楽ばかりです。
examplePolite.english: Do you listen to Western or Japanese music? I mostly listen to Japanese.

items.notes: Dotchi is the casual form of dochira (which of two).

blocks.label: Tastes differ
blocks.rationale: Say that opinions split without saying anyone is wrong.
blocks.interference: wakareru (split, divide) vs wakaru (understand).

items.english: everyone's different; to each their own
items.use: Ends a debate politely or avoids judging someone's choice.

example.romaji: maa, konomi wa hito sorezore da kara ne.
example.ja: まあ、好みは人それぞれだからね。
example.english: Well, everyone has their own taste.

examplePolite.romaji: kangaekata wa hito sorezore desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 考え方は人それぞれですよね。
examplePolite.english: Everyone thinks differently, don't they?

items.notes: Sorezore means 'each'; it also works alone: sorezore no iken (each person's view).

items.romaji: suki na hito wa suki da yo ne
items.polite: suki na hito wa suki desu yo ne
items.english: it's not for everyone, but fans love it
items.use: A tactful verdict on something niche or odd that you don't love yourself.
items.ja: 好きな人は好きだよね
items.kana: すきなひとはすきだよね
items.politeJa: 好きな人は好きですよね

example.romaji: ano bando, suki na hito wa suki da yo ne.
example.ja: あのバンド、好きな人は好きだよね。
example.english: That band's not for everyone, but their fans love them.

examplePolite.romaji: kou iu aji wa, suki na hito wa suki desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: こういう味は、好きな人は好きですよね。
examplePolite.english: This kind of flavour isn't for everyone, but some people love it.

items.notes: Usually hints that you're not one of those fans.

items.english: people either love it or hate it; it divides opinion
items.use: Describes polarising food, films or styles without saying which side you're on.

example.romaji: pakuchii wa, kekkou konomi ga wakareru yo ne.
example.ja: パクチーは、結構好みが分かれるよね。
example.english: Coriander really divides people, doesn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono eiga wa, konomi ga wakaremasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この映画は、好みが分かれますね。
examplePolite.english: People are split on this film.

items.notes: Konomi means 'taste, preference'; wakareru means 'to split'.

items.english: it's hit and miss; some are good, some aren't
items.use: Describes things that vary in quality, like a chain's branches, a series or second-hand goods.
items.politeJa: 当たり外れがあります

example.romaji: kono shiriizu, kekkou atari hazure ga aru yo.
example.ja: このシリーズ、結構当たり外れがあるよ。
example.english: This series is pretty hit and miss.

examplePolite.romaji: furugi wa atari hazure ga arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 古着は当たり外れがありますね。
examplePolite.english: Second-hand clothes are hit and miss.

items.notes: Atari is a hit or win, hazure a miss; atari! is what you say when you get a good one.

blocks.label: Picking a side
blocks.rationale: Ask which option someone prefers and lean one way yourself.
blocks.interference: dotchi? (which one) vs dotchika (either one); ha is 'camp' (派), not the particle wa.

items.polite: dochira ga ii to omoimasu ka?
items.english: which do you think is better?
items.use: Asks a friend to help you choose between two things: clothes, dates, plans.
items.kana: どっちがいいとおもう？
items.politeJa: どちらがいいと思いますか？

example.romaji: kono futatsu, dotchi ga ii to omou?
example.ja: この二つ、どっちがいいと思う？
example.english: Which of these two do you think is better?

examplePolite.romaji: kono futatsu, dochira ga ii to omoimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この二つ、どちらがいいと思いますか？
examplePolite.english: Which of these two do you think is better?

items.notes: Dotchi is casual for dochira; for three or more options ask dore ga ii?

items.english: if anything; I'd lean toward; if I had to choose
items.use: Starts a mild preference when you're not strongly on either side.

example.romaji: dotchi ka tte iu to, natsu yori fuyu ga suki.
example.ja: どっちかっていうと、夏より冬が好き。
example.english: If anything, I prefer winter to summer.

examplePolite.romaji: dochira ka to iu to, natsu yori fuyu ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: どちらかと言うと、夏より冬が好きです。
examplePolite.english: If anything, I prefer winter to summer.

items.notes: Often ends with ... ha kana or ... no hou ga suki.

items.english: which side are you on?; which do you go for?
items.use: Comes after two options to ask which camp someone is in; answer with ... ha kana.

example.romaji: raamen to udon nara, dotchi ha?
example.ja: ラーメンとうどんなら、どっち派？
example.english: Ramen or udon: which are you?

examplePolite.romaji: raamen to udon nara, dochira ha desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ラーメンとうどんなら、どちら派ですか？
examplePolite.english: Ramen or udon: which do you prefer?

items.notes: Dotchi is casual for dochira.

items.english: I'm more of a ... person, I guess
items.use: Answers a this-or-that question with your side; kana softens it.

example.romaji: watashi wa koohii yori koucha ha kana.
example.ja: 私はコーヒーより紅茶派かな。
example.english: I'm more of a tea person than coffee, I guess.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa koohii yori koucha ha desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私はコーヒーより紅茶派ですね。
examplePolite.english: I'm more of a tea person than a coffee person.

items.notes: Ha (派) means 'camp, side' and is said ha, unlike the topic particle wa.

blocks.label: Rating words
blocks.rationale: Shade a verdict up or down with a small degree word.
blocks.interference: futsuu ni can mean 'honestly, really', not just 'normally'.

items.use: Softens a description, often to say something is better than expected.

example.romaji: kono hen, warito shizuka de sumiyasui yo.
example.ja: この辺、わりと静かで住みやすいよ。
example.english: This area's fairly quiet and easy to live in.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hen wa warito shizuka desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この辺はわりと静かですよ。
examplePolite.english: This area's fairly quiet.

items.notes: Wari ni means the same; kekkou is a bit stronger.

items.use: Marks something that breaks your expectations, good or bad.

example.romaji: kono mise, igai to yasukatta ne.
example.ja: この店、意外と安かったね。
example.english: This place was surprisingly cheap.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, igai to yasukatta desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、意外と安かったですね。
examplePolite.english: This place was surprisingly cheap.

items.notes: Igai ni means the same; igai na (unexpected) goes before a noun.

items.use: In young people's speech it upgrades praise: futsuu ni oishii means 'actually tasty', not 'average'.

example.romaji: kore, futsuu ni oishii ne. bikkuri.
example.ja: これ、普通においしいね。びっくり。
example.english: This is actually really good. I'm surprised.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, futsuu ni oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、普通においしいですね。
examplePolite.english: This is genuinely tasty.

items.notes: The older sense 'normally, in the usual way' is still common: futsuu ni aruite (just walk normally).

items.use: Compares a result with what you'd expect: nedan no wari ni wa oishii (tasty for the price).

example.romaji: nedan no wari ni wa, kekkou oishii ne.
example.ja: 値段の割には、結構おいしいね。
example.english: It's pretty tasty for the price.

examplePolite.romaji: nedan no wari ni wa, oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 値段の割には、おいしいですね。
examplePolite.english: It's tasty for the price.

items.notes: After an adjective or verb, drop the no: yasui wari ni wa (for something so cheap).

blocks.label: Kind of like
blocks.rationale: Describe something by likeness when you lack the exact word.
blocks.interference: trailing mitai na ('like, ...') vs mitai (want to see).

items.use: Attaches to a noun to say something has that quality: kodomoppoi (childish), kazeppoi (feels like a cold).

example.romaji: kare, chotto kodomoppoi tokoro aru yo ne.
example.ja: 彼、ちょっと子供っぽいところあるよね。
example.english: He can be a bit childish, can't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto kazeppoi n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと風邪っぽいんです。
examplePolite.english: I think I'm coming down with a cold today.

items.notes: Also a casual hedge on news: ashita ameppoi yo (looks like rain tomorrow).

items.use: Ends a quote or rough idea to keep it vague or playful.

example.romaji: tsukarete, mou dou demo ii, mitai na.
example.ja: 疲れて、もうどうでもいい、みたいな。
example.english: I was so tired, like, I just didn't care anymore.

items.notes: Before a noun it means 'like, similar to': neko mitai na hito (a cat-like person).

items.english: it's like ...; it looks like ...; it's similar to ...
items.use: Compares looks, taste or style; for family it means 'takes after': haha ni niteru.

example.romaji: kare, ano haiyuu ni niteru to omowanai?
example.ja: 彼、あの俳優に似てると思わない？
example.english: Don't you think he looks like that actor?

examplePolite.romaji: kono ryouri, tai ryouri ni nite imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この料理、タイ料理に似ていますね。
examplePolite.english: This dish is a lot like Thai food.

items.notes: Use niteru (nite iru), not plain niru, to say two things look alike.

blocks.label: Weighing their point
blocks.rationale: Acknowledge someone's view before adding your own.
blocks.interference: iitai koto wa wakaru signals a 'but' is coming, not full agreement.

items.english: I see what you're getting at (but ...); I get your point
items.use: Acknowledges someone's point before disagreeing; a kedo usually follows.
items.ja: 言いたいことは分かる
items.kana: いいたいことはわかる
items.politeJa: 言いたいことは分かります

example.romaji: iitai koto wa wakaru kedo, chotto kibishii yo.
example.ja: 言いたいことは分かるけど、ちょっと厳しいよ。
example.english: I get your point, but that's a bit harsh.

examplePolite.romaji: iitai koto wa wakarimasu kedo, ima wa jikan ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 言いたいことは分かりますけど、今は時間がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I see your point, but we just don't have time right now.

items.notes: The wa means 'that much I get', so it rarely signals full agreement.

items.romaji: sou iu kangaekata mo aru ne
items.polite: sou iu kangaekata mo arimasu ne
items.english: that's one way to look at it; fair point
items.use: Accepts another view as valid without fully agreeing; useful to cool a debate.
items.ja: そういう考え方もあるね
items.kana: そういうかんがえかたもあるね
items.politeJa: そういう考え方もありますね

example.romaji: naruhodo ne. sou iu kangaekata mo aru ne.
example.ja: なるほどね。そういう考え方もあるね。
example.english: I see. That's one way to look at it.

examplePolite.romaji: naruhodo, sou iu kangaekata mo arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: なるほど、そういう考え方もありますね。
examplePolite.english: I see, that's one way to look at it.

items.notes: The mo (also) keeps your own view standing; a flat tone can sound dismissive.

items.english: I'd never thought about that; that never occurred to me
items.use: Reacts with real surprise to a new angle or question, often after e or naruhodo.
items.kana: かんがえたことなかった
items.politeJa: 考えたことなかったです

example.romaji: e, sou ka. sonna no kangaeta koto nakatta.
example.ja: え、そうか。そんなの考えたことなかった。
example.english: Oh, right. I'd never thought about that.

examplePolite.romaji: naruhodo, sore wa kangaeta koto nakatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: なるほど、それは考えたことなかったです。
examplePolite.english: I see, I'd never thought of that.

items.notes: -ta koto nai means 'have never ...': itta koto nai (I've never been).

items.polite: sore wa sore de ii desu ne
items.english: that's good in its own way; that works too
items.use: Accepts an outcome or idea that isn't what you planned but has its own appeal.
items.politeJa: それはそれでいいですね

example.romaji: ame de dekakerarenai kedo, sore wa sore de ii ka.
example.ja: 雨で出かけられないけど、それはそれでいいか。
example.english: We can't go out in the rain, but that's fine in its own way.

examplePolite.romaji: shizuka na kurisumasu mo, sore wa sore de ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 静かなクリスマスも、それはそれでいいですね。
examplePolite.english: A quiet Christmas is nice in its own way.

items.notes: Sore wa sore de alone means 'in its own way': sore wa sore de taihen (that's tough in its own way).

blocks.label: Impressions and stereotypes
blocks.rationale: Share an impression or doubt while flagging it may be unfair.
blocks.interference: imeeji means impression, not picture.

items.english: I picture it as ...; my impression is ...
items.use: Shares your general picture of a place, group or thing, often inviting the other person to confirm or correct it.
items.politeJa: 〜というイメージがあります

example.romaji: igirisu tte, itsumo ame futteru tte imeeji ga aru.
example.ja: イギリスって、いつも雨降ってるってイメージがある。
example.english: I picture Britain as always rainy.

examplePolite.romaji: igirisu wa itsumo ame to iu imeeji ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: イギリスはいつも雨というイメージがあります。
examplePolite.english: My image of Britain is that it's always raining.

items.notes: Imeeji means 'impression, mental picture', not a photo.

items.english: it's not what I imagined; not what I expected
items.use: Said when a place, person or product turns out different from your picture of it, good or bad.

example.romaji: nihon no fuyu, kekkou samui ne. imeeji to chigau.
example.ja: 日本の冬、結構寒いね。イメージと違う。
example.english: Japanese winters are pretty cold. Not what I imagined.

examplePolite.romaji: jissai ni kite mitara, imeeji to chigaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 実際に来てみたら、イメージと違いました。
examplePolite.english: Once I actually came, it wasn't what I'd imagined.

items.notes: Omotteta to chigau (not what I thought) means the same.

items.romaji: ... tte iu hito mo iru kedo
items.polite: ... to iu hito mo imasu kedo
items.use: Brings up another view so you can disagree with it without owning it.

example.romaji: takai tte iu hito mo iru kedo, watashi wa yasui to omou.
example.ja: 高いって言う人もいるけど、私は安いと思う。
example.english: Some say it's pricey, but I think it's cheap.

examplePolite.romaji: fuben da to iu hito mo imasu kedo, watashi wa suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 不便だと言う人もいますけど、私は好きです。
examplePolite.english: Some people say it's inconvenient, but I like it.

items.notes: Tte is the casual form of the quoting to.

items.english: I'm not so sure about ...; I have my doubts about ...
items.use: Indirect criticism of a choice or behaviour; it sounds mild but clearly means you disapprove.

example.romaji: kaigi de sore iu no wa, dou ka to omou yo.
example.ja: 会議でそれ言うのは、どうかと思うよ。
example.english: I'm not sure saying that in a meeting is a good idea.

examplePolite.romaji: sono iikata wa, chotto dou ka to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: その言い方は、ちょっとどうかと思います。
examplePolite.english: I have my doubts about putting it that way.

items.notes: Not a question despite dou ka; chotto before it softens it further.

items.english: this might be a stereotype, but ...; maybe I'm biased, but ...
items.use: Softens a generalisation about a group or place before you say it.
items.ja: 偏見かもしれないけど
items.kana: へんけんかもしれないけど
items.politeJa: 偏見かもしれませんけど

example.romaji: henken kamo shirenai kedo, oosaka no hito tte omoshiroi yo ne.
example.ja: 偏見かもしれないけど、大阪の人って面白いよね。
example.english: Maybe it's a stereotype, but people from Osaka are funny, right?

examplePolite.romaji: henken kamo shiremasen kedo, toukyou no hito wa aruku no ga hayai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 偏見かもしれませんけど、東京の人は歩くのが速いですね。
examplePolite.english: Maybe it's a stereotype, but people in Tokyo walk fast.

items.notes: Henken means 'prejudice'; kamo shirenai (might be) is often shortened to kamo.

blocks.label: Shrugging it off
blocks.rationale: Let a point go or play something down.
blocks.interference: saa can mean 'who knows' or 'come on, let's go'.

items.use: Self-talk as you decide to let something go.

example.romaji: densha itchatta. maa ii ka, tsugi matou.
example.ja: 電車行っちゃった。まあいいか、次待とう。
example.english: Missed the train. Oh well, I'll wait for the next one.

items.english: it's no big deal; nothing serious
items.use: Plays down a problem, an injury, or praise.
items.politeJa: 大したことありません

example.romaji: kega? taishita koto nai yo.
example.ja: けが？大したことないよ。
example.english: The injury? It's nothing serious.

examplePolite.romaji: taishita koto arimasen yo. daijoubu desu.
examplePolite.ja: 大したことありませんよ。大丈夫です。
examplePolite.english: It's nothing serious. I'm fine.

items.notes: About someone else's work it's a put-down: 'not that impressive'.

items.use: Accept or explain something you can't change, often as sou iu mon da yo.

example.romaji: shigoto nante, sou iu mon da yo.
example.ja: 仕事なんて、そういうもんだよ。
example.english: That's just how work is.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto wa, sou iu mono desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 仕事は、そういうものですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's just how work is.

items.notes: mon is a casual squeeze of mono (thing).

items.english: well, who knows; come on, let's go
items.use: With a shrug it dodges a question you can't answer; said briskly it gets people moving.

example.romaji: saa, doko itta n darou. shiranai.
example.ja: さあ、どこ行ったんだろう。知らない。
example.english: Who knows where he went. No idea.

examplePolite.romaji: saa, chotto wakarimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: さあ、ちょっとわかりませんね。
examplePolite.english: Hmm, I'm not really sure.

items.notes: A bare saa can sound dismissive; add chotto wakaranai to soften it.

blocks.label: Days off and plans
blocks.rationale: Ask about days off and say you've got nothing on.
blocks.interference: yotei (plans) vs yoyaku (booking).

items.polite: toku ni yotei wa nai desu
items.use: Answering 'doing anything this weekend?'; it also hints you're free to meet.

example.romaji: shuumatsu? toku ni yotei nai yo. nande?
example.ja: 週末？特に予定ないよ。なんで？
example.english: This weekend? No plans, really. Why?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu desu ka? toku ni yotei wa nai desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 週末ですか？特に予定はないですけど。
examplePolite.english: This weekend? I don't have any plans, no.

items.notes: Yotei aru? is the question that usually comes right before an invitation.

items.english: are you off today?; is it your day off?
items.use: Asked when you bump into someone at a time they'd usually be working.

example.romaji: are, kyou wa yasumi? shigoto ja nai no?
example.ja: あれ、今日は休み？仕事じゃないの？
example.english: Oh, are you off today? No work?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa oyasumi desu ka? ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はお休みですか？いいですね。
examplePolite.english: Are you off today? Nice.

items.notes: About a shop, the same words ask whether it's closed today.

items.romaji: yasumi no hi wa nani shiteru?
items.polite: oyasumi no hi wa nani o shite imasu ka?
items.english: what do you do on your days off?
items.use: The usual getting-to-know-you way to ask about hobbies without saying 'hobby'.
items.kana: やすみのひはなにしてる？
items.politeJa: お休みの日は何をしていますか？

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa nani shiteru? yoku dekakeru?
example.ja: 休みの日は何してる？よく出かける？
example.english: What do you do on your days off? Go out much?

examplePolite.romaji: oyasumi no hi wa nani o shite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お休みの日は何をしていますか？
examplePolite.english: What do you do on your days off?

items.notes: Shumi wa nan desu ka? asks the same but sounds stiffer, like an interview.

items.use: A half-joking mid-week grumble to friends or coworkers, or to yourself.
items.ja: 早く週末にならないかな
items.kana: はやくしゅうまつにならないかな

example.romaji: mada suiyoubi ka. hayaku shuumatsu ni naranai kana.
example.ja: まだ水曜日か。早く週末にならないかな。
example.english: Only Wednesday? I can't wait for the weekend.

items.notes: Works for any day or event: hayaku natsuyasumi ni naranai kana.

blocks.label: Seeing someone again
blocks.rationale: Greet a friend you haven't seen in a long time.
blocks.interference: nannenburi (how many years) vs hisashiburi (long time no see).

items.english: you look well; you seem good
items.use: Said on meeting someone after a while; reply un, genki da yo, or okagesama de in polite talk.

example.romaji: hisashiburi! sugoku genkisou da ne.
example.ja: 久しぶり！すごく元気そうだね。
example.english: Long time no see! You look great.

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. ogenkisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気そうですね。
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. You look well.

items.notes: -sou means 'looks like': tanoshisou (looks fun), oishisou (looks tasty).

items.use: Said at a reunion, usually as a warm compliment; also about a place.

example.romaji: uwa, zenzen kawatte nai ne!
example.ja: うわ、全然変わってないね！
example.english: Wow, you haven't changed at all!

examplePolite.romaji: sensei, zenzen kawatte imasen ne!
examplePolite.ja: 先生、全然変わっていませんね！
examplePolite.english: You haven't changed at all, sensei!

items.notes: Can also tease: still the same old you.

items.english: how many years has it been?
items.use: Said with surprise when meeting someone after years; answer with a guess like gonenburi kana.

example.romaji: uwa, hisashiburi! nannenburi? gonen kurai?
example.ja: うわ、久しぶり！何年ぶり？五年くらい？
example.english: Wow, long time! How long has it been? Five years?

examplePolite.romaji: sotsugyou irai desu ne. nannenburi deshou.
examplePolite.ja: 卒業以来ですね。何年ぶりでしょう。
examplePolite.english: Not since graduation, right? How many years has it been?

items.notes: -buri marks the time since last: mikkaburi (first time in three days), hisashiburi (in ages).

blocks.label: Asking about their people
blocks.rationale: Ask after someone's family, partner or a mutual friend.
blocks.interference: dou shiteru (how are they doing) vs dou shita (what happened).

items.use: Asked of a friend you haven't seen for a while; answer un, minna genki da yo (yeah, everyone's well).
items.politeJa: ご家族はお元気ですか？

example.romaji: sou ieba, kazoku wa genki? okaasan mo?
example.ja: そういえば、家族は元気？お母さんも？
example.english: By the way, how's your family? Your mum too?

examplePolite.romaji: sou ieba, gokazoku wa ogenki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そういえば、ご家族はお元気ですか？
examplePolite.english: By the way, how is your family?

items.notes: The polite form honours their family with go- and o-; never use those for your own family.

items.english: how are they doing?; what are you up to these days?
items.use: Asks about someone's life now, often about a person who isn't there.

example.romaji: sotsugyou shite kara, minna dou shiteru?
example.ja: 卒業してから、みんなどうしてる？
example.english: How's everyone been since graduation?

examplePolite.romaji: sotsugyou shite kara, minasan dou shite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 卒業してから、皆さんどうしていますか？
examplePolite.english: How is everyone doing since graduation?

items.notes: Often with kana: ima dou shiteru kana (I wonder how they're doing).

items.use: A personal question, often from relatives or older friends, about whether you have a partner.

example.romaji: saikin dou? dareka ii hito iru?
example.ja: 最近どう？誰かいい人いる？
example.english: How are things? Seeing anyone?

items.notes: Ii hito also just means 'a nice person', as in ii hito da ne.

blocks.label: Casual check-in texts
blocks.rationale: Send or answer the light check-ins friends drop by message.
blocks.interference: gohan tabeta? is a caring check-in, not an invitation to eat.

items.english: what are you up to?; what are you doing now?
items.use: An opening text or call to a friend or partner, often before inviting them out.

example.romaji: ima nani shiteru? hima nara gohan ikanai?
example.ja: 今何してる？暇ならご飯行かない？
example.english: What are you up to? If you're free, want to grab food?

items.notes: A common answer is betsu ni or nani mo shitenai (nothing much).

items.use: A caring check-in from family or close friends, often leading to an invitation to eat.

example.romaji: gohan tabeta? mada nara issho ni tabeyou.
example.ja: ご飯食べた？まだなら一緒に食べよう。
example.english: Have you eaten? If not, let's eat together.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan tabemashita ka? mada nara issho ni dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ご飯食べましたか？まだなら一緒にどうですか？
examplePolite.english: Have you eaten? If not, would you like to join me?

items.notes: Answer mada ('not yet') or mou tabeta ('already ate'). Gohan here means any meal, not just rice.

items.use: A parent's or close friend's worry when you seem thin, busy or are living alone.

example.romaji: kaze hiite nai? chanto tabeteru?
example.ja: 風邪ひいてない？ちゃんと食べてる？
example.english: You're not sick, are you? Eating properly?

items.notes: Chanto means 'properly, as you should': chanto nete ne, 'get proper sleep'.

blocks.label: Noticing changes
blocks.rationale: Comment on a new haircut or look, or on your own weight.
blocks.interference: kitta (cut) vs kita (came, wore).

items.use: A friendly remark when you notice a new haircut, usually followed by a compliment.

example.romaji: are, kami kitta? niau ne!
example.ja: あれ、髪切った？似合うね！
example.english: Oh, did you get a haircut? It suits you!

examplePolite.romaji: are, kami kirimashita ka? niaimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、髪切りましたか？似合いますね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, did you get your hair cut? It looks good.

items.notes: Kiru covers a salon cut too; there's no separate 'have it cut' form.

items.english: you look different; you seem different
items.use: Said when someone's look or vibe has changed since you last met.
items.politeJa: 雰囲気変わりましたね

example.romaji: hisashiburi! nanka fun'iki kawatta ne.
example.ja: 久しぶり！なんか雰囲気変わったね。
example.english: Long time no see! You look different somehow.

examplePolite.romaji: ohisashiburi desu. fun'iki kawarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。雰囲気変わりましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's been a while. You look different.

items.notes: Usually meant kindly; add ii ne to make it a clear compliment.

items.use: A common compliment between friends after time apart; reply e, hontou? or sukoshi ne (a little).

example.romaji: are, yaseta? nanka sukkiri shita ne.
example.ja: あれ、痩せた？なんかすっきりしたね。
example.english: Oh, have you lost weight? You look trimmer.

examplePolite.romaji: are, yasemashita ka? sukkiri shimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、痩せましたか？すっきりしましたね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, have you lost weight? You look trimmer.

items.notes: Yaseta is the change; yaseteru (slim) describes a body type.

items.english: I've put on a bit of weight lately
items.use: Self-deprecating small talk about yourself; don't ask futotta? of others, it's rude.
items.ja: 最近ちょっと太っちゃった
items.kana: さいきんちょっとふとっちゃった
items.politeJa: 最近ちょっと太ってしまいました

example.romaji: shougatsu tabesugite, saikin chotto futotchatta.
example.ja: 正月食べすぎて、最近ちょっと太っちゃった。
example.english: I ate too much over New Year, so I've put on a bit of weight.

examplePolite.romaji: shougatsu ni tabesugite, chotto futotte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 正月に食べすぎて、ちょっと太ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I ate too much over New Year and put on a bit of weight.

items.notes: -chatta (from -te shimatta) adds an 'oops, it happened' feel.

blocks.label: Time flies
blocks.rationale: Remark on how fast the year goes and ask about holiday plans.
blocks.interference: kaeru (go home) sounds the same as kaeru (change).

items.polite: jikan ga tatsu no wa hayai desu ne
items.use: Said when you notice how long it's been, like meeting an old friend or seeing a child grown up.
items.kana: じかんたつのはやいね
items.politeJa: 時間が経つのは早いですね

example.romaji: mou ichinen? jikan tatsu no hayai ne.
example.ja: もう一年？時間経つの早いね。
example.english: A year already? Time flies, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: mou ichinen desu ka. jikan ga tatsu no wa hayai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もう一年ですか。時間が経つのは早いですね。
examplePolite.english: A year already. Time really flies.

items.notes: Tatsu here is 'pass' (time), a different word from tatsu 'stand' with the same sound.

items.romaji: kotoshi mo ato sukoshi da ne
items.polite: kotoshi mo ato sukoshi desu ne
items.use: Standard December small talk at work, in shops and with neighbours.
items.kana: ことしもあとすこしだね
items.politeJa: 今年もあと少しですね

example.romaji: kotoshi mo ato sukoshi da ne. hayakatta naa.
example.ja: 今年もあと少しだね。早かったなあ。
example.english: The year's almost over. That went fast.

examplePolite.romaji: kotoshi mo ato sukoshi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今年もあと少しですね。
examplePolite.english: The year's nearly over, isn't it.

items.notes: Often paired with yoi otoshi o, 'have a good new year', said before the year ends.

items.use: Asked in December, since many people go back to their parents' home for the New Year holidays.
items.kana: おしょうがつはかえるの？

example.romaji: oshougatsu wa kaeru no? jikka doko dakke?
example.ja: お正月は帰るの？実家どこだっけ？
example.english: Going home for New Year? Where's your family from again?

examplePolite.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お正月は実家に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going back to your family home for New Year?

items.notes: Kaeru here means going back to your hometown; jikka is your parents' home.

blocks.label: No way unbelievable
blocks.rationale: Reacts strongly to something shocking or outrageous.
blocks.interference: iya iya also brushes off compliments; arienai can mean outrageous, not just surprising.

items.english: no way; that's impossible; that's outrageous
items.use: Reacts to something hard to believe or hard to accept.

example.romaji: kyuuryou ga sagaru no? arienai!
example.ja: 給料が下がるの？ありえない！
example.english: Our pay's going down? That's outrageous!

examplePolite.romaji: kyuuryou ga sagaru n desu ka? arienai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 給料が下がるんですか？ありえないです。
examplePolite.english: Our pay's going down? That's unbelievable.

items.notes: Young people also use it as praise: arienai kurai oishii (unbelievably good).

items.english: no, no; not at all; oh, come on
items.use: Modest denial when you're praised or thanked; also brushes off a silly idea.

example.romaji: iya iya, sonna koto nai yo.
example.ja: いやいや、そんなことないよ。
example.english: No, no, not at all.

examplePolite.romaji: iya iya, sonna koto nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いやいや、そんなことないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Oh no, not at all.

items.notes: In polite talk, ie ie is a softer choice.

items.use: For shocking news, good or bad.

example.romaji: uso, shinjirarenai! takarakuji atatta no?
example.ja: うそ、信じられない！宝くじ当たったの？
example.english: No way, I can't believe it! You won the lottery?

examplePolite.romaji: shinjiraremasen. takarakuji ga atatta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 信じられません。宝くじが当たったんですか？
examplePolite.english: I can't believe it. You won the lottery?

items.notes: Said with a frown it scolds, like 'how could you?'.

items.english: it's unreal; I can hardly believe it
items.use: Said about something too good or too strange to believe, like happy news or a stunning view.

example.romaji: goukaku shita nante, uso mitai.
example.ja: 合格したなんて、嘘みたい。
example.english: I can't believe I actually passed.

examplePolite.romaji: goukaku shita nante, uso mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 合格したなんて、嘘みたいです。
examplePolite.english: I can hardly believe I passed.

items.notes: It doesn't accuse anyone of lying; uso! alone is the everyday 'no way!'.

blocks.label: What you're kidding
blocks.rationale: Challenges something odd or cheeky someone just said.
blocks.interference: nani sore can sound scornful; uso tsuke is playful only with close friends.

items.english: what's that?!; what's that supposed to mean
items.use: Reacts to something surprising the other person shows or says; your tone shows if you're curious or annoyed.

example.romaji: nani sore, kawaii! doko de katta no?
example.ja: 何それ、かわいい！どこで買ったの？
example.english: What's that? So cute! Where'd you buy it?

examplePolite.romaji: sore, nan desu ka? kawaii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それ、何ですか？かわいいですね。
examplePolite.english: What's that? It's cute.

items.notes: Said flatly, it means 'that's ridiculous'.

items.english: are you serious?; you're not joking?
items.use: Reacting to news so surprising you suspect a joke; among friends only.

example.romaji: kaisha yameru no? maji de itteru?
example.ja: 会社辞めるの？マジで言ってる？
example.english: You're quitting your job? Are you serious?

items.notes: Shorter: maji de? or just maji? Politely, say hontou desu ka?

items.use: Playfully calling out an obvious fib or brag among close friends.

example.romaji: kyou wa nomanai? uso tsuke.
example.ja: 今日は飲まない？嘘つけ。
example.english: You're not drinking today? Yeah, right.

items.notes: It's a command form, so it can sound harsh to people you don't know well. Uso tsuki is the noun 'liar'.

items.use: Shocked reaction to news; with a sharp tone it challenges what someone just said.

example.romaji: nan datte? kekkon suru no?
example.ja: なんだって？結婚するの？
example.english: What?! You're getting married?

items.notes: Asked calmly, it asks what someone else said: sensei, nan datte? (what did the teacher say?)

blocks.label: Wow and whoa
blocks.rationale: Gives a quick gut reaction to something you see or hear.
blocks.interference: uwa can be delight or disgust; ara sounds older or feminine.

items.use: Surprise or delight at something you see, like a view, a gift or food arriving.

example.romaji: waa, kirei! mite, umi ga mieru yo.
example.ja: わあ、きれい！見て、海が見えるよ。
example.english: Wow, beautiful! Look, you can see the sea.

examplePolite.romaji: waa, kirei desu ne! umi ga miemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: わあ、きれいですね！海が見えますよ。
examplePolite.english: Wow, how beautiful! You can see the sea.

items.notes: uwa! leans toward shock or disgust; waa is usually pleasant.

items.use: Shock or amazement; with a grimace it means disgust.

example.romaji: uwa, kyou hito ga ooi na!
example.ja: うわっ、今日人が多いな！
example.english: Whoa, it's so crowded today!

examplePolite.romaji: uwa, kyou wa hito ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: うわっ、今日は人が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: Wow, it's really crowded today.

items.notes: Drawn out, uwaa is awe: uwaa, kirei (wow, beautiful).

items.use: Opens a comment with feeling; also a bashful start to answering praise.

example.romaji: iyaa, kyou wa atsui ne.
example.ja: いやー、今日は暑いね。
example.english: Man, it's hot today.

examplePolite.romaji: iyaa, kyou wa atsui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: いやー、今日は暑いですね。
examplePolite.english: My, it's hot today.

items.notes: Not 'no': short iya means no, drawn-out iyaa is a filler.

items.use: A light 'oh' when you notice something good or see someone arrive.

example.romaji: o! ii no aru jan.
example.ja: おっ！いいのあるじゃん。
example.english: Oh! There's a good one.

examplePolite.romaji: o, ii no ga arimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: おっ、いいのがありますね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, there's a nice one.

items.notes: a! is for sudden realization or alarm; o! is for pleasant noticing.

items.use: Mild surprise, typically from women, like running into someone you know.

example.romaji: ara, hisashiburi ne. genki?
example.ja: あら、久しぶりね。元気？
example.english: Oh, long time no see. How are you?

examplePolite.romaji: ara, ohisashiburi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あら、お久しぶりですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, it's been a long time.

items.notes: Men rarely say it; are? is the neutral 'huh?'.

blocks.label: Well done never mind
blocks.rationale: Responds to how someone did, whether they nailed it or missed.
blocks.interference: yatta ne is 'you did it', yatta is 'I did it'; yoku yatta can sound top-down.

items.use: Casual, slightly teasing praise when a friend does better than expected.

example.romaji: zenbu seikai? yaru jan!
example.ja: 全部正解？やるじゃん！
example.english: All correct? Nice going!

items.notes: It implies surprise, so don't say it to a superior; politely, say sugoi desu ne.

items.english: you did it!; way to go
items.use: Congratulates a friend on a success; yatta alone is your own win.

example.romaji: goukaku shita no? yatta ne!
example.ja: 合格したの？やったね！
example.english: You passed? You did it!

examplePolite.romaji: goukaku shita n desu ka? yarimashita ne!
examplePolite.ja: 合格したんですか？やりましたね！
examplePolite.english: You passed? That's great!

items.use: Comforting someone right after a small slip, especially in sports or games.

example.romaji: donmai! tsugi wa ganbarou yo.
example.ja: ドンマイ！次は頑張ろうよ。
example.english: Don't worry about it! We'll get it next time.

items.notes: From English 'don't mind', but only used this way; for bigger worries say ki ni shinaide.

items.use: Praise from a parent, coach, or boss to someone below them.

example.romaji: yoku yatta! zenbu hitori de yatta no?
example.ja: よくやった！全部一人でやったの？
example.english: Well done! You did it all by yourself?

examplePolite.romaji: yoku yarimashita ne. taihen datta deshou.
examplePolite.ja: よくやりましたね。大変だったでしょう。
examplePolite.english: Well done. That must have been tough.

items.notes: It talks down, so don't say it to a boss; use otsukaresama deshita instead.

items.use: Said when someone guesses right; also heard at prize draws and on winning tickets.

example.romaji: sou, atari! yoku wakatta ne.
example.ja: そう、当たり！よくわかったね。
example.english: Yep, you got it! How did you guess?

examplePolite.romaji: hai, atari desu. yoku wakarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: はい、当たりです。よくわかりましたね。
examplePolite.english: Yes, that's right. Well guessed.

items.notes: The opposite is hazure: 'wrong guess' or 'a dud'.

blocks.label: Yes I did it
blocks.rationale: Celebrates your own win or a bit of luck.
blocks.interference: yossha sounds masculine; dekita also means 'it's ready'.

items.use: Shouted when something good happens to you or you pull something off.

example.romaji: yatta! shiken ni ukatta yo!
example.ja: やった！試験に受かったよ！
example.english: Yes! I passed the exam!

examplePolite.romaji: yatta! shiken ni ukarimashita!
examplePolite.ja: やった！試験に受かりました！
examplePolite.english: Yes! I passed the exam!

items.notes: It's the past of yaru (do), but as a shout it just means joy. To cheer someone else, say yatta ne.

items.use: A punchy shout when you win or something goes your way, like a fist pump.

example.romaji: yossha, kore de owari da!
example.ja: よっしゃ、これで終わりだ！
example.english: All right, that's it, done!

items.notes: Sounds a bit macho; yatta is the neutral choice.

items.use: Said when something goes your way by chance.

example.romaji: rakkii! saigo no hitotsu datta.
example.ja: ラッキー！最後の一つだった。
example.english: Lucky! It was the last one.

examplePolite.romaji: rakkii deshita. saigo no hitotsu deshita yo.
examplePolite.ja: ラッキーでした。最後の一つでしたよ。
examplePolite.english: I got lucky. It was the last one.

items.use: Said to yourself before starting something, or when something turns out well.

example.romaji: yoshi, ja hajimeyou ka.
example.ja: よし、じゃ始めようか。
example.english: Right, let's get started.

examplePolite.romaji: yoshi, sore dewa hajimemashou.
examplePolite.ja: よし、それでは始めましょう。
examplePolite.english: Right, let's begin then.

items.notes: Doubled, yoshi yoshi soothes or praises a child or pet.

items.english: done; I did it; it's ready
items.use: Said when you finish making or managing something, often while showing it.

example.romaji: dekita! mite, kore jibun de tsukutta.
example.ja: できた！見て、これ自分で作った。
example.english: Done! Look, I made this myself.

examplePolite.romaji: dekimashita. mite kudasai, jibun de tsukurimashita.
examplePolite.ja: できました。見てください、自分で作りました。
examplePolite.english: Done. Have a look, I made it myself.

items.notes: Also 'it's ready' for food: gohan dekita yo (dinner's ready).

blocks.label: Oh that's all
blocks.rationale: Reacts when the story or news turns out smaller than expected.
blocks.interference: naanda can be relief or letdown; haa? with a rising tone sounds rude.

items.english: oh, is that all?; oh, it's only that
items.use: Said when something turns out less serious or exciting than you thought, in relief or disappointment.

example.romaji: naanda, sonna koto ka. shinpai shite sonshita.
example.ja: なーんだ、そんなことか。心配して損した。
example.english: Oh, is that all? I worried for nothing.

items.notes: A short, rising nan da? means 'what is it?' when someone calls you.

items.use: Said when something is smaller, shorter or less than you expected.

example.romaji: e, sore dake? motto aru to omotta.
example.ja: え、それだけ？もっとあると思った。
example.english: Wait, that's it? I thought there'd be more.

examplePolite.romaji: e, sore dake desu ka? motto aru to omoimashita.
examplePolite.ja: え、それだけですか？もっとあると思いました。
examplePolite.english: Oh, that's all? I thought there'd be more.

items.notes: Without the surprised e, sore dake? can be a plain check: 'is that everything?'

items.use: Rising and sharp, it's an annoyed 'huh?!'; long and falling, it's a sigh.

example.romaji: haa? nani itten no?
example.ja: はあ？何言ってんの？
example.english: Huh? What are you talking about?

items.notes: A flat haa to a request is a reluctant 'uh, okay'; the rising haa? is rude.

blocks.label: Huh that's odd
blocks.rationale: Voices puzzlement at something strange.
blocks.interference: nani kore is about a thing in front of you, nani sore about what they said.

items.use: Reacts to something right in front of you, in surprise, delight, or disgust.

example.romaji: nani kore, sugoku oishii!
example.ja: 何これ、すごくおいしい！
example.english: What is this? It's so good!

examplePolite.romaji: kore, nan desu ka? sugoku oishii desu.
examplePolite.ja: これ、何ですか？すごくおいしいです。
examplePolite.english: What is this? It's really good.

items.notes: kore is near you; sore is near the other person.

items.use: Disbelief at an unlikely story or a run of bad luck; it isn't a real question.

example.romaji: mata densha tomatta no? sonna koto aru?
example.ja: また電車止まったの？そんなことある？
example.english: The train stopped again? How is that even possible?

items.notes: Don't mix up with sonna koto nai yo, 'that's not true' or 'not at all'.

items.use: Puzzled self-talk when something isn't where or how it should be.

example.romaji: okashii na, koko ni oita no ni.
example.ja: おかしいな、ここに置いたのに。
example.english: That's strange, I put it right here.

examplePolite.romaji: okashii desu ne, koko ni oita n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: おかしいですね、ここに置いたんですが。
examplePolite.english: That's odd, I put it right here.

items.notes: okashii also means funny: okashii hanashi (a funny story).

blocks.label: Oops oh no
blocks.rationale: Reacts to small mistakes and mishaps.
blocks.interference: shimatta is your own slip; arara reacts to anyone's small mishap.

items.use: Said when you realize you've made a mistake or forgotten something.

example.romaji: shimatta, saifu ie ni wasureta.
example.ja: しまった、財布家に忘れた。
example.english: Oh no, I left my wallet at home.

examplePolite.romaji: a, shimatta. saifu o ie ni wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: あ、しまった。財布を家に忘れました。
examplePolite.english: Oh no. I left my wallet at home.

items.notes: For your own slip-ups; yabai is the more casual everyday version.

items.use: Sympathetic or teasing reaction to a small mishap, usually someone else's.

example.romaji: arara, juusu koboshichatta ne.
example.ja: あらら、ジュースこぼしちゃったね。
example.english: Oh dear, you spilled your juice.

examplePolite.romaji: arara, juusu ga koborete shimaimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: あらら、ジュースがこぼれてしまいましたね。
examplePolite.english: Oh dear, the juice spilled.

items.use: A quick reflex when you nearly drop, bump into, or let slip something.

example.romaji: otto, abunai. ki o tsukete.
example.ja: おっと、危ない。気をつけて。
example.english: Whoa, careful. Watch out.

examplePolite.romaji: otto, sumimasen, shitsurei shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: おっと、すみません、失礼しました。
examplePolite.english: Oops, sorry, excuse me.

items.english: got me!; they got us; I've been had
items.use: When you're beaten, tricked, or caught out.

example.romaji: yarareta! mata kare ni damasareta.
example.ja: やられた！また彼にだまされた。
example.english: He got me! Fooled by him again.

examplePolite.romaji: yararemashita. mata kare ni damasaremashita.
examplePolite.ja: やられました。また彼にだまされました。
examplePolite.english: He got me. I fell for it again.

items.notes: In action films it also means 'I'm hit'.

blocks.label: What's new with you
blocks.rationale: Catches up on what a friend has been up to.
blocks.interference: nanika atta asks if something's wrong; nanka ii koto atta asks about something good.

items.polite: nani shite ita n desu ka?
items.english: what were you up to?; what were you doing?
items.use: Asking what someone was doing at a certain time, like when they didn't pick up or turned up late.

example.romaji: denwa shita noni. nani shiteta no?
example.ja: 電話したのに。何してたの？
example.english: I called you. What were you up to?

examplePolite.romaji: denwa shita n desu kedo, nani shite ita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 電話したんですけど、何していたんですか？
examplePolite.english: I called you. What were you doing?

items.notes: Said sharply, it can sound like an accusation: 'where were you?!'

items.use: Following up on something you both know about, like an illness, a breakup or a new job.

example.romaji: kaze, are kara dou? mou daijoubu?
example.ja: 風邪、あれからどう？もう大丈夫？
example.english: How's your cold since then? All better?

examplePolite.romaji: kaze wa are kara dou desu ka? mou daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 風邪はあれからどうですか？もう大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: How has your cold been since then? Are you better?

items.notes: Are kara points back to something you both know; sore kara just means 'and then'.

items.english: did something happen?; is something wrong?
items.use: Asked when someone looks upset or calls out of the blue.

example.romaji: genki nai ne. nanika atta?
example.ja: 元気ないね。何かあった？
example.english: You seem down. Did something happen?

examplePolite.romaji: kaoiro ga warui desu yo. nanika atta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔色が悪いですよ。何かあったんですか？
examplePolite.english: You look pale. Did something happen?

items.notes: Nanika atta no? is the softer, more caring version; dou shita no? (what's wrong?) is close.

items.use: Said when someone looks happier than usual, smiling or humming.
items.ja: なんかいいことあった？
items.kana: なんかいいことあった？
items.politeJa: 何かいいことありましたか？

example.romaji: nikoniko shite, nanka ii koto atta?
example.ja: ニコニコして、なんかいいことあった？
example.english: You're all smiles. Did something good happen?

examplePolite.romaji: ureshisou desu ne. nanika ii koto arimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 嬉しそうですね。何かいいことありましたか？
examplePolite.english: You look happy. Did something good happen?

items.notes: Nanka is the casual nanika ('something'); it's also the filler 'like'.

blocks.label: Since when who told
blocks.rationale: Digs into the details behind a piece of news or gossip.
blocks.interference: nande shitteru no can sound accusing without a smile.

items.use: Asking when something started, like a symptom, a relationship or a new habit.

example.romaji: atama itai no? itsu kara?
example.ja: 頭痛いの？いつから？
example.english: Your head hurts? Since when?

examplePolite.romaji: itami wa itsu kara desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 痛みはいつからですか？
examplePolite.english: When did the pain start?

items.notes: Doctors ask itsu kara desu ka? about symptoms, so expect to hear it there.

items.use: Asking what someone means when they react without saying what, like 'that's weird!'.

example.romaji: e, nani ga? zenzen wakannai.
example.ja: え、何が？全然わかんない。
example.english: Wait, what is? I don't get it at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, nani ga desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、何がですか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, what is?

items.notes: Said flat, it can sound defensive: 'what's your problem?'

items.polite: dare kara kiita n desu ka?
items.use: Asking where news or gossip came from, often with some surprise.
items.politeJa: 誰から聞いたんですか？

example.romaji: sono hanashi, dare kara kiita no?
example.ja: その話、誰から聞いたの？
example.english: Who told you that?

examplePolite.romaji: sono hanashi, dare kara kiita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: その話、誰から聞いたんですか？
examplePolite.english: Who did you hear that from?

items.notes: Kiku means both 'hear' and 'ask'; dare ni kiita no? is 'who did you ask?'

items.polite: doushite shitte iru n desu ka?
items.use: Said in surprise when someone knows something you didn't tell them.
items.politeJa: どうして知っているんですか？

example.romaji: e, nande shitteru no? dare ni mo itte nai noni.
example.ja: え、なんで知ってるの？誰にも言ってないのに。
example.english: Wait, how do you know? I didn't tell anyone.

examplePolite.romaji: e, doushite shitte iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、どうして知っているんですか？
examplePolite.english: Oh, how do you know that?

items.notes: 'Know' is shitteru; shiru alone means 'find out'.

blocks.label: Asking first asking advice
blocks.rationale: Opens a question, checks it's okay, or asks for advice.
blocks.interference: ii no? checks it's really okay; ii yo is the reply 'it's fine'.

items.use: Lead-in before a personal or awkward question.

example.romaji: chotto kiite mo ii? kanojo iru?
example.ja: ちょっと聞いてもいい？彼女いる？
example.english: Can I ask you something? Do you have a girlfriend?

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu kiite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一つ聞いてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Can I ask you one thing?

items.notes: Very polite version: ukagatte mo yoroshii desu ka.

items.use: Asks someone for advice when you're stuck or don't know the next step.
items.politeJa: どうしたらいいですか

example.romaji: kagi nakushichatta. dou shitara ii?
example.ja: 鍵なくしちゃった。どうしたらいい？
example.english: I lost my keys. What should I do?

examplePolite.romaji: kagi o nakushite shimatta n desu ga, dou shitara ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 鍵をなくしてしまったんですが、どうしたらいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I've lost my key. What should I do?

items.notes: Dou sureba ii? means the same.

items.english: are you sure?; is it really okay?
items.use: Checks that someone means it when they offer you something or do you a favour; follow with thanks.

example.romaji: e, ogori? ii no?
example.ja: え、おごり？いいの？
example.english: Wait, your treat? Are you sure?

examplePolite.romaji: e, ii n desu ka? arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: え、いいんですか？ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Oh, are you sure? Thank you.

items.notes: Also asks permission after a -te verb: kore tabete ii no? (can I eat this?).

blocks.label: Fair point
blocks.rationale: Concedes a good point in a discussion.
blocks.interference: sore wa aru means 'that's a factor'; aru aru means 'so relatable'.

items.use: Concede a point, often before a but: sore wa sou da kedo...

example.romaji: sore wa sou da kedo, ima wa okane ga nai.
example.ja: それはそうだけど、今はお金がない。
example.english: That's true, but I don't have the money right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa sou desu kedo, ima wa okane ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: それはそうですけど、今はお金がないんです。
examplePolite.english: That's true, but I don't have the money right now.

items.notes: Online, sore wa sou alone is a stock 'fair point'.

items.english: that could be it; that's part of it
items.use: Granting that something someone mentions is part of the reason.

example.romaji: a, sore wa aru kamo. saikin nete nai shi.
example.ja: あ、それはあるかも。最近寝てないし。
example.english: Oh, that could be it. I haven't been sleeping.

examplePolite.romaji: a, sore wa arimasu ne. saikin nete inai node.
examplePolite.ja: あ、それはありますね。最近寝ていないので。
examplePolite.english: Oh, that's a factor. I haven't been sleeping lately.

items.notes: Sore mo aru adds one more reason: 'that's part of it too'.

items.use: Agreeing that a remark is spot on, often something you hadn't put into words yourself.

example.romaji: ieteru. ano hito, itsumo okureru yo ne.
example.ja: 言えてる。あの人、いつも遅れるよね。
example.english: You said it. That guy's always late.

items.notes: Politely, say tashika ni or sou desu ne instead.

items.use: Changing your mind a little when someone gives a good counterpoint.

example.romaji: sore mo sou da ne. ja, ashita ni shiyou.
example.ja: それもそうだね。じゃ、明日にしよう。
example.english: Fair point. Let's do it tomorrow then.

examplePolite.romaji: sore mo sou desu ne. ja, ashita ni shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: それもそうですね。じゃ、明日にしましょう。
examplePolite.english: That's true. Let's make it tomorrow, then.

items.notes: Sore wa sou da kedo is the opposite move: granting the point, then pushing back.

items.use: Said when someone points out something you hadn't noticed but now see is true.

example.romaji: iwarete mireba, saikin kare minai ne.
example.ja: 言われてみれば、最近彼見ないね。
example.english: Now that you mention it, I haven't seen him lately.

examplePolite.romaji: iwarete mireba, saikin mikakemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 言われてみれば、最近見かけませんね。
examplePolite.english: Now that you mention it, I haven't seen him around lately.

items.notes: Often followed by tashika ni, 'that's true'.

blocks.label: I don't think so
blocks.rationale: Disagrees firmly or corrects a claim.
blocks.interference: sore wa nai rejects an idea, not a person; chigau chigau corrects a fact.

items.use: Disagreeing with someone's opinion, clearly but without attacking it.

example.romaji: uun, watashi wa sou wa omowanai kana.
example.ja: うーん、私はそうは思わないかな。
example.english: Hmm, I don't really think so.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa sou wa omoimasen kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 私はそうは思いませんけど。
examplePolite.english: I don't see it that way, myself.

items.notes: Adding kana or kedo softens it a lot; said bare, it can sound blunt.

items.use: Quick correction, often with a hand wave, when someone guesses or does it wrong.

example.romaji: chigau chigau, sotchi ja nakute kotchi!
example.ja: 違う違う、そっちじゃなくてこっち！
example.english: No, no, not that one, this one!

items.notes: Politely, a single iie, chigaimasu. chigau also means 'different'.

items.english: no way; that's not fair; that won't happen
items.use: Rejects an idea as impossible or unfair.

example.romaji: e, ashita made? sore wa nai yo.
example.ja: え、明日まで？それはないよ。
example.english: What, by tomorrow? No way.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita made desu ka? sore wa nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日までですか？それはないですよ。
examplePolite.english: By tomorrow? That's not fair.

items.use: Saying a fact or opinion is wrong; to omou keeps it from sounding like a flat correction.
items.kana: それはちがうとおもう
items.politeJa: それは違うと思います

example.romaji: iya, sore wa chigau to omou. kare wa warukunai yo.
example.ja: いや、それは違うと思う。彼は悪くないよ。
example.english: No, I don't think that's right. It's not his fault.

examplePolite.romaji: iie, sore wa chigau to omoimasu. kare wa warukunai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いいえ、それは違うと思います。彼は悪くないですよ。
examplePolite.english: No, I don't think that's right. He's not to blame.

items.notes: Chigau also means 'different'; here it means 'wrong'.

blocks.label: Getting to the point
blocks.rationale: Lets you sum up, give the reason, or reveal what really happened.
blocks.interference: honto wa (the truth is) is easy to mix up with the reaction honto? (really?).

items.use: Introduces what really happened or what you really want, against what was said or assumed.

example.romaji: honto wa, ikitakunakatta n da.
example.ja: ほんとは、行きたくなかったんだ。
example.english: Actually, I didn't want to go.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou wa, ikitakunakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 本当は、行きたくなかったんです。
examplePolite.english: To be honest, I didn't want to go.

items.notes: Hontou wa is the full form, used in careful speech.

items.use: Sums up what you or someone else said in a few words.

example.romaji: yousuru ni, okane ga nai tte koto?
example.ja: 要するに、お金がないってこと？
example.english: So basically, you're out of money?

examplePolite.romaji: yousuru ni, jikan ga tarinai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 要するに、時間が足りないんです。
examplePolite.english: In short, there isn't enough time.

items.notes: Used on someone else's long story, it can sound impatient.

items.use: Sets up an explanation and buys you a second to build it; finish with '...kara' or '...n da'.

example.romaji: nande ka tte iu to, kare ga uso tsuita kara.
example.ja: なんでかっていうと、彼が嘘ついたから。
example.english: And the reason is, he lied.

examplePolite.romaji: naze ka to iu to, jikan ga nakatta kara desu.
examplePolite.ja: なぜかというと、時間がなかったからです。
examplePolite.english: The reason is, there wasn't enough time.

items.notes: The same frame works with other question words: 'doko ga ii ka tte iu to' (what's good about it is...).

items.english: ...and that's the story; I hear that...
items.use: Wraps up a story with its point, or passes on something you heard.

example.romaji: de, kekkyoku saifu wa ie ni atta tte hanashi.
example.ja: で、結局財布は家にあったって話。
example.english: So the wallet was at home the whole time. That's the story.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkyoku, saifu wa ie ni atta tte hanashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: 結局、財布は家にあったって話です。
examplePolite.english: In the end, the wallet was at home all along.

items.notes: As hearsay: raigetsu kekkon suru tte hanashi da yo, 'I hear they're marrying next month'.

blocks.label: Opening a story
blocks.rationale: Lets you launch into a story or hook the listener before you start.
blocks.interference: mou ittakke? (did I tell you?) is easy to confuse with mou itta (I already said it).

items.english: a lot happened, so...; it's a long story
items.use: Hints at trouble without explaining; listeners usually don't press.

example.romaji: maa, iroiro atte, shigoto yameta n da.
example.ja: まあ、いろいろあって、仕事辞めたんだ。
example.english: Well, a lot happened, and I quit my job.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, iroiro atte, shigoto o yamemashita.
examplePolite.ja: まあ、いろいろあって、仕事を辞めました。
examplePolite.english: Well, it's a long story, but I quit my job.

items.notes: iroiro is 'all sorts'; iroiro arigatou is 'thanks for everything'.

items.use: Checks before sharing news so you don't repeat yourself; they'll say 'kiitenai' (you didn't) or 'kiita yo' (you did).

example.romaji: atarashii shigoto kimatta no, mou ittakke?
example.ja: 新しい仕事決まったの、もう言ったっけ？
example.english: Did I tell you I got a new job?

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu hikkosu koto, mou iimashitakke?
examplePolite.ja: 来月引っ越すこと、もう言いましたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Did I mention I'm moving next month?

items.notes: Itta (said) and itta (went) sound the same; context tells them apart.

items.use: Builds suspense before the payoff of a story; the listener answers 'e, dou natta no?'.
items.politeJa: どうなったと思いますか？

example.romaji: de, sono ato dou natta to omou?
example.ja: で、その後どうなったと思う？
example.english: So guess what happened after that?

examplePolite.romaji: sore de, kekka dou natta to omoimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それで、結果どうなったと思いますか？
examplePolite.english: And guess how it turned out?

items.notes: Swap in other question words: 'nani shita to omou?' (guess what he did?).

blocks.label: Own little slip-ups
blocks.rationale: Lets you own up to small everyday mistakes when you tell what happened.
blocks.interference: The -chatta endings blur together, and tsui ... shichatta needs a verb in the gap.

items.english: oops, I got it wrong; I made a mistake
items.use: Admit a slip like a wrong number, train or answer; the -chatta adds an 'oops'.

example.romaji: a, densha machigaechatta. tsugi de oriyou.
example.ja: あ、電車間違えちゃった。次で降りよう。
example.english: Oh, I got on the wrong train. Let's get off at the next stop.

examplePolite.romaji: a, densha o machigaete shimaimashita. tsugi de orimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、電車を間違えてしまいました。次で降ります。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I took the wrong train. I'll get off at the next stop.

items.notes: machigaeru is 'get something wrong'; machigatteru is 'it's wrong'.

items.use: The standard excuse for being late in the morning.

example.romaji: gomen, nebou shita! juppun okureru.
example.ja: ごめん、寝坊した！十分遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I overslept! I'll be ten minutes late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, nebou shimashita. juppun hodo okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、寝坊しました。十分ほど遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I overslept. I'll be about ten minutes late.

items.english: I couldn't help it; I ended up doing it without meaning to
items.use: Put tsui before a verb in -chatta to admit something you did on impulse: 'tsui tabechatta'.
items.politeJa: つい〜してしまいました

example.romaji: gomen, keeki tsui zenbu tabechatta.
example.ja: ごめん、ケーキつい全部食べちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I couldn't help eating all the cake.

examplePolite.romaji: seeru de tsui kaisugite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: セールでつい買いすぎてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I ended up buying too much at the sale.

items.notes: Tsui adds 'without meaning to'; -chatta alone already sounds a little regretful. Often said with a sheepish laugh.

items.english: I left something behind; I forgot something
items.use: When you realize you left something at home, on a train or in a shop.

example.romaji: a, wasuremono shita! chotto modoru ne.
example.ja: あ、忘れ物した！ちょっと戻るね。
example.english: Oh, I forgot something! I'll run back.

examplePolite.romaji: a, wasuremono o shimashita. chotto modorimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あ、忘れ物をしました。ちょっと戻ります。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I left something behind. I'll just go back.

items.notes: On trains you'll hear owasuremono in announcements reminding you not to leave things behind.

blocks.label: Hazy memory and hindsight
blocks.rationale: Lets you hedge details you are not sure of and look back on events.
blocks.interference: tashika (if I remember right) is not tashikani (certainly; true).

items.english: if I remember right; I'm pretty sure
items.use: Put it at the start to flag that you're going from memory and might be slightly off.

example.romaji: tashika raishuu no kayoubi datta yo.
example.ja: 確か来週の火曜日だったよ。
example.english: If I remember right, it's next Tuesday.

examplePolite.romaji: tashika sangatsu ni hikkoshita to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 確か三月に引っ越したと思います。
examplePolite.english: I'm pretty sure they moved in March.

items.notes: 'Tashika ni' is a different use: 'true, good point'. 'Tashika na' means 'certain, reliable'.

items.polite: yoku oboete inai n desu kedo
items.use: Hedges before a fuzzy memory so you're not held to the details.
items.kana: よくおぼえてないけど
items.politeJa: よく覚えていないんですけど

example.romaji: yoku oboetenai kedo, tabun gonen mae kana.
example.ja: よく覚えてないけど、たぶん五年前かな。
