example.english: I don't remember exactly, but maybe five years ago.

examplePolite.romaji: yoku oboete inai n desu kedo, tashika eki no chikaku deshita.
examplePolite.ja: よく覚えていないんですけど、確か駅の近くでした。
examplePolite.english: I don't remember well, but I think it was near the station.

items.notes: Oboeteru = 'remember (still have in mind)'; plain oboeru means 'to learn, memorize'.

items.use: Telling about a brief scare or mix-up; the thing you wrongly thought goes in the gap.
items.kana: いっしゅん〜かとおもった

example.romaji: isshun saifu otoshita ka to omotta.
example.ja: 一瞬財布落としたかと思った。
example.english: For a second I thought I'd lost my wallet.

examplePolite.romaji: isshun saifu o otoshita ka to omoimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一瞬財布を落としたかと思いました。
examplePolite.english: For a moment I thought I'd dropped my wallet.

items.notes: Isshun alone means 'an instant': isshun de, 'in no time'.

items.use: Opens a reflection on the past, often a mild regret or a late realization.

example.romaji: ima omoeba, ano toki yamete yokatta.
example.ja: 今思えば、あの時やめてよかった。
example.english: Looking back, I'm glad I quit back then.

examplePolite.romaji: ima omoeba, ii keiken deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 今思えば、いい経験でした。
examplePolite.english: Looking back, it was a good experience.

blocks.label: Had enough
blocks.rationale: Lets you vent that you are fed up or have reached your limit.
blocks.interference: The mou set starts alike: muri (can't), yada (hate it), dame (hopeless), ii (forget it); hottoite is harsh.

items.use: Give up on food, work or a situation; young people say it about small things too.

example.romaji: mou muri, kore ijou taberarenai.
example.ja: もう無理、これ以上食べられない。
example.english: I can't, I can't eat any more.

items.notes: muri is 'impossible'; muri shinaide is 'don't push yourself'.

items.english: ugh, I've had it; I hate this
items.use: Vents when something keeps going wrong or you're fed up; said to yourself or a close friend.

example.romaji: mata densha okureteru. mou yada!
example.ja: また電車遅れてる。もうやだ！
example.english: The train's late again. Ugh, I've had it!

items.notes: Yada is casual for iya da (I don't want it). Depending on tone it's playful or close to tears.

items.english: I can't go on; it's hopeless; I'm done for
items.use: Said when you're exhausted, overwhelmed or think it's all over.

example.romaji: mou dame, ashi ga ugokanai.
example.ja: もうダメ、足が動かない。
example.english: I can't go on, my legs won't move.

items.notes: dame alone is 'no good' or 'not allowed'; mou adds 'any more'.

items.use: Ends an argument or a request in frustration; it can sound cold.

example.romaji: mou ii, jibun de yaru.
example.ja: もういい、自分でやる。
example.english: Forget it, I'll do it myself.

examplePolite.romaji: mou ii desu. jibun de yarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: もういいです。自分でやります。
examplePolite.english: Never mind. I'll do it myself.

items.notes: Said calmly, mou ii desu politely turns down more food. As a question, mou ii? means 'ready?' or 'is that enough?'.

items.english: leave me alone; mind your own business
items.use: Pushes someone away when you're upset or don't want their help.
items.politeJa: 放っておいてください

example.romaji: mou hottoite yo. hitori ni shite.
example.ja: もうほっといてよ。一人にして。
example.english: Just leave me alone. Let me be by myself.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, shibaraku houtte oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、しばらく放っておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, please leave me be for a while.

items.notes: Short for houtte oite, from houtte oku (leave alone); hottoku is the spoken form.

blocks.label: Checking on someone
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask if a friend is okay or doing better.
blocks.interference: daijoubu desu ka is polite; with friends just daijoubu? is enough.

items.english: are you all right?; are you okay?
items.use: Said to a stranger or someone older who fell, looks unwell or seems lost; with friends just daijoubu?

example.romaji: a, daijoubu desu ka? tatemasu ka?
example.ja: あ、大丈夫ですか？立てますか？
example.english: Oh, are you all right? Can you stand?

items.notes: Daijoubu desu as an answer often means no thanks, as when you're offered a bag.

items.use: Notices a friend seems low and opens the door to talk; they answer 'chotto ne' or 'daijoubu'.

example.romaji: dou shita no? kyou genki nai ne.
example.ja: どうしたの？今日元気ないね。
example.english: What's up? You seem down today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa genki nai desu ne. daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は元気ないですね。大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: You seem down today. Are you okay?

items.notes: Not about health: genki here is energy and mood.

items.english: are you feeling better now?; are you okay now?
items.use: Asked after someone was sick, hurt or upset; the answer is un, mou daijoubu.

example.romaji: kaze, mou daijoubu? kinou tsurasou datta kedo.
example.ja: 風邪、もう大丈夫？昨日つらそうだったけど。
example.english: Is your cold better? You looked rough yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: ashi wa mou daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 足はもう大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: Is your leg okay now?

items.notes: As a statement, mou daijoubu means it's all right now, said to calm someone.

items.use: Asked right after someone falls or there's an accident.
items.politeJa: お怪我はありませんか

example.romaji: abunakatta! daijoubu? kega nai?
example.ja: 危なかった！大丈夫？ケガない？
example.english: That was close! Are you okay? Are you hurt?

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu ka? okega wa arimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですか？お怪我はありませんか？
examplePolite.english: Are you all right? Are you hurt?

items.notes: Kega means injury; kega shita means I got hurt.

blocks.label: Oh no moments
blocks.rationale: Lets you voice panic, nerves or being stuck.
blocks.interference: dou shiyou (what do I do?) is not dou suru? (what shall we do?).

items.english: what do I do?; oh no
items.use: Panicky self-talk when you're in trouble and don't know what to do.

example.romaji: dou shiyou, kagi nakushita.
example.ja: どうしよう、鍵なくした。
example.english: What do I do? I lost my keys.

examplePolite.romaji: dou shimashou, kagi o nakushite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: どうしましょう、鍵をなくしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: What should I do? I've lost my keys.

items.notes: Asked calmly, dou shiyou ka? just means 'what shall we do?' when planning.

items.use: Before an interview, a speech or meeting someone important; kinchou shiteru is 'I'm nervous right now'.

example.romaji: ashita mensetsu da kara, sugoku kinchou suru.
example.ja: 明日面接だから、すごく緊張する。
example.english: I've got an interview tomorrow, so I'm really nervous.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita mensetsu na node, totemo kinchou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日面接なので、とても緊張します。
examplePolite.english: I have an interview tomorrow, so I'm very nervous.

items.notes: Not 'excited': wakuwaku suru is the happy kind of nerves.

items.english: this is a problem; what do I do now?
items.use: Muttered when you're stuck; someone nearby may offer help: dou shita n desu ka? (what's wrong?).

example.romaji: komatta na, kagi ga mitsukaranai.
example.ja: 困ったな、鍵が見つからない。
example.english: This is a problem, I can't find my keys.

examplePolite.romaji: komarimashita ne, kagi ga mitsukarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 困りましたね、鍵が見つかりません。
examplePolite.english: This is a problem. I can't find my keys.

items.notes: Staff offer help with nanika okomari desu ka? (is something wrong?).

items.english: I won't make it in time; there's not enough time
items.use: Panic about a train or deadline; ma ni atta is 'made it!'

example.romaji: yabai, kono mama ja ma ni awanai!
example.ja: やばい、このままじゃ間に合わない！
example.english: Oh no, at this rate I won't make it!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kono mama da to ma ni aimasen.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、このままだと間に合いません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, at this rate I won't make it in time.

items.notes: ma ni atte imasu also politely declines: 'I'm fine, thanks, I have enough'.

blocks.label: Feeling relieved
blocks.rationale: Lets you say the worry is over.
blocks.interference: anshin shita and hotto shita are near-synonyms, and raku ni natta also means it got easier.

items.english: what a relief; I feel reassured
items.use: When news or someone's words remove a worry; tell others anshin shite (don't worry).

example.romaji: kekka, daijoubu datta. anshin shita.
example.ja: 結果、大丈夫だった。安心した。
example.english: The results were fine. What a relief.

examplePolite.romaji: kekka ga daijoubu de, anshin shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 結果が大丈夫で、安心しました。
examplePolite.english: I'm relieved the results were fine.

items.notes: The opposite is shinpai (worry).

items.use: The sigh when a worry ends: a test passed, someone arrived safe.

example.romaji: buji de yokatta. hotto shita yo.
example.ja: 無事でよかった。ほっとしたよ。
example.english: I'm so glad you're safe. What a relief.

examplePolite.romaji: buji de yokatta desu. hotto shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 無事でよかったです。ほっとしました。
examplePolite.english: I'm glad you're safe. What a relief.

items.notes: Close to anshin shita; hotto shita is the instant release, anshin the calm that follows.

items.english: I feel better; it got easier
items.use: After medicine, rest or a weight off your mind; also when a task gets easier.

example.romaji: kusuri nondara, daibu raku ni natta.
example.ja: 薬飲んだら、だいぶ楽になった。
example.english: After the medicine, I feel a lot better.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri o nondara, daibu raku ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 薬を飲んだら、だいぶ楽になりました。
examplePolite.english: I took the medicine and feel much better.

items.notes: raku is 'ease': raku ni shite kudasai is 'make yourself comfortable'.

blocks.label: Low moods
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you are down, torn or unmotivated.
blocks.interference: ochikonderu (feeling down) and nayanderu (torn, worrying over something) get swapped.

items.use: Says you're low after a setback; asked as 'ochikonderu?' to check on someone.

example.romaji: shiken ochite, chotto ochikonderu.
example.ja: 試験落ちて、ちょっと落ち込んでる。
example.english: I failed the exam, so I'm a bit down.

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto de shippai shite, ochikonde imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 仕事で失敗して、落ち込んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I messed up at work, and I'm feeling down.

items.notes: From ochikomu (to sink, get depressed); 'ochikomanaide' is 'don't be down'.

items.use: Complains you can't get started on work, study or chores.

example.romaji: ame da shi, nanka yaruki ga denai.
example.ja: 雨だし、なんかやる気が出ない。
example.english: It's raining, and I just can't get motivated.

examplePolite.romaji: getsuyoubi wa nakanaka yaruki ga demasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 月曜日はなかなかやる気が出ませんね。
examplePolite.english: It's hard to get motivated on Mondays.

items.notes: Yaruki = the drive to do something; 'yaruki aru ne' praises someone keen. Ga is often dropped: 'yaruki denai'.

items.english: I'm torn; something's weighing on me
items.use: Says you're stuck on a decision or worried about a problem; 'nani nayanderu no?' asks what's bothering someone.

example.romaji: tenshoku suru ka dou ka, zutto nayanderu.
example.ja: 転職するかどうか、ずっと悩んでる。
example.english: I keep going back and forth on whether to change jobs.

examplePolite.romaji: dore ni suru ka nayande imasu.
examplePolite.ja: どれにするか悩んでいます。
examplePolite.english: I can't decide which one to pick.

items.notes: Covers small choices (which dessert) and real worries; nayami is 'a worry'.

items.use: Turns down an activity because of how you feel right now, not because you're busy.
items.kana: そんなきぶんじゃない
items.politeJa: そんな気分じゃないです

example.romaji: gomen, kyou wa sonna kibun ja nai.
example.ja: ごめん、今日はそんな気分じゃない。
example.english: Sorry, I'm not in the mood today.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima wa chotto sonna kibun ja nai desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今はちょっとそんな気分じゃないです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm not really in the mood right now.

items.notes: Flip it for a craving: 'raamen no kibun' is 'I'm in the mood for ramen'.

blocks.label: Easing someone up
blocks.rationale: Lets you tell someone to relax, slow down or stop overthinking.
blocks.interference: yukkuri de ii yo and aseranakute ii yo mean the same, and ochitsuite can sound like a scolding.

items.use: Tells someone who's worrying that it's not as big a deal as they think.

example.romaji: daremo mitenai tte. ki ni shisugi da yo.
example.ja: 誰も見てないって。気にしすぎだよ。
example.english: Nobody's looking. You're overthinking it.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto nai desu yo. ki ni shisugi desu.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことないですよ。気にしすぎです。
examplePolite.english: That's not true. You're overthinking it.

items.notes: From ki ni suru (to worry about) plus -sugi (too much); 'ki ni shinaide' is 'don't worry about it'.

items.use: Encourages someone, or yourself, to relax about a task or situation.

example.romaji: shippai shite mo ii kara, kiraku ni ikou.
example.ja: 失敗してもいいから、気楽にいこう。
example.english: It's fine if it goes wrong, so let's take it easy.

examplePolite.romaji: hajimete desu kara, kiraku ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 初めてですから、気楽にいきましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's the first time, so let's keep it relaxed.

items.notes: Kiraku = carefree; 'kiraku ni ne' is a shorter, softer version.

items.use: Said to someone hurrying for your sake; people often say it when you're searching for words.
items.politeJa: ゆっくりでいいですよ

example.romaji: isoganakute ii kara, yukkuri de ii yo.
example.ja: 急がなくていいから、ゆっくりでいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to hurry. Take your time.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo, yukkuri de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ、ゆっくりでいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's all right, take your time.

items.notes: To ask someone to slow down: mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai.

items.use: Said to someone panicking, angry or rushing; soothing when said softly, sharp when shouted.

example.romaji: chotto ochitsuite. yukkuri hanashite.
example.ja: ちょっと落ち着いて。ゆっくり話して。
example.english: Calm down a bit. Talk slowly.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu kara, ochitsuite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですから、落ち着いてください。
examplePolite.english: It's okay, so please calm down.

items.notes: Ochitsuita describes a calm person or a quiet, relaxed place.

items.use: Reassures someone who is hurrying or panicking.
items.politeJa: 焦らなくていいですよ

example.romaji: jikan aru kara, aseranakute ii yo.
example.ja: 時間あるから、焦らなくていいよ。
example.english: We've got time, no need to rush.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan wa arimasu kara, aseranakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 時間はありますから、焦らなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: There's time, so no need to rush.

items.notes: Built from aseru (to panic, rush) plus -nakute ii (you don't have to).

blocks.label: Too much food or drink
blocks.rationale: Lets you say you are full, stuffed or drunk.
blocks.interference: tabesugita and nomisugita differ by one verb, and onaka ippai (full) is not mou ippai (one more).

items.use: Say when you can't eat any more, or to turn down seconds.

example.romaji: mou onaka ippai, taberarenai.
example.ja: もうお腹いっぱい、食べられない。
example.english: I'm full, I can't eat another bite.

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka ippai desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹いっぱいです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm full. Thank you for the meal.

items.notes: Also figurative: 'I've had enough of that'.

items.use: Groaned after a big meal; half complaint, half compliment to the cook.

example.romaji: aa, tabesugita. onaka ippai.
example.ja: あー、食べ過ぎた。お腹いっぱい。
example.english: Ugh, I ate too much. I'm stuffed.

examplePolite.romaji: oishikute, tabesugimashita.
examplePolite.ja: おいしくて、食べ過ぎました。
examplePolite.english: It was so good I ate too much.

items.notes: Onaka ippai means I'm full.

items.use: Groaned the night of or the morning after.

example.romaji: kinou nomisugita... atama itai.
example.ja: 昨日飲み過ぎた…頭痛い。
example.english: I drank too much last night... my head hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa chotto nomisugimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はちょっと飲み過ぎました。
examplePolite.english: I had a bit too much to drink yesterday.

items.notes: -sugita works on any verb: tabesugita (ate too much). A hangover is futsukayoi.

items.use: Say you've had too much; chotto yopparatta is 'I'm a bit tipsy'.

example.romaji: chotto yopparatta kamo. mizu choudai.
example.ja: ちょっと酔っ払ったかも。水ちょうだい。
example.english: I might be a bit drunk. Can I have some water?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto yopparatte shimaimashita. omizu o kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと酔っ払ってしまいました。お水をください。
examplePolite.english: I've had a bit too much. Could I have some water?

items.notes: yotta is a milder 'tipsy', and also means carsick or seasick.

items.use: Said when you're full and someone offers more.

example.romaji: gomen, mou taberarenai. onaka ippai.
example.ja: ごめん、もう食べられない。お腹いっぱい。
example.english: Sorry, I can't eat any more. I'm stuffed.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, mou taberaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう食べられません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I couldn't eat another thing.

items.notes: Many speakers drop the ra: mou taberenai.

blocks.label: Being moved
blocks.rationale: Lets you say a show, song or moment got to you.
blocks.interference: nakeru (it makes you cry) is not naku (to cry), and tereru is about your own blushing.

items.english: it makes you cry; such a tearjerker
items.use: Praise for a moving film, song or story; 'kono eiga, nakeru' is a recommendation.

example.romaji: kono eiga, saigo ga maji de nakeru.
example.ja: この映画、最後がマジで泣ける。
example.english: This movie's ending will totally make you cry.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hon wa hontou ni nakemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この本は本当に泣けますよ。
examplePolite.english: This book really makes you cry.

items.notes: Potential form of naku (to cry). Also sarcastic about something pathetic: 'how sad'.

items.english: so soothing; it melts my stress away
items.use: Reacts to something calming or cute: a cat video, a hot bath, a quiet café. Often drawn out: 'iyasareru~'.

example.romaji: kono neko no douga, hontou ni iyasareru.
example.ja: この猫の動画、本当に癒される。
example.english: This cat video is so soothing.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ongaku, iyasaremasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この音楽、癒されますね。
examplePolite.english: This music is so relaxing.

items.notes: Passive of iyasu (to heal); the noun iyashi means comfort, and 'iyashi-kei' is a soothing kind of person or thing.

items.use: Your shy reaction to a compliment; friends may tease back with 'tereteru!' (you're blushing!).

example.romaji: sonna ni homenaide yo, tereru.
example.ja: そんなに褒めないでよ、照れる。
example.english: Don't praise me so much, you're making me blush.

examplePolite.romaji: sou iwareru to teremasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そう言われると照れますね。
examplePolite.english: Hearing that makes me a little shy.

items.notes: Tereru is shyness at attention; for shame or awkwardness use 'hazukashii'.

blocks.label: Cheering someone on
blocks.rationale: Lets you encourage effort and praise it afterwards.
blocks.interference: yoku ganbatta ne is for effort already made, faito for effort ahead.

items.english: you did really well; great effort
items.use: Praise after someone finishes something hard, win or lose; often to kids or juniors.

example.romaji: shiai, oshikatta kedo yoku ganbatta ne.
example.ja: 試合、惜しかったけどよく頑張ったね。
example.english: The game was close, but you did really well.

examplePolite.romaji: nagai aida, yoku ganbarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 長い間、よく頑張りましたね。
examplePolite.english: You worked so hard for so long.

items.notes: It praises effort, not results. To a superior, otsukaresama deshita is safer.

items.english: don't overdo it; don't push yourself
items.use: Said to someone sick, tired or overworking; also to let someone off an invitation.
items.politeJa: 無理しないでください

example.romaji: netsu aru n desho? muri shinaide ne.
example.ja: 熱あるんでしょ？無理しないでね。
example.english: You've got a fever, right? Don't push yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii to omoimasu ga, muri shinaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 忙しいと思いますが、無理しないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: I know you're busy, but please don't overdo it.

items.notes: Muri means too much or impossible; muri! on its own means no way!

items.english: go for it!; you can do it!
items.use: Called out to cheer someone on in sport or before a challenge.

example.romaji: ashita shiken desho? faito!
example.ja: 明日試験でしょ？ファイト！
example.english: Your exam's tomorrow, right? You've got this!

items.notes: From English fight, but it means keep going. Ganbatte is the everyday word.

blocks.label: Inviting someone out
blocks.rationale: Lets you invite a friend to eat, drink or come along.
blocks.interference: The -nai? ending is an invitation, not "aren't you going?".

items.use: Casual invitation to eat out with a friend or coworker; the ni is dropped.

example.romaji: kondo no doyoubi, gohan ikanai?
example.ja: 今度の土曜日、ご飯行かない？
example.english: Want to get something to eat this Saturday?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, kondo gohan ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、今度ご飯行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you're free, would you like to get a meal sometime?

items.notes: Kondo gohan ikou ne can be a vague pleasantry rather than a real plan.

items.english: want to go for a drink?
items.use: Invites a friend or coworker out drinking; the negative question makes it easy to say no.

example.romaji: shigoto owattara, nomi ni ikanai?
example.ja: 仕事終わったら、飲みに行かない？
example.english: Want to go for a drink after work?

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, nomi ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今度、飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for a drink sometime?

items.notes: A nomikai is an organised drinking party with work or a club.

items.english: how about a tea or something?; want to grab a coffee?
items.use: Low-pressure invitation to sit and chat over a drink, at home or at a cafe.
items.politeJa: お茶でもいかがですか

example.romaji: jikan aru nara, ocha demo dou?
example.ja: 時間あるなら、お茶でもどう？
example.english: If you've got time, how about a coffee?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, ocha demo ikaga desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、お茶でもいかがですか？
examplePolite.english: If you like, would you care for some tea?

items.notes: Ocha suru means stopping at a cafe, not only drinking tea.

items.use: Invites someone to join something you're already going to do; 'iku iku!' is the eager yes.

example.romaji: ima kara konbini iku kedo, issho ni kuru?
example.ja: 今からコンビニ行くけど、一緒に来る？
example.english: I'm heading to the convenience store. Want to come along?

examplePolite.romaji: kore kara shokuji ni ikimasu kedo, issho ni kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これから食事に行きますけど、一緒に来ますか？
examplePolite.english: We're going to eat now. Would you like to come along?

items.notes: Use kuru when you're going and they join you; 'issho ni ikanai?' (shall we go together?) when it's a joint plan.

items.use: Invites a friend to your place; uchi here means 'my home', and dropping ni is normal in speech.

example.romaji: atarashii geemu katta n da. uchi kuru?
example.ja: 新しいゲーム買ったんだ。うち来る？
example.english: I bought a new game. Want to come over?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, kondo uchi ni kimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、今度うちに来ませんか？
examplePolite.english: If you'd like, why not come over sometime?

items.notes: Uchi can also mean 'our family' or 'our company', depending on context.

blocks.label: Finding a time and place
blocks.rationale: Lets you check if someone is free and pin down when and where.
blocks.interference: aiteru? (are you free?) is easy to mix up with aite (partner).

items.use: Asked before an invitation, with the day first: 'doyoubi aiteru?'. Answer 'aiteru yo' or 'gomen, chotto...'.

example.romaji: doyoubi no yoru, aiteru?
example.ja: 土曜日の夜、空いてる？
example.english: Are you free Saturday night?

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu no getsuyoubi wa aite imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 来週の月曜日は空いていますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you free next Monday?

items.notes: Also used for seats and rooms: 'kono seki aite imasu ka?' is 'is this seat free?'.

items.use: A soft lead-in to an invitation, usually with a time; answer 'betsu ni nai yo' (not really) if you're free.

example.romaji: kondo no nichiyoubi, nanika yotei aru?
example.ja: 今度の日曜日、何か予定ある？
example.english: Got any plans this Sunday?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no yoru wa nanika yotei arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日の夜は何か予定ありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any plans tonight?

items.english: when works for you?; when's good?
items.use: Asked when setting a date; answer with a day + ga ii, or X wa dou?

example.romaji: kondo nomi ni ikou yo. itsu ga ii?
example.ja: 今度飲みに行こうよ。いつがいい？
example.english: Let's go for a drink sometime. When works for you?

examplePolite.romaji: uchiawase wa itsu ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 打ち合わせはいつがいいですか？
examplePolite.english: When is good for the meeting?

items.notes: At work, itsu ga yoroshii desu ka is more polite.

items.use: Asked once you've picked a day; answer with a time, or suggest one: rokuji wa dou?

example.romaji: doyoubi ne. jaa, nanji ga ii?
example.ja: 土曜日ね。じゃあ、何時がいい？
example.english: Saturday, then. So what time works for you?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa nanji ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は何時がいいですか？
examplePolite.english: What time is good for you tomorrow?

items.notes: Nanji is what time; don't confuse it with nanjikan (how many hours).

items.use: Asked when making plans; answer with a place, or suggest one: eki de ii?
items.politeJa: どこで会いましょうか

example.romaji: doyoubi, doko de au? shibuya de ii?
example.ja: 土曜日、どこで会う？渋谷でいい？
example.english: Where shall we meet on Saturday? Is Shibuya okay?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa doko de aimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はどこで会いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: Where shall we meet tomorrow?

items.notes: Machiawase is the arrangement to meet; machiawase basho is the meeting spot.

blocks.label: Saying yes to plans
blocks.rationale: Lets you accept an invite with enthusiasm.
blocks.interference: tsukiau (keep you company) also means to date someone.

items.english: yeah, I can make it; sure, easy
items.use: A quick, upbeat yes when asked if you can make it, or encouragement that something is doable.

example.romaji: shichiji? ikeru ikeru, daijoubu.
example.ja: 7時？行ける行ける、大丈夫。
example.english: Seven? Yeah, I can make it, no problem.

items.notes: Also said about food or a challenge: 'kore ikeru' is 'this is pretty good' or 'I can do this'.

items.use: Jumps on board with a plan or idea someone just pitched; sounds keen and a bit playful.

example.romaji: onsen ryokou? sono hanashi, notta!
example.ja: 温泉旅行？その話、乗った！
example.english: A hot spring trip? Count me in!

items.notes: From noru (to get on board). Just 'notta!' works too.

items.english: I'll come along; I'll keep you company
items.use: Offers to join someone for something they need or want to do: shopping, a drink, waiting.

example.romaji: kaimono? ii yo, tsukiau yo.
example.ja: 買い物？いいよ、付き合うよ。
example.english: Shopping? Sure, I'll come with you.

examplePolite.romaji: yokereba, saigo made otsukiai shimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: よければ、最後までお付き合いしますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you like, I'll keep you company to the end.

items.notes: With a person, 'X to tsukiau' means 'to date X', and 'tsukiatte kudasai' can be a love confession, so watch the context.

items.use: An eager yes to an invitation or a request for help.

example.romaji: sasotte kurete arigatou. yorokonde iku yo!
example.ja: 誘ってくれてありがとう。喜んで行くよ！
example.english: Thanks for inviting me. I'd love to come!

examplePolite.romaji: yorokonde otetsudai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 喜んでお手伝いします。
examplePolite.english: I'd be glad to help.

items.notes: Some izakaya staff shout hai, yorokonde! when they take an order.

blocks.label: Turning down softly
blocks.rationale: Lets you say no to an invite without bluntness.
blocks.interference: kyou wa chotto works because it trails off, so don't finish the sentence.

items.use: Turns down an invitation by trailing off; the unfinished sentence is the polite no, so no long excuse is needed.

example.romaji: gomen, kyou wa chotto... ashita nara ii yo.
example.ja: ごめん、今日はちょっと…明日ならいいよ。
example.english: Sorry, today's not great... tomorrow works, though.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyou wa chotto...
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今日はちょっと…
examplePolite.english: Sorry, today's a bit difficult...

items.notes: Chotto... alone works for any request you'd rather refuse.

items.use: The standard soft refusal: say it and trail off, and the other person understands it's a no.

example.romaji: ikitai kedo, ashita hayai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 行きたいけど、明日早いんだよね。
example.english: I'd love to, but I've got an early start tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ikitai n desu kedo, sono hi wa chotto...
examplePolite.ja: 行きたいんですけど、その日はちょっと…
examplePolite.english: I'd love to, but that day's a bit...

items.notes: Leaving the sentence hanging is the polite part; you don't have to spell out the reason.

items.use: A light, friendly way to skip an outing without a long excuse; fine with friends, too blunt with a boss.

example.romaji: gomen, tsukareteru kara kyou wa pasu.
example.ja: ごめん、疲れてるから今日はパス。
example.english: Sorry, I'm tired, so I'll pass today.

items.notes: Pasu works for anything you skip: food, a turn in a game, a question you won't answer.

items.use: Polite no to an offer or invitation, softer than kekkou desu.
items.kana: えんりょしておきます

example.romaji: kyou wa enryo shite okimasu. mata sasotte kudasai.
example.ja: 今日は遠慮しておきます。また誘ってください。
example.english: I'll pass today. Please ask me again.

items.notes: Casual version: enryo shitoku. Enryo means holding back.

blocks.label: Deciding what to do
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask what to do and show you are easy either way.
blocks.interference: dou suru? (what shall we do?) is not dou shiyou (what do I do?!).

items.english: what do you want to do?; what shall we do?
items.use: Asks a friend to decide or pick between options; answer with your choice plus ni suru, or dotchi demo ii.

example.romaji: ame da kedo, dou suru? ie de eiga miru?
example.ja: 雨だけど、どうする？家で映画見る？
example.english: It's raining. What do you want to do? Watch a movie at home?

examplePolite.romaji: ame desu ne. dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨ですね。どうしますか？
examplePolite.english: It's raining. What shall we do?

items.notes: Dou shiyou (what do I do?) is the worried version you say to yourself.

items.use: Tells someone you don't mind which; add yo to sound easygoing rather than bored.

example.romaji: ramen demo sushi demo, dotchi demo ii yo.
example.ja: ラーメンでも寿司でも、どっちでもいいよ。
example.english: Ramen or sushi, either's fine with me.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa dochira demo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私はどちらでもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Either is fine with me.

items.notes: Said flatly it can sound like you don't care. Nan demo ii means anything is fine.

items.english: what shall we eat?; what are you having?
items.use: Asks a friend what they want for a meal or what they're ordering.

example.romaji: hirugohan, nani taberu? ramen?
example.ja: 昼ご飯、何食べる？ラーメン？
example.english: What should we have for lunch? Ramen?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no hirugohan, nani tabemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日の昼ご飯、何食べますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you having for lunch today?

items.notes: With a menu in hand, nani ni suru? (what are you getting?) is just as common.

items.english: I'll fit around you; whatever suits you
items.use: Your answer when someone asks when or where to meet, handing them the choice.

example.romaji: itsu demo ii yo. sotchi ni awaseru yo.
example.ja: いつでもいいよ。そっちに合わせるよ。
example.english: Any time's fine. I'll fit around you.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa itsu demo daijoubu desu. awasemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 私はいつでも大丈夫です。合わせますよ。
examplePolite.english: Any time works for me. I'll fit around you.

items.notes: Literally 'I'll match (you)'. The polite version is often 'sochira ni awasemasu'.

items.use: Said with confidence when you take on a job someone is worried about.

example.romaji: ryouri? makasete! tokui da kara.
example.ja: 料理？任せて！得意だから。
example.english: Cooking? Leave it to me, I'm good at it.

examplePolite.romaji: sono ken wa watashi ni makasete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: その件は私に任せてください。
examplePolite.english: Please leave that to me.

items.notes: Makaseru means to entrust. Omakase at a sushi bar means chef's choice.

blocks.label: Settling the plan
blocks.rationale: Lets you agree on a choice and lock it in.
blocks.interference: sou shiyou (let's do that) and sou suru (I'll do that) differ in who acts.

items.use: Agrees to a plan someone just suggested.

example.romaji: ii ne, sou shiyou!
example.ja: いいね、そうしよう！
example.english: Good idea, let's do that!

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne. sou shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: いいですね。そうしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Sounds good. Let's do that.

items.notes: Sou suru (I'll do that) is about your own action only, e.g. when you take someone's advice.

items.use: Settles a plan or choice someone just suggested; to staff add onegai shimasu.
items.politeJa: じゃあそれでお願いします

example.romaji: rokuji ni eki? un, jaa sore de.
example.ja: 6時に駅？うん、じゃあそれで。
example.english: Six at the station? Okay, let's go with that.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, sore de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、それでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Okay, I'll go with that, please.

items.use: Closes the planning once everyone agrees on a time or place; often 'jaa, kimari ne!'.

example.romaji: jaa, doyoubi no juuniji ni eki de. kimari!
example.ja: じゃあ、土曜日の12時に駅で。決まり！
example.english: So, noon Saturday at the station. It's a deal!

items.notes: From kimaru (to be decided); 'mou kimatteru' means it's already settled.

items.use: Seals a plan or favour so the other person can't back out; they answer 'un, yakusoku'.

example.romaji: kondo wa zettai kite ne. yakusoku ne.
example.ja: 今度は絶対来てね。約束ね。
example.english: You'd better come next time. Promise?

examplePolite.romaji: kondo wa zettai kite kudasai ne. yakusoku desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今度は絶対来てくださいね。約束ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please make sure you come next time. It's a promise.

items.notes: Yakusoku suru is 'to promise'; 'yakusoku ga aru' means 'I have plans with someone'.

blocks.label: On the way
blocks.rationale: Lets you check where someone is and report where you are.
blocks.interference: tsuita (I've arrived) and tsuku (I will arrive) get swapped.

items.use: The standard text or call when meeting up; answer with a place + da yo, or ima mukatteru.

example.romaji: ima doko? mou eki ni tsuita yo.
example.ja: 今どこ？もう駅に着いたよ。
example.english: Where are you? I'm already at the station.

examplePolite.romaji: ima doko desu ka? kaisatsu no mae ni imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今どこですか？改札の前にいます。
examplePolite.english: Where are you now? I'm in front of the ticket gates.

items.notes: To someone senior, ima dochira desu ka sounds more polite.

items.use: Texted or said when someone asks where you are; add a place + ni to say where you're heading.

example.romaji: ima mukatteru! juppun gurai de tsuku.
example.ja: 今向かってる！10分ぐらいで着く。
example.english: I'm on my way! I'll be there in about ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: ima eki ni mukatte imasu. sugu tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今駅に向かっています。すぐ着きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm heading to the station now. I'll be there soon.

items.notes: Mukau means head toward. Ima iku is closer to I'm coming right now.

items.use: Texted or said when you're close; often with yo, or kara to mean so hang on.

example.romaji: mou sugu tsuku yo. ato gofun.
example.ja: もうすぐ着くよ。あと5分。
example.english: I'm almost there. Five more minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, mou sugu tsukimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、もうすぐ着きます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm almost there.

items.notes: Mou sugu means very soon and works with other verbs: mou sugu owaru (almost done).

items.use: Texted or said when you reach the meeting place; add where: eki ni tsuita yo.

example.romaji: tsuita yo. kitaguchi no mae ni iru.
example.ja: 着いたよ。北口の前にいる。
example.english: I'm here. I'm in front of the north exit.

examplePolite.romaji: ima tsukimashita. iriguchi no mae ni imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今着きました。入口の前にいます。
examplePolite.english: I just got here. I'm in front of the entrance.

items.notes: Past tense because you've already arrived. Mou tsuita? means are you there yet?

items.english: I'll be waiting; I'll wait for you
items.use: Said to someone on their way, or warmly at a goodbye to mean see you then.

example.romaji: wakatta. jaa, kafe de matteru ne.
example.ja: わかった。じゃあ、カフェで待ってるね。
example.english: Okay. I'll wait for you at the café, then.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita. robii de matte imasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: わかりました。ロビーで待っていますね。
examplePolite.english: Understood. I'll be waiting in the lobby.

items.notes: To customers or seniors, omachi shite imasu is the humble version.

blocks.label: No I mean
blocks.rationale: Corrects yourself or takes something back.
blocks.interference: sou ja nakute fixes your own words; chotto chigau kana gently fixes theirs.

items.english: no, I mean...; that's not what I meant
items.use: Correct a misunderstanding, then say what you actually meant.

example.romaji: sou ja nakute, ashita no hanashi da yo.
example.ja: そうじゃなくて、明日の話だよ。
example.english: No, I mean tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: sou ja nakute, ashita no hanashi desu.
examplePolite.ja: そうじゃなくて、明日の話です。
examplePolite.english: No, I'm talking about tomorrow.

items.notes: In formal talk: sou de wa nakute.

items.use: A soft way to say someone's guess or summary is off, or to correct your own word.
items.politeJa: ちょっと違うかもしれません

example.romaji: un, demo chotto chigau kana.
example.ja: うん、でもちょっと違うかな。
example.english: Yeah, but not quite, I think.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa chotto chigau kamo shiremasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: それはちょっと違うかもしれませんね。
examplePolite.english: That might not be quite right.

items.notes: A flat 'chigau' (wrong) to someone's face sounds harsh; chotto and kana soften it.

items.english: scratch that; forget what I said
items.use: Takes back something you just said or did, like an embarrassing slip or a bad move in a game.

example.romaji: a, gomen, ima no nashi! wasurete.
example.ja: あ、ごめん、今のなし！忘れて。
example.english: Oh, sorry, scratch that! Forget it.

items.notes: Nashi = 'doesn't count'; its opposite ari means 'allowed': 'sore ari?' is 'is that allowed?'.

items.use: Said when someone asks what's wrong or what you said, and you'd rather drop it.

example.romaji: e? a, nan demo nai. ki ni shinaide.
example.ja: え？あ、何でもない。気にしないで。
example.english: Huh? Oh, it's nothing. Don't worry.

examplePolite.romaji: a, nan demo arimasen. ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: あ、何でもありません。気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Oh, it's nothing. Please don't worry.

items.notes: Don't confuse with nan demo ii (anything is fine).

blocks.label: Did I get it
blocks.rationale: Checks you understood or were understood.
blocks.interference: atteru asks if you're right; kikoeru is for bad audio or calls.

items.english: is that right?; did I get it right?
items.use: Checks your guess, answer, route or pronunciation; the answer is 'atteru yo' (right) or 'chotto chigau' (not quite).

example.romaji: kono michi de atteru?
example.ja: この道で合ってる？
example.english: Is this the right way?

examplePolite.romaji: kono hatsuon de atte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この発音で合っていますか？
examplePolite.english: Is my pronunciation right?

items.notes: 'X de atteru?' = 'is X right?'. Also used for fit: 'saizu atteru' (the size fits).

items.use: Checks that a clumsy explanation landed; the answer is 'un, wakaru wakaru' if it did.
items.politeJa: 言いたいことわかりますか？

example.romaji: umaku ienai kedo, iitai koto wakaru?
example.ja: うまく言えないけど、言いたいことわかる？
example.english: I can't put it well, but you know what I mean?

examplePolite.romaji: setsumei ga heta desu kedo, iitai koto wakarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 説明が下手ですけど、言いたいことわかりますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm bad at explaining, but do you see what I mean?

items.notes: Said sharply in an argument, it becomes a challenge: 'do you get it?'.

items.use: Said on a bad phone or video call; the answer is kikoeru yo or kikoenai.

example.romaji: moshimoshi? kikoeru? denpa warui mitai.
example.ja: もしもし？聞こえる？電波悪いみたい。
example.english: Hello? Can you hear me? The signal seems bad.

examplePolite.romaji: moshimoshi, kikoemasu ka? koe ga tooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もしもし、聞こえますか？声が遠いですね。
examplePolite.english: Hello, can you hear me? You sound far away.

items.notes: Kikoeru means can be heard, so the sound takes ga: koe ga kikoeru. It also asks did you hear that? about a noise.

blocks.label: Joking around
blocks.rationale: Lets you mark a joke, ask for the punchline, or admit one bombed.
blocks.interference: uso uso (just kidding) is not the reaction uso! (no way!).

items.use: Take back a tease, or a joke someone took seriously.

example.romaji: uso uso, joudan da yo. okotta?
example.ja: うそうそ、冗談だよ。怒った？
example.english: Nah, just kidding. Are you mad?

examplePolite.romaji: joudan desu yo. ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談ですよ。気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Just kidding. Don't take it seriously.

items.notes: uso uso (literally 'lie, lie') is another quick 'just kidding'.

items.use: Takes back a tease or a fake-out right after saying it, usually with a laugh.

example.romaji: ashita tesuto da yo. uso uso, joudan.
example.ja: 明日テストだよ。うそうそ、冗談。
example.english: There's a test tomorrow. Just kidding, joking!

items.notes: A single 'uso!' is the opposite move: 'no way!' when you hear surprising news.

items.use: A teasing demand at the end of a flat story; Japanese banter expects stories to land on a payoff.

example.romaji: e, sore de owari? ochi wa?
example.ja: え、それで終わり？オチは？
example.english: Wait, that's it? Where's the punchline?

items.notes: Kansai-flavoured but heard everywhere. Ochi = the payoff of a story or joke.

items.english: that joke bombed; it fell flat
items.use: Admits or points out that a joke got no laugh; saying it about yourself helps you recover.

example.romaji: daremo warawanai... kanzen ni subetta.
example.ja: 誰も笑わない…完全にすべった。
example.english: Nobody's laughing... that totally bombed.

items.notes: Literally 'slipped', so it also means 'I slipped'. The opposite is ukeru: the joke lands.

items.use: Said while revealing something you're proud of.

example.romaji: jaan! kore, tezukuri no keeki.
example.ja: ジャーン！これ、手作りのケーキ。
example.english: Ta-da! I made this cake myself.

examplePolite.romaji: jaan! kore, tezukuri no keeki desu.
examplePolite.ja: ジャーン！これ、手作りのケーキです。
examplePolite.english: Ta-da! I made this cake myself.

items.notes: jajaan adds more drama.

blocks.label: Laughing it off
blocks.rationale: Lets you deny or shrug off teasing.
blocks.interference: sore ga nanika? (so what?) can sound combative if said flat.

items.english: no way; not at all; nope
items.use: Laughs off a suggestion, like being asked if you're dating someone.

example.romaji: kanojo? nai nai, tada no tomodachi.
example.ja: 彼女？ないない、ただの友達。
example.english: Girlfriend? No way, she's just a friend.

examplePolite.romaji: nai nai, tada no tomodachi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ないない、ただの友達ですよ。
examplePolite.english: No, no, she's just a friend.

items.notes: Also said while searching: 'it's not here, not here'.

items.use: Reassures someone that what they noticed or feared isn't real; also a teasing brush-off.

example.romaji: futotta? ki no sei da yo.
example.ja: 太った？気のせいだよ。
example.english: 'Have I put on weight?' Nah, it's just your imagination.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai shinakute ii desu yo. ki no sei desu.
examplePolite.ja: 心配しなくていいですよ。気のせいです。
examplePolite.english: No need to worry. It's just your imagination.

items.notes: Ki no sei says it isn't real at all; 'ki ni shisugi' says it's real but small.

items.use: Playful disbelief when someone flatters you or brags.

example.romaji: mata mata, joudan bakkari.
example.ja: またまた、冗談ばっかり。
example.english: Oh, come on, always joking.

examplePolite.romaji: mata mata, joudan deshou?
examplePolite.ja: またまた、冗談でしょう？
examplePolite.english: Oh, come on, you're joking.

items.notes: Not 'again' here, though mata alone means again.

items.english: so what?; is there a problem?
items.use: Cool, defensive comeback when someone points something out about you.

example.romaji: hitori de kita yo. sore ga nanika?
example.ja: 一人で来たよ。それが何か？
example.english: I came alone. So what?

examplePolite.romaji: hitori de kimashita kedo, sore ga nanika?
examplePolite.ja: 一人で来ましたけど、それが何か？
examplePolite.english: I came alone. Is there a problem?

items.notes: Sounds icy even in polite speech.

blocks.label: Stop teasing me
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask someone to ease off when they tease you.
blocks.interference: yamete can sound truly upset, so tone carries the playfulness.

items.use: Tell someone to stop, from playful teasing to real danger.

example.romaji: chotto, yamete yo! kusuguttai!
example.ja: ちょっと、やめてよ！くすぐったい！
example.english: Hey, stop it! That tickles!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sore, yamete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、それ、やめてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please stop that.

items.notes: yamero is the harsh command form you'll hear in dramas; yamete is softer and used by anyone.

items.use: A half-laughing protest when friends tease you, especially about love or a slip-up.
items.politeJa: からかわないでください

example.romaji: mou, karakawanaide yo! sonna n ja nai tte.
example.ja: もう、からかわないでよ！そんなんじゃないって。
example.english: Come on, stop teasing me! It's not like that.

examplePolite.romaji: senpai, karakawanaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: 先輩、からかわないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Come on, stop teasing me.

items.notes: Karakau = to tease; 'karakatta dake' is 'I was only teasing'.

items.use: An exasperated plea when something is too much: more work, a bad joke, another delay.

example.romaji: mata zangyou? kanben shite yo.
example.ja: また残業？勘弁してよ。
example.english: Overtime again? Give me a break.

examplePolite.romaji: kore ijou wa kanben shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これ以上は勘弁してください。
examplePolite.english: Please, no more than this.

items.notes: Kanben is forgiveness, so it's literally 'spare me'.

blocks.label: Told you so
blocks.rationale: Lets you gloat when you were right or a habit repeats.
blocks.interference: hora ne (see? told you) is not hora (look!).

items.use: Said when something turns out just as you predicted.

example.romaji: hora ne, yappari ame futta.
example.ja: ほらね、やっぱり雨降った。
example.english: See? It rained, just like I said.

examplePolite.romaji: hora ne, yappari ame ga furimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ほらね、やっぱり雨が降りました。
examplePolite.english: See? It rained after all.

items.notes: hora alone means 'look' or 'here you go': hora, kore.

items.polite: dakara itta ja nai desu ka
items.use: Said, a bit reproachfully, when someone ignored your warning.
items.ja: だから言ったじゃない
items.kana: だからいったじゃない
items.politeJa: だから言ったじゃないですか

example.romaji: dakara itta ja nai. kasa iru tte.
example.ja: だから言ったじゃない。傘いるって。
example.english: I told you so. I said you'd need an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: dakara itta ja nai desu ka. kasa ga iru tte.
examplePolite.ja: だから言ったじゃないですか。傘がいるって。
examplePolite.english: I told you. I said you'd need an umbrella.

items.notes: Men often say dakara itta daro.

items.use: An eye-roll reaction when someone starts their usual rant, boast or habit, often said to a third person.

example.romaji: mata hajimatta yo, buchou no jiman banashi.
example.ja: また始まったよ、部長の自慢話。
example.english: Here we go again, the boss bragging.

blocks.label: Calling out bragging
blocks.rationale: Lets you poke fun at someone showing off.
blocks.interference: yoku iu (look who's talking) uses the same words as yoku iu (often say).

items.use: A teasing comeback when a friend shows off; they may deny it ('chigau yo!') or own it ('jiman da yo').

example.romaji: mata atarashii fuku? sore jiman?
example.ja: また新しい服？それ自慢？
example.english: New clothes again? Are you showing off?

items.notes: Jiman suru is 'to brag'; 'jiman no ...' means 'my prized ...'.

items.use: A playful jab when someone praises themselves, like calling themselves good-looking or a genius.

example.romaji: tensai tte, sore jibun de iu?
example.ja: 天才って、それ自分で言う？
example.english: Calling yourself a genius? Really?

items.english: look who's talking; you've got some nerve
items.use: Sarcastic reply when someone says something shameless or hypocritical.

example.romaji: yoku iu yo, jibun mo okureta kuse ni.
example.ja: よく言うよ、自分も遅れたくせに。
example.english: Look who's talking, you were late too.

examplePolite.romaji: yoku iimasu ne. jibun mo okureta no ni.
examplePolite.ja: よく言いますね。自分も遅れたのに。
examplePolite.english: You've got some nerve. You were late too.

items.notes: In a plain statement, yoku iu means 'people often say'.

items.use: Puts down someone getting too full of themselves after a success; among friends it's often a joke.

example.romaji: ichido katta dake de choushi ni noru na yo.
example.ja: 一度勝っただけで調子に乗るなよ。
example.english: You won once, don't get cocky.

items.notes: The softer version is 'choushi ni noranaide'; 'choushi notteru' means 'getting carried away' or 'on a roll'.

blocks.label: Managing a long story
blocks.rationale: Hands the turn over, takes it back, and keeps a long story on track.
blocks.interference: kke marks trying to recall (doko made hanashita kke), not a plain question.

items.use: Wraps up a story or explanation and signals you're done talking; also a vague 'something like that'.

example.romaji: de, kekkyoku wakareta. maa, sonna kanji.
example.ja: で、結局別れた。まあ、そんな感じ。
example.english: So in the end we broke up. So yeah, that's about it.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin no shigoto wa maa, sonna kanji desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近の仕事はまあ、そんな感じです。
examplePolite.english: So that's work lately, more or less.

items.notes: 'Sonna kanji?' as a question asks 'like this?' when you check a rough idea.

items.use: Tells someone to carry on after an interruption, or to keep telling their story.

example.romaji: gomen, jama shita. tsuzukete.
example.ja: ごめん、邪魔した。続けて。
example.english: Sorry for interrupting. Go on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, douzo tsuzukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、どうぞ続けてください。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, please go on.

items.notes: From tsuzukeru (to continue something); 'tsuzuki wa?' asks 'and then what?'.

items.english: I'm all ears; tell me about it
items.use: Offers to listen to someone who's upset or has something on their mind.

example.romaji: nanka atta? hanashi kiku yo.
example.ja: なんかあった？話聞くよ。
example.english: Something happen? I'm here to listen.

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, ohanashi kikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、お話聞きますよ。
examplePolite.english: If you'd like, I'm happy to listen.

items.use: Warns the listener before a long explanation and checks they have time.

example.romaji: nagaku naru kedo, kiite kureru?
example.ja: 長くなるけど、聞いてくれる？
example.english: It's a long story, but will you hear me out?

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi ga nagaku narimasu kedo, ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 話が長くなりますけど、いいですか？
examplePolite.english: It'll take a while to explain. Is that okay?

items.notes: 'Hanashi ga nagai' is a complaint about someone: 'they talk too long'.

items.use: Pick up a story after an interruption.
items.kana: どこまではなしたっけ
items.politeJa: どこまで話しましたっけ

example.romaji: etto, doko made hanashita kke?
example.ja: えっと、どこまで話したっけ？
example.english: Um, where was I?

examplePolite.romaji: etto, doko made hanashimashita kke?
examplePolite.ja: えっと、どこまで話しましたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Um, where was I?

items.notes: kke turns a question into 'what was it again?': namae nan datta kke?

blocks.label: Got a minute
blocks.rationale: Opens a request, a serious talk, or a call for attention.
blocks.interference: chotto hanashi ga aru can sound ominous; nanka you? is blunt.

items.english: is now a good time?; got a minute?
items.use: Asked at the start of a call or before interrupting someone; answer un, daijoubu or gomen, ato de.

example.romaji: moshimoshi, ima daijoubu? chotto kikitai koto ga atte.
example.ja: もしもし、今大丈夫？ちょっと聞きたいことがあって。
example.english: Hi, is now a good time? There's something I want to ask.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima daijoubu desu ka? sugu sumimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今大丈夫ですか？すぐ済みます。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, do you have a moment? It won't take long.

items.notes: To a boss or client, ima ojikan yoroshii desu ka is safer.

items.romaji: chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo
items.polite: chotto ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo
items.english: there's something I want to talk to you about
items.use: Asks for a serious talk, and can make the listener nervous; they'll answer 'nani?' or 'ima?'.
items.ja: ちょっと話があるんだけど
items.kana: ちょっとはなしがあるんだけど
items.politeJa: ちょっとお話があるんですけど

example.romaji: ima ii? chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: 今いい？ちょっと話があるんだけど。
example.english: Got a sec? There's something I need to talk about.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっとお話があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, there's something I'd like to discuss.

items.notes: Ending on kedo leaves the request hanging, which is the polite part.

items.romaji: onegai ga aru n da kedo
items.polite: onegai ga aru n desu ga
items.english: I have a favour to ask
items.use: Opens a bigger favour; the other person usually answers nani? and then you explain.
items.ja: お願いがあるんだけど
items.kana: おねがいがあるんだけど
items.politeJa: お願いがあるんですが

example.romaji: nee, chotto onegai ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ねえ、ちょっとお願いがあるんだけど。
example.english: Hey, I've got a favour to ask.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, onegai ga aru n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お願いがあるんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, I have a favour to ask.

items.use: Call to someone far off or not paying attention; also 'anyone there?'

example.romaji: ooi, kotchi da yo! hayaku oide!
example.ja: おーい、こっちだよ！早くおいで！
example.english: Hey, over here! Come on!

items.notes: To get a stranger's attention, say sumimasen instead.

items.english: what do you want?; what is it?
items.use: Asked when someone calls you or turns up; can sound curt depending on tone.

example.romaji: nanka you? ima chotto isogashii n da kedo.
example.ja: 何か用？今ちょっと忙しいんだけど。
example.english: What is it? I'm a bit busy right now.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika goyou desu ka? ima chotto isogashii n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: 何かご用ですか？今ちょっと忙しいんですが。
examplePolite.english: Can I help you? I'm a bit busy right now.

items.notes: nanika you? is the same, a touch less blunt. Staff use the polite form to mean 'Can I help you?'.

blocks.label: Late or out of touch
blocks.rationale: Lets you apologise for keeping someone waiting or going quiet.
blocks.interference: matta? (did you wait?) is not matte (wait).

items.use: Said as you arrive late; the usual answer is ii yo or daijoubu.

example.romaji: okurete gomen! densha ga tomatteta n da.
example.ja: 遅れてごめん！電車が止まってたんだ。
example.english: Sorry I'm late! The train was stopped.

examplePolite.romaji: okurete sumimasen. michi ni mayotte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 遅れてすみません。道に迷ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry I'm late. I got lost.

items.notes: At work, okurete moushiwake arimasen is the stronger apology.

items.english: sorry to keep you waiting; here I am
items.use: Said when you reach a friend who has been waiting, even a minute; they often answer zenzen (not at all).

example.romaji: gomen, omatase! ikou ka.
example.ja: ごめん、お待たせ！行こうか。
example.english: Sorry to keep you waiting! Shall we go?

examplePolite.romaji: omatase shimashita. sumimasen, densha ga okurete.
examplePolite.ja: お待たせしました。すみません、電車が遅れて。
examplePolite.english: Sorry to keep you waiting. My train was late.

items.notes: Also said when handing over something people were waiting for, like food you cooked.

items.english: did you wait long?; have you been waiting?
items.use: Asked when you meet someone who got there first; the classic answer is uun, ima kita tokoro (no, I just got here).

example.romaji: gomen, matta? uun, ima kita tokoro.
example.ja: ごめん、待った？ううん、今来たところ。
example.english: Sorry, did you wait long? No, I just got here.

items.notes: Shouted, matta! means hold on! or wait!

items.english: sorry I haven't been in touch
items.use: Opens a message or meeting with a friend you've gone quiet on; they'll usually brush it off with 'ii yo, ii yo'.
items.kana: れんらくしなくてごめん
items.politeJa: 連絡しなくてすみません

example.romaji: zutto renraku shinakute gomen ne. genki datta?
example.ja: ずっと連絡しなくてごめんね。元気だった？
example.english: Sorry I haven't been in touch for so long. How've you been?

examplePolite.romaji: nagai aida renraku shinakute sumimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 長い間連絡しなくてすみませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry I haven't been in touch for so long.

items.notes: With people you should be formal with, the set phrase is 'gobusata shite imasu'.

items.use: Said or texted when you call back after missing someone's call.
items.ja: 電話出られなくてごめん
items.kana: でんわでられなくてごめん
items.politeJa: お電話に出られずすみませんでした

example.romaji: denwa derarenakute gomen. dou shita no?
example.ja: 電話出られなくてごめん。どうしたの？
example.english: Sorry I missed your call. What's up?

examplePolite.romaji: sakki wa odenwa ni derarezu sumimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: さっきはお電話に出られずすみませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry I couldn't take your call earlier.

items.notes: Denwa ni deru means answer the phone; casual speech drops the ni.

blocks.label: At the table
blocks.rationale: Lets you toast, treat, and call people to eat.
blocks.interference: ogoru (to treat) and okoru (to get angry) sound close.

items.use: The toast that starts the drinking; wait until everyone has a glass before the first sip.

example.romaji: jaa minna, otsukaresama! kanpai!
example.ja: じゃあみんな、お疲れさま！乾杯！
example.english: Okay everyone, good work today! Cheers!

examplePolite.romaji: dewa minasan, kanpai shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: では皆さん、乾杯しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Well, everyone, let's raise a toast.

items.notes: At work dinners someone usually gives a short toast speech first.

items.use: Offers to pay for a friend's food or drinks; they usually answer ii no? before accepting.

example.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga ogoru yo.
example.ja: 今日は私がおごるよ。
example.english: Today's on me.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gochisou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は私がごちそうします。
examplePolite.english: Today's my treat.

items.notes: The treat itself is ogori; ogotte means treat me.

items.use: Called out at home, usually by a parent, to get everyone to the table.

example.romaji: minna, gohan da yo! hayaku kite.
example.ja: みんな、ご飯だよ！早く来て。
example.english: Everyone, food's ready! Come quick.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan desu yo. douzo suwatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯ですよ。どうぞ座ってください。
examplePolite.english: The meal's ready. Please sit down.

items.notes: Gohan means a meal as well as cooked rice.

items.use: Said by the cook at home as they serve, usually douzo meshiagare, often in reply to itadakimasu.
items.politeJa: 召し上がってください

example.romaji: hai, dekita yo. douzo meshiagare.
example.ja: はい、できたよ。どうぞ召し上がれ。
example.english: Okay, it's ready. Dig in.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo, meshiagatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞ、召し上がってください。
examplePolite.english: Please, go ahead and eat.

items.notes: Homey and a little playful; staff and formal hosts say meshiagatte kudasai instead.

items.use: Urges someone to start eating or drinking now; usually followed by douzo or tabete.
items.politeJa: 冷めないうちにどうぞ

example.romaji: hora, samenai uchi ni tabete.
example.ja: ほら、冷めないうちに食べて。
example.english: Come on, eat it while it's hot.

examplePolite.romaji: samenai uchi ni douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 冷めないうちにどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: Please, have it before it gets cold.

items.notes: -nai uchi ni means before something happens: kuraku naranai uchi ni (before it gets dark).

blocks.label: Asking a favour
blocks.rationale: Lets you ask a friend for help or for something.
blocks.interference: choudai (give me) gets mixed up with chotto (a bit).

items.use: Softens a favour or a no to a friend; say it first, then the request or refusal.

example.romaji: warui kedo, mado shimete kureru?
example.ja: 悪いけど、窓閉めてくれる？
example.english: Sorry, could you close the window?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen ga, mado o shimete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみませんが、窓を閉めてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you close the window?

items.notes: Warui ne afterwards means sorry about that.

items.english: give me a hand for a sec
items.use: Quick call for help to family, friends or a close coworker.
items.politeJa: ちょっと手伝ってもらえますか

example.romaji: chotto tetsudatte! kore omoi.
example.ja: ちょっと手伝って！これ重い。
example.english: Give me a hand! This is heavy.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと手伝ってもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you give me a hand?

items.notes: Add kureru? to soften it: chotto tetsudatte kureru?

items.use: Presses a request on a friend or junior, or tells them you're relying on them; the answer is makasete.

example.romaji: ashita no junbi, tanomu yo.
example.ja: 明日の準備、頼むよ。
example.english: I'm counting on you to get things ready for tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no junbi, onegai shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の準備、お願いしますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll leave tomorrow's prep to you, then.

items.notes: Women usually say onegai ne instead.

items.use: Soft, homey request to family and close friends, after a thing (sore choudai) or a -te verb (matte choudai).

example.romaji: sore choudai! nodo kawaita.
example.ja: それちょうだい！喉渇いた。
example.english: Give me that! I'm thirsty.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sore o kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、それをください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, that one, please.

items.notes: Can sound childlike or motherly; adults asking strangers use kudasai.

blocks.label: Take care wishes
blocks.rationale: Lets you wish someone well when you part.
blocks.interference: ki o tsukete (take care) gets mixed up with ki ni shinaide (don't worry).

items.use: Said when you won't see someone for a long time, like before a move or at the end of a trip.

example.romaji: mukou de mo genki de ne.
example.ja: 向こうでも元気でね。
example.english: Take care of yourself over there.

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii shigoto, ganbatte kudasai. ogenki de.
examplePolite.ja: 新しい仕事、頑張ってください。お元気で。
examplePolite.english: Good luck with the new job. Take care.

items.notes: Not for an ordinary daily goodbye; it implies a long time apart.

items.polite: okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai
items.english: look after yourself; take care of your health
items.use: Said at a goodbye before a long gap, or to someone busy or getting older; also ends letters.
items.politeJa: お体に気をつけてください

example.romaji: samuku natta kara, karada ni ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: 寒くなったから、体に気をつけてね。
example.english: It's gotten cold, so look after yourself.

examplePolite.romaji: isogashii jiki desu ga, okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 忙しい時期ですが、お体に気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: It's a busy time, but please take care of yourself.

items.notes: Ki o tsukete alone means be careful, or take care as a goodbye.

items.polite: kaze o hikanai you ni ki o tsukete kudasai
items.english: don't catch a cold; stay warm
items.use: A caring send-off when it's cold or someone's heading out in the rain.
items.ja: 風邪ひかないようにね
items.kana: かぜひかないようにね
items.politeJa: 風邪をひかないように気をつけてください

example.romaji: kyou samui kara, kaze hikanai you ni ne.
example.ja: 今日寒いから、風邪ひかないようにね。
example.english: It's cold today, so don't catch a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hikanai you ni ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひかないように気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Be careful not to catch a cold.

items.notes: Catching a cold is kaze o hiku, literally 'pull a cold'.

items.use: Polite send-off to someone leaving: a guest, a customer, a coworker going on a trip.

example.romaji: kyou wa arigatou gozaimashita. oki o tsukete.
example.ja: 今日はありがとうございました。お気をつけて。
example.english: Thank you for today. Take care.

items.notes: Casual form: ki o tsukete.

blocks.label: Offering help
blocks.rationale: Lets you offer a hand and thank someone for theirs.
blocks.interference: tetsudaou ka (shall I help?) is not tetsudatte (help me).

items.english: shall I help?; want a hand?
items.use: Offers help to someone carrying, cooking or struggling with something.

example.romaji: omosou da ne. tetsudaou ka?
example.ja: 重そうだね。手伝おうか？
example.english: That looks heavy. Want a hand?

examplePolite.romaji: omosou desu ne. tetsudaimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: 重そうですね。手伝いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: That looks heavy. Shall I help?

items.notes: Humbler still: otetsudai shimashou ka. Nanika tetsudau? means anything I can do?

items.english: let me know if you need anything
items.use: Friendly offer of ongoing help, said when leaving someone to get on with things.
items.ja: 何かあったら言ってね
items.kana: なにかあったらいってね
items.politeJa: 何かあったら言ってください

example.romaji: nanika attara itsu demo itte ne.
example.ja: 何かあったらいつでも言ってね。
example.english: If you need anything, just say so, anytime.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara itsu demo itte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったらいつでも言ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know anytime if you need anything.

items.notes: Literally if anything happens, tell me, so it's also said to someone sick or worried.

items.use: Praises someone who did something helpful without being asked, like bringing an umbrella or refilling drinks.

example.romaji: mizu katte kita no? ki ga kiku ne.
example.ja: 水買ってきたの？気が利くね。
example.english: You bought water? How thoughtful.

examplePolite.romaji: arigatou gozaimasu. ki ga kikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます。気が利きますね。
examplePolite.english: Thank you. That's very thoughtful.

items.notes: 'Ki ga kikanai' is the criticism: someone who doesn't notice what others need.

blocks.label: Heading off
blocks.rationale: Lets you leave before others or part for longer.
blocks.interference: osaki ni (I'm off first) is not osaki ni douzo (after you).

items.english: I'm heading off (before you); after you
items.use: Short form for leaving before others, or with douzo for letting someone go first.

example.romaji: jaa, osaki ni! otsukare.
example.ja: じゃあ、お先に！お疲れ。
example.english: Okay, I'm heading off! Good work.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お先に失礼します。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'll be leaving before you.

items.notes: Also before eating or bathing first: osaki ni itadakimasu.

items.use: Goodbye to people you see weekly: classmates, a teacher, coworkers on a Friday.

example.romaji: otsukare! mata raishuu ne.
example.ja: お疲れ！また来週ね。
example.english: Good work! See you next week.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou mo arigatou gozaimashita. mata raishuu yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日もありがとうございました。また来週よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Thanks again for today. See you next week.

items.english: say hi to them for me
items.use: Sends your regards to someone who isn't there, usually as you part: X ni yoroshiku tsutaete.
items.politeJa: よろしくお伝えください

example.romaji: okaasan ni yoroshiku tsutaete ne.
example.ja: お母さんによろしく伝えてね。
example.english: Say hi to your mom for me.

examplePolite.romaji: okusan ni yoroshiku otsutae kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 奥さんによろしくお伝えください。
examplePolite.english: Please give my regards to your wife.

items.notes: Often cut to just X ni yoroshiku.

items.use: Sounds final or formal: teachers and pupils at the end of the school day, or a goodbye for a long time.

example.romaji: minna, sayounara! ki o tsukete kaette ne.
example.ja: みんな、さようなら！気をつけて帰ってね。
example.english: Bye, everyone! Get home safe.

items.notes: Friends rarely say it day to day, and between partners it can sound like a breakup. Use mata ne instead.

blocks.label: Congratulations
blocks.rationale: Lets you congratulate a friend on a milestone.
blocks.interference: omedetou and arigatou both end in -ou and can slip.

items.use: The answer is arigatou; add gozaimasu for anyone you speak politely to.
items.kana: おたんじょうびおめでとう
items.politeJa: お誕生日おめでとうございます

example.romaji: otanjoubi omedetou! kyou wa ogoru yo.
example.ja: お誕生日おめでとう！今日はおごるよ。
example.english: Happy birthday! Today's on me.

examplePolite.romaji: otanjoubi omedetou gozaimasu. kyou wa watashi ga gochisou shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お誕生日おめでとうございます。今日は私がごちそうします。
examplePolite.english: Happy birthday. Today is my treat.

items.notes: Friends often shorten it to tanjoubi omedetou or just omedetou.

items.use: For passing an entrance exam, a certification test, or an audition.
items.politeJa: 合格おめでとうございます

example.romaji: goukaku omedetou! yoku ganbatta ne.
example.ja: 合格おめでとう！よく頑張ったね。
example.english: Congrats on passing! You worked so hard.

examplePolite.romaji: goukaku omedetou gozaimasu. yoku ganbarimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 合格おめでとうございます。よく頑張りましたね。
examplePolite.english: Congratulations on passing. You worked really hard.

items.use: Heard most in March, Japan's graduation season.
items.kana: そつぎょうおめでとう
items.politeJa: ご卒業おめでとうございます

example.romaji: sotsugyou omedetou! haru kara shakaijin da ne.
example.ja: 卒業おめでとう！春から社会人だね。
example.english: Congrats on graduating! You start working this spring.

examplePolite.romaji: gosotsugyou omedetou gozaimasu. haru kara oshigoto desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ご卒業おめでとうございます。春からお仕事ですね。
examplePolite.english: Congratulations on graduating. You start work in spring, right?

items.use: To a friend getting married; the polite form with go- is what goes on cards and at the reception.
items.politeJa: ご結婚おめでとうございます

example.romaji: kekkon omedetou! shiawase ni ne.
example.ja: 結婚おめでとう！幸せにね。
example.english: Congrats on getting married! Be happy.

examplePolite.romaji: gokekkon omedetou gozaimasu. oshiawase ni.
examplePolite.ja: ご結婚おめでとうございます。お幸せに。
examplePolite.english: Congratulations on your marriage. Wishing you every happiness.

blocks.label: Visiting a home
blocks.rationale: Lets you enter and leave a friend's place politely.
blocks.interference: ojama shimasu is for arriving, ojama shimashita for leaving.

items.use: Said by a guest stepping into someone's home or office, or joining a group.

example.romaji: ojama shimasu. kore, minna de tabete kudasai.
example.ja: お邪魔します。これ、みんなで食べてください。
example.english: Thanks for having me. Here's something for everyone.

items.notes: Friends just say ojama. Plain jama means 'in the way', and jama da! is rude.

items.use: A host greets a visitor at the door, or a small shop owner greets customers; the guest answers ojama shimasu.

example.romaji: irasshai! samukatta deshou, haitte.
example.ja: いらっしゃい！寒かったでしょう、入って。
example.english: Welcome! You must be cold, come in.

examplePolite.romaji: irasshaimase. nanmeisama desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか？
examplePolite.english: Welcome. How many in your party?

items.notes: Shop staff's irasshaimase needs no reply; a nod is fine.

items.use: Said by a guest at the door when leaving someone's home; the host answers mata kite ne.

example.romaji: kyou wa ojama shimashita. tanoshikatta desu.
example.ja: 今日はお邪魔しました。楽しかったです。
example.english: Thanks for having me today. It was fun.

items.notes: The pair: ojama shimasu coming in, ojama shimashita going out.

items.use: A host invites you up from the entryway into the house; take your shoes off and say ojama shimasu.

example.romaji: douzo, oagari kudasai. surippa, kochira desu.
example.ja: どうぞ、お上がりください。スリッパ、こちらです。
example.english: Please, come on in. Here are some slippers.

items.notes: Casual: agatte, agatte. Agaru is stepping up from the entryway.

items.use: Welcoming someone to a place, event or group, as in youkoso nihon e; you answer with arigatou or a bow.
items.politeJa: ようこそいらっしゃいました

example.romaji: youkoso, uchi no saakuru e!
example.ja: ようこそ、うちのサークルへ！
example.english: Welcome to our club!

examplePolite.romaji: youkoso irasshaimashita. douzo kochira e.
examplePolite.ja: ようこそいらっしゃいました。どうぞこちらへ。
examplePolite.english: Welcome. This way, please.

items.notes: Not for someone coming home (okaeri) or into a shop (irasshaimase).

blocks.label: Go ahead and help yourself
blocks.rationale: Lets you put a guest or friend at ease.
blocks.interference: enryo shinaide (don't hold back) is not enryo shite okimasu (I'll pass).

items.use: Warmly lets someone go first, sit down or take something; doubling it makes it eager.

example.romaji: douzo douzo, saki ni haitte.
example.ja: どうぞどうぞ、先に入って。
example.english: Go ahead, you go in first.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo douzo, saki ni haitte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞどうぞ、先に入ってください。
examplePolite.english: Please, go on in first.

items.notes: A single douzo is the everyday here you go when handing something over.

items.english: help yourself if you like; please have some
items.use: Offers food, a seat or a spare item without pressure, e.g. passing snacks round at work; answer arigatou, itadakimasu.

example.romaji: okashi katte kita kara, yokattara douzo.
example.ja: お菓子買ってきたから、よかったらどうぞ。
example.english: I bought some snacks, help yourselves.

examplePolite.romaji: omiyage desu. yokattara douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お土産です。よかったらどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: It's a little souvenir. Please have some.

items.use: A host or friend urging you to eat, sit or ask for something; accept with jaa, enryo naku.

example.romaji: takusan aru kara, enryo shinaide tabete.
example.ja: たくさんあるから、遠慮しないで食べて。
example.english: There's plenty, so don't be shy, eat up.

examplePolite.romaji: takusan arimasu kara, goenryo naku douzo.
examplePolite.ja: たくさんありますから、ご遠慮なくどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: There's plenty, so please help yourself.

items.notes: Enryo is holding back out of politeness; guests decline once, so hosts insist.

items.use: A host tells a guest to sit however they like, often to someone kneeling formally.

example.romaji: ashi kuzushite, raku ni shite ne.
example.ja: 足崩して、楽にしてね。
example.english: Stretch your legs out, make yourself comfortable.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo oraku ni. ocha iremasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞお楽に。お茶入れますね。
examplePolite.english: Please, make yourself comfortable. I'll make some tea.

items.notes: Doctors say it too: raku ni shite kudasai (relax).

items.use: Letting someone go first at a door, lift or till; they answer sumimasen or doumo.

example.romaji: watashi wa ato de ii kara, osaki ni douzo.
example.ja: 私は後でいいから、お先にどうぞ。
example.english: I can go later, so go ahead.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa ato de daijoubu desu kara, osaki ni douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 私は後で大丈夫ですから、お先にどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm fine going later, so please go ahead.

items.notes: A host may also offer you the bath first with it.

blocks.label: Sounding unimpressed
blocks.rationale: Recognise or voice a cool, dismissive take.
blocks.interference: dou demo ii (don't care) sounds cold; nandemo ii (anything's fine) is the friendly one.

items.english: I mean, it's fine, but ...; whatever, fine
items.use: Agrees while hinting you're not thrilled; tone decides whether it sounds relaxed or sulky.

example.romaji: ashita ni suru? betsu ni ii kedo.
example.ja: 明日にする？別にいいけど。
example.english: Make it tomorrow? Fine by me, I guess.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa betsu ni ii desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 私は別にいいですけど。
examplePolite.english: I don't mind, I suppose.

items.notes: Betsu ni ii n da kedo leads into a small complaint instead; a bare betsu ni ('not really') can sound cold.

items.english: whatever; I don't care; it doesn't matter
items.use: Dismisses something as unimportant; to someone's face it can sound rude.

example.romaji: sonna koto, dou demo ii yo.
example.ja: そんなこと、どうでもいいよ。
example.english: I don't care about that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto wa dou demo ii desu.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことはどうでもいいです。
examplePolite.english: That doesn't matter.

items.notes: Don't confuse with nan demo ii (anything is fine), the friendly way to say you have no preference.

items.use: The humble reply to a compliment (iie, mada mada desu), or says something is far from good enough; said about someone else it's a put-down.

example.romaji: shiai ni katta kedo, mada mada da na.
example.ja: 試合に勝ったけど、まだまだだな。
example.english: We won the match, but we've still got a long way to go.

examplePolite.romaji: shiai ni wa kachimashita ga, mada mada desu.
examplePolite.ja: 試合には勝ちましたが、まだまだです。
examplePolite.english: We won the match, but we've still got a long way to go.

items.notes: Also 'still lots more': mada mada aru (there's plenty left).

items.english: how stupid; I feel so dumb; ridiculous
items.use: Mostly about yourself or a situation, once you realize you wasted your effort.

example.romaji: ichinichi matteta. baka mitai.
example.ja: 一日待ってた。バカみたい。
example.english: I waited all day. I feel so stupid.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinichi matte ita nante, baka mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 一日待っていたなんて、バカみたいです。
examplePolite.english: Waiting all day like that, I feel so stupid.

items.notes: Said about another person, it's an insult.

blocks.label: Polite small talk
blocks.rationale: Handle formal small talk with older people or acquaintances.
blocks.interference: desu ne is polite; with friends it drops to atsui ne.

items.use: The default summer opener with neighbours, shop staff or coworkers; agree with hontou ni, atsui desu ne.

example.romaji: kyou mo atsui desu ne. ase ga tomaranai desu.
example.ja: 今日も暑いですね。汗が止まらないです。
example.english: Hot again today, isn't it? I can't stop sweating.

items.notes: With friends: atsui ne. Hot food and baths are atsui too.

items.use: The winter version of atsui desu ne; an easy way to greet anyone.

example.romaji: kesa wa hontou ni samui desu ne.
example.ja: 今朝は本当に寒いですね。
example.english: It's really cold this morning, isn't it?

items.notes: With friends: samui ne. For cold drinks or water, use tsumetai, not samui.

items.use: Light opener with a neighbour or someone at a bus stop; agree with sou desu ne.

example.romaji: kyou wa ii tenki desu ne. osanpo desu ka?
example.ja: 今日はいい天気ですね。お散歩ですか？
example.english: Lovely day today. Out for a walk?

items.notes: With friends: ii tenki da ne.

items.english: I'm well, thank you; thanks to you
items.use: Polite answer when asked how you or your family are, or when congratulated.

example.romaji: okagesama de, kodomo mo genki desu.
example.ja: おかげさまで、子供も元気です。
example.english: We're well, thank you. The kids are fine too.

items.notes: Thanks for general goodwill, not for something they actually did.

blocks.label: Ugh damn ouch
blocks.rationale: Lets out frustration or pain.
blocks.interference: kuso and chikushou are rough; mou is mild annoyance.

items.use: Annoyed outburst at someone's behavior, often from women or kids.

example.romaji: mou! mata okureta no?
example.ja: もうっ！また遅れたの？
example.english: Ugh! You're late again?

items.notes: Same word as mou (already; anymore), but snapped out on its own.

items.use: Muttered in frustration when something goes wrong; in slang it also intensifies, as in kuso muzui (damn hard).

example.romaji: kuso, mata maketa! mou ikkai!
example.ja: クソ、また負けた！もう一回！
example.english: Damn, lost again! One more time!

items.notes: Literally 'dung'. Good to recognize, risky to say: it sounds harsh, especially from a learner.

items.use: Muttered or shouted in frustration at losing or failing.

example.romaji: chikushou, mata maketa yo.
example.ja: ちくしょう、また負けたよ。
example.english: Damn it, lost again.

items.notes: Literally 'beast'; kuso is even cruder.

items.use: Reflex shout at a sudden small pain.

example.romaji: ite! houchou de yubi kitchatta.
example.ja: イテッ！包丁で指切っちゃった。
example.english: Ouch! I cut my finger with the knife.

items.notes: A clipped itai (it hurts); ita! and itai! are the same reflex.

blocks.label: Doing things together
blocks.rationale: Covers the little noises of handling things side by side.
blocks.interference: kore kore can also scold ('now, now'); seeno times a group action.
