items.english: let's see; let me have a look
items.use: Said as you lean in to look at something someone wants to show you.

example.romaji: dore dore, chotto misete.
example.ja: どれどれ、ちょっと見せて。
example.english: Let's see, show me.

examplePolite.romaji: dore dore, chotto misete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どれどれ、ちょっと見せてください。
examplePolite.english: Let's see, may I have a look?

items.notes: Sounds a little like a parent or teacher checking something.

items.use: Excited when you find exactly what you wanted.

example.romaji: kore kore! kono aji ga tabetakatta.
example.ja: これこれ！この味が食べたかった。
example.english: This is it! This is the taste I've been craving.

examplePolite.romaji: kore kore! kono aji ga tabetakatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: これこれ！この味が食べたかったんです。
examplePolite.english: This is it! This is the taste I wanted.

items.notes: From an older person to a child, it's a gentle 'now, now' scolding.

items.english: ready, one, two, three!; on three
items.use: Signals everyone to act at once: lifting together, shouting together.

example.romaji: ja, issho ni mochiageyou. seeno!
example.ja: じゃ、一緒に持ち上げよう。せーの！
example.english: OK, let's lift it together. One, two, three!

examplePolite.romaji: ja, issho ni mochiagemashou. seeno!
examplePolite.ja: じゃ、一緒に持ち上げましょう。せーの！
examplePolite.english: OK, let's lift it together. One, two, three!

items.notes: Act on the 'no'; there's no count after it.

items.use: Said while lifting something, standing up, or sitting down.

example.romaji: yoisho. kono hako, omoi na.
example.ja: よいしょ。この箱、重いな。
example.english: Oof. This box is heavy.

examplePolite.romaji: yoisho. kono hako, omoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: よいしょ。この箱、重いですね。
examplePolite.english: Oof. This box is heavy.

items.notes: Saying it as you sit down is a classic, often joked-about sign of getting older.

items.use: Hushes someone, often with a finger to the lips.

example.romaji: shii! akachan neteru kara.
example.ja: シーッ！赤ちゃん寝てるから。
example.english: Shh! The baby's sleeping.

examplePolite.romaji: shii! shizuka ni onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: シーッ！静かにお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Shh! Quiet, please.

blocks.label: Framing a story
blocks.rationale: Lets you play a story down or mark it as an aside or a secret.
blocks.interference: betsu ni ii n da kedo softens the start, but betsu ni alone sounds curt.

items.romaji: betsu ni ii n da kedo
items.polite: betsu ni ii n desu kedo
items.english: it's not a big deal, but...
items.use: Softens the small complaint or request that follows; said with a sigh, it means you do mind.

example.romaji: betsu ni ii n da kedo, henji kurai shite yo.
example.ja: 別にいいんだけど、返事くらいしてよ。
example.english: It's no big deal, but at least reply to me.

examplePolite.romaji: betsu ni ii n desu kedo, ichiou oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 別にいいんですけど、一応教えてください。
examplePolite.english: It's not a big deal, but please let me know anyway.

items.notes: A bare 'betsu ni' (not really) can sound cold or sulky.

items.english: keep it a secret; it's a secret
items.use: Before or after sharing something private; naisho! alone refuses to tell.

example.romaji: kore, minna ni wa naisho da yo.
example.ja: これ、みんなにはないしょだよ。
example.english: Don't tell anyone about this.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, minna ni wa naisho desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: これ、みんなにはないしょですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please keep this between us.

items.english: just so you know; let me tell you
items.use: Flags a warning or something you want on record; can sound pushy.

example.romaji: ittoku kedo, watashi wa kankei nai kara ne.
example.ja: 言っとくけど、私は関係ないからね。
example.english: Just so you know, this has nothing to do with me.

items.notes: Short for itte oku kedo; the polite version is itte okimasu ga.

items.polite: ochi wa nai n desu kedo
items.english: there's no punchline, but... (it's just a story)
items.use: A disclaimer before or after a story with no big payoff, to head off 'ochi wa?'.
items.politeJa: オチはないんですけど

example.romaji: ochi nai n da kedo, kinou hen na yume mita.
example.ja: オチないんだけど、昨日変な夢見た。
example.english: There's no punchline, but I had a weird dream last night.

examplePolite.romaji: ochi wa nai n desu kedo, kinou omoshiroi hito ni aimashita.
examplePolite.ja: オチはないんですけど、昨日面白い人に会いました。
examplePolite.english: There's no real punchline, but I met an interesting person yesterday.

items.notes: Here it's the noun ochi plus nai, not ochinai (doesn't fall); they sound alike.

blocks.label: Things gone wrong
blocks.rationale: Lets you report a lost, broken or missed thing in a story.
blocks.interference: nakushita (lost it) and wasureta (forgot it) get swapped, as do kowareta (broke) and ugokanai (won't run).

items.use: A common late-night problem: trains stop around midnight, leaving a taxi, a net cafe or a long walk.

example.romaji: yabai, shuuden nogashita. takushii shika nai.
example.ja: やばい、終電逃した。タクシーしかない。
example.english: Crap, I missed the last train. It's a taxi now.

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden o nogashita node, takushii de kaerimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 終電を逃したので、タクシーで帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I missed the last train, so I'll take a taxi home.

items.notes: shuuden is the last train; the first one of the day is shihatsu.

items.use: Say a thing has broken or stopped working.

example.romaji: aa, sumaho kowareta. gamen ga tsukanai.
example.ja: ああ、スマホ壊れた。画面がつかない。
example.english: Ugh, my phone's broken. The screen won't turn on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho ga kowaremashita. gamen ga tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: スマホが壊れました。画面がつきません。
examplePolite.english: My phone broke. The screen won't turn on.

items.notes: kowasu is 'break (something)': kowashichatta, 'I broke it'.

items.use: Tell a friend, staff or the police box (kouban) that your wallet is gone.

example.romaji: yabai, saifu nakushita kamo. doko da?
example.ja: やばい、財布なくしたかも。どこだ？
example.english: Oh no, I think I lost my wallet. Where is it?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, saifu o nakushite shimatta n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、財布をなくしてしまったんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, I've lost my wallet.

items.notes: nakusu is 'lose'; otoshita (dropped it) is just as common.

items.english: it won't work; it won't move; it's stuck
items.use: For machines that won't run, doors or lids that won't budge, or a body part you can't move.

example.romaji: kono kopiiki, mata ugokanai yo.
example.ja: このコピー機、また動かないよ。
example.english: This copier's not working again.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kono kopiiki ga ugokanai n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、このコピー機が動かないんですが。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, this copier isn't working.

items.notes: For screens and lights that won't come on, use tsukanai.

blocks.label: Feeling refreshed
blocks.rationale: Lets you say something left you feeling better or revived.
blocks.interference: sukkiri (clear, unburdened) and sappari (clean, fresh) sound alike.

items.english: that feels better; I feel refreshed; that cleared things up
items.use: After a shower, a good cry, a clean-up or finally getting an answer: anything that clears a heavy or cluttered feeling.

example.romaji: heya katazuketara, sukkiri shita.
example.ja: 部屋片付けたら、すっきりした。
example.english: I tidied my room and feel so much better.

examplePolite.romaji: heya o katazuketara, sukkiri shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋を片付けたら、すっきりしました。
examplePolite.english: I tidied my room and feel much better.

items.notes: sappari is close but leans to feeling physically clean or fresh.

items.use: After a bath, a haircut or a light, clean-tasting meal.

example.romaji: kami kitte, sugoku sappari shita yo.
example.ja: 髪切って、すごくさっぱりしたよ。
example.english: I got a haircut and feel so fresh.

examplePolite.romaji: kami o kitte, sugoku sappari shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 髪を切って、すごくさっぱりしました。
examplePolite.english: I got a haircut and feel really fresh.

items.notes: With a negative it means 'not at all': sappari wakaranai (no idea at all).

items.english: I feel alive again; that hit the spot
items.use: Said after a cold drink on a hot day, a hot bath or a break; literally 'came back to life'.

example.romaji: aa, tsumetai biiru, ikikaetta!
example.ja: ああ、冷たいビール、生き返った！
example.english: Ah, an ice-cold beer. I feel alive again!

items.notes: In stories it's literal: someone came back to life.

blocks.label: Get well wishes
blocks.rationale: Lets you wish a sick friend a quick recovery.
blocks.interference: odaiji ni is only for illness or injury, not a general take care.

items.use: Said to someone sick or hurt as you part; clinic and pharmacy staff say it as you leave, and you answer arigatou gozaimasu.

example.romaji: kaze hiita no? odaiji ni ne.
example.ja: 風邪ひいたの？お大事にね。
example.english: You caught a cold? Get well soon.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze desu ka? douzo odaiji ni.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪ですか？どうぞお大事に。
examplePolite.english: A cold? Please take care.

items.notes: Only for illness or injury, not a general goodbye.

items.use: To someone sick or injured, as you leave or end a call.
items.politeJa: 早く良くなってくださいね

example.romaji: kaze? hayaku yoku natte ne.
example.ja: 風邪？早く良くなってね。
example.english: A cold? Get better soon.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku yoku natte kudasai ne. odaiji ni.
examplePolite.ja: 早く良くなってくださいね。お大事に。
examplePolite.english: Get well soon. Take care.

items.notes: odaiji ni (take care of yourself) is the standard set phrase to anyone unwell.

items.use: Said to someone sick, tired, or done with a hard stretch of work.
items.politeJa: ゆっくり休んでください

example.romaji: kyou wa hayaku nete, yukkuri yasunde ne.
example.ja: 今日は早く寝て、ゆっくり休んでね。
example.english: Go to bed early tonight and get some good rest.

examplePolite.romaji: konshuu wa taihen deshita ne. yukkuri yasunde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今週は大変でしたね。ゆっくり休んでください。
examplePolite.english: This week was tough. Please get some good rest.

items.notes: Yasumu means rest, and also take a day off.

blocks.label: Comforting someone upset
blocks.rationale: Lets you comfort a friend who is down or in tears.
blocks.interference: yoshi yoshi is for kids and pets and can sound patronising to an adult.

items.use: Said to someone sad or discouraged, often after a failure or a breakup.
items.politeJa: 元気を出してください

example.romaji: sonna ni ochikomanaide. genki dashite yo.
example.ja: そんなに落ち込まないで。元気出してよ。
example.english: Don't be so down. Cheer up.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi ga arimasu yo. genki o dashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次がありますよ。元気を出してください。
examplePolite.english: There's always next time. Please cheer up.

items.notes: Genki here means energy or spirits; genki nai ne means you seem down.

items.english: don't let it get you down; don't lose heart
items.use: Comfort after a failure or disappointment, like a lost game or a rejection.
items.politeJa: 気を落とさないでください

example.romaji: tsugi ga aru kara, ki o otosanaide.
example.ja: 次があるから、気を落とさないで。
example.english: There's always next time, don't let it get you down.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi ga arimasu kara, ki o otosanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次がありますから、気を落とさないでください。
examplePolite.english: There will be a next time, so please don't lose heart.

items.notes: Friends often say ki ni shinaide (don't worry about it) instead.

items.use: Said gently to someone crying, often a child or partner.

example.romaji: mou nakanaide. watashi ga iru kara.
example.ja: もう泣かないで。私がいるから。
example.english: Don't cry anymore. I'm here for you.

examplePolite.romaji: douka nakanaide kudasai. daijoubu desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: どうか泣かないでください。大丈夫ですから。
examplePolite.english: Please don't cry. It's going to be okay.

items.notes: The -naide ending means don't, as in shinpai shinaide and muri shinaide.

items.english: there, there; good boy, good girl
items.use: Said while patting a crying child or a pet; to an adult only as a joke.

example.romaji: yoshi yoshi, mou daijoubu da yo.
example.ja: よしよし、もう大丈夫だよ。
example.english: There, there, it's all right now.

items.notes: A single yoshi! means right!, said when starting something.

blocks.label: Maybe next time
blocks.rationale: Lets you leave the door open when you can't or won't commit.
blocks.interference: mata kondo can be a polite no rather than a real promise.

items.use: Puts a plan off to some later time; also the soft way to turn down an invitation.

example.romaji: kyou wa muri da kedo, mata kondo ne.
example.ja: 今日は無理だけど、また今度ね。
example.english: I can't today, but next time.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto... mata kondo onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと…また今度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Today's a bit... maybe another time.

items.notes: Often a polite no: don't expect a date to follow.

items.use: Softens a no: you can't make it this time but want to be asked again. Also said when you hear about a fun outing you missed.

example.romaji: kyou wa muri da kedo, mata kondo sasotte.
example.ja: 今日は無理だけど、また今度誘って。
example.english: I can't today, but invite me next time.

examplePolite.romaji: zannen desu. mata kondo sasotte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 残念です。また今度誘ってください。
examplePolite.english: That's a shame. Please invite me next time.

items.notes: Sasou is 'to invite'; 'sasotte kurete arigatou' is 'thanks for inviting me'.

items.use: A non-committal maybe about going or doing something; it can work as a polite no.

example.romaji: ki ga muitara iku kamo.
example.ja: 気が向いたら行くかも。
example.english: I might go if I feel like it.

examplePolite.romaji: ki ga muitara, itsu demo asobi ni kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 気が向いたら、いつでも遊びに来てください。
examplePolite.english: Drop by any time you feel like it.

items.notes: Ki ga muku = to feel inclined. Also an easygoing invite: 'ki ga muitara kite ne' (come if you feel like it).

blocks.label: Delays and call-backs
blocks.rationale: Lets you handle running late, dropping out, or calling later.
blocks.interference: ato de denwa suru (I'll call) and ato de kakenaosu (I'll call back) overlap.

items.use: Texted or said before you arrive, usually with gomen and how long.

example.romaji: gomen, chotto okureru. juppun gurai.
example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと遅れる。10分ぐらい。
example.english: Sorry, I'll be a bit late. About ten minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, densha ga okurete ite, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、電車が遅れていて、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my train's delayed, so I'll be a little late.

items.notes: Okureru is also used for trains: densha ga okureteru (the train's late).

items.english: I can't make it after all
items.use: Said to cancel a plan you agreed to, usually with gomen and a short reason.

example.romaji: gomen, kyuu ni shigoto ga haitte ikenaku natta.
example.ja: ごめん、急に仕事が入って行けなくなった。
example.english: Sorry, something came up at work and I can't make it.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ashita ikenaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、明日行けなくなりました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I can't make it tomorrow after all.

items.notes: The -naku natta ending says things changed, which sounds softer than a flat ikenai.

items.use: Said to friends or family when you can't talk now or want to talk later, often with ne.

example.romaji: ima isogashii kara, ato de denwa suru ne.
example.ja: 今忙しいから、後で電話するね。
example.english: I'm busy now, so I'll call you later.

examplePolite.romaji: kaigi no ato de denwa shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 会議の後で電話します。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you after the meeting.

items.notes: To a client or senior, ato de odenwa shimasu is the humble version.

items.use: Said when you can't talk right now; usually with ne.

example.romaji: gomen, ima densha. ato de kakenaosu ne.
example.ja: ごめん、今電車。後でかけ直すね。
example.english: Sorry, I'm on the train. I'll call you back later.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima te ga hanasenai node, ato de kakenaoshimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今手が離せないので、後でかけ直します。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm tied up right now, so I'll call you back later.

items.notes: Kakenaosu means call again; kakeru alone means make a call.

items.english: go on ahead; go without me
items.use: Said when you'll catch up later; the other person may answer jaa, matteru ne.
items.politeJa: 先に行っていてください

example.romaji: wasuremono shita. saki ni ittete!
example.ja: 忘れ物した。先に行ってて！
example.english: I forgot something. Go on ahead!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, saki ni itte ite kudasai. sugu oikakemasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、先に行っていてください。すぐ追いかけます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, please go on ahead. I'll catch up soon.

items.notes: Don't mix it up with osaki ni, which you say when you leave before others.

blocks.label: End of the night
blocks.rationale: Lets you suggest leaving, offer a ride home, or order one more.
blocks.interference: mou ippai (one more drink) is not onaka ippai (I'm full).

items.use: Suggests to the group that it's time to leave, or to move on to the next place.
items.politeJa: そろそろ行きましょうか

example.romaji: mou juuji da. sorosoro ikou ka.
example.ja: もう十時だ。そろそろ行こうか。
example.english: It's already ten. Shall we get going?

examplePolite.romaji: mou juuji desu ne. sorosoro ikimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: もう十時ですね。そろそろ行きましょうか。
examplePolite.english: It's already ten. Shall we get going?

items.notes: Swap the verb: sorosoro kaerou ka (shall we head home?).

items.english: are you okay for the last train?
items.use: Asked late in the evening so nobody gets stranded; answer with your cut-off, e.g. 'juuichiji made daijoubu'.
items.kana: しゅうでんだいじょうぶ？

example.romaji: mou juuji sugiteru kedo, shuuden daijoubu?
example.ja: もう10時過ぎてるけど、終電大丈夫？
example.english: It's past ten. Are you okay for the last train?

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro jikan desu kedo, shuuden daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ時間ですけど、終電大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: It's getting late. Will you make the last train?

items.notes: Shuuden = the last train of the night; missing it means a taxi, a karaoke booth or an all-nighter.

items.english: I'll walk you home; I'll drive you
items.use: Offers to see someone home or to the station at the end of the night; the polite refusal is 'ii yo, daijoubu'.

example.romaji: mou osoi kara, eki made okuru yo.
example.ja: もう遅いから、駅まで送るよ。
example.english: It's late, so I'll walk you to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma de ie made okurimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 車で家まで送りますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'll drive you home.

items.notes: Okuru also means 'to send': 'shashin okuru ne' is 'I'll send you the photos'.

items.use: Orders or offers another glass or bowl; add kudasai to staff.

example.romaji: mou ippai nomou yo.
example.ja: もう一杯飲もうよ。
example.english: Let's have one more.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, biiru mou ippai kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ビールもう一杯ください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, another beer, please.

items.notes: Ippai on its own also means full or lots; the mou tells you it's one more.

blocks.label: Spoilers and killjoys
blocks.rationale: Lets you handle someone spoiling the fun or the mood.
blocks.interference: nori warui (no fun) has nothing to do with noru meaning to ride.

items.use: Stops someone before they give away the plot of a show, film or game.
items.politeJa: ネタバレしないでください

example.romaji: mada mitenai kara, netabare shinaide!
example.ja: まだ見てないから、ネタバレしないで！
example.english: I haven't seen it yet, so no spoilers!

examplePolite.romaji: mada yonde inai node, netabare shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: まだ読んでいないので、ネタバレしないでください。
examplePolite.english: I haven't read it yet, so please don't spoil it.

items.notes: Netabare is the noun 'spoiler'; 'netabare chuui' is a spoiler warning.

items.use: Grumbled at someone who won't join in or play along; the opposite is 'nori ii' (up for anything).

example.romaji: e, mou kaeru no? nori warui naa.
example.ja: え、もう帰るの？ノリ悪いなあ。
example.english: What, you're leaving already? You're no fun.

items.notes: Nori is the group's vibe or momentum; 'nori de' means 'on impulse, in the moment'.

items.use: Tells someone they're missing the group's mood, like joking at a serious moment.

example.romaji: ima sono hanashi? chotto kuuki yonde yo.
example.ja: 今その話？ちょっと空気読んでよ。
example.english: That topic, now? Read the room a bit.

items.notes: Someone who can't read the room is 'kuuki yomenai', once shortened to the slang 'KY'.

blocks.label: Hey, cut that out
blocks.rationale: Lets you recognise rough calls to stop or pay attention.
blocks.interference: These are mostly for hearing; kora and iikagen ni shiro sound like scolding.

items.use: Said in shock or annoyance when you catch someone doing something odd or wrong.

example.romaji: chotto, nani yatten no! abunai yo.
example.ja: ちょっと、何やってんの！危ないよ。
example.english: Hey, what are you doing?! That's dangerous.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto, nani yatteru n desu ka! abunai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと、何やってるんですか！危ないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Hey, what are you doing? That's dangerous.

items.notes: For a neutral 'what are you up to?', ask nani shiteru no?

items.english: hey, hey; come on; whoa, whoa
items.use: Mild protest when someone does something careless or over the top.

example.romaji: oioi, sore ore no biiru da yo.
example.ja: おいおい、それ俺のビールだよ。
example.english: Hey, hey, that's my beer.

items.notes: Softer and more joking than a single oi.

items.use: Calls or warns someone sharply; normal between close male friends, rude otherwise.

example.romaji: oi, chotto matte yo.
example.ja: おい、ちょっと待ってよ。
example.english: Hey, wait a sec.

items.notes: To get a stranger's attention say sumimasen instead.

items.use: An adult catching a child or pet misbehaving; playful between friends.

example.romaji: kora! sonna tokoro ni nobotcha dame!
example.ja: こら！そんなところに登っちゃダメ！
example.english: Hey! You can't climb up there!

items.notes: Don't use it to call adults; ooi is the neutral calling 'hey'.

items.use: Angry order to stop something that has gone on too long.
items.politeJa: いい加減にしてください

example.romaji: iikagen ni shiro, nankaime da!
example.ja: いいかげんにしろ、何回目だ！
example.english: Knock it off! How many times is this?

examplePolite.romaji: mou iikagen ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: もういい加減にしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please, that's enough now.

items.notes: iikagen ni shite is the softer everyday version.

blocks.label: Rough comebacks
blocks.rationale: Lets you recognise harsh retorts and how hard they hit.
blocks.interference: baka ja nai no can be fond or cutting depending on tone, and shiru ka is ruder than shiranai.

items.english: so annoying; you're such a pain
items.use: Snapped at someone or something irritating; teens toss it at friends, but it stings, so learn to recognise it first.

example.romaji: nankai mo kikanaide yo, uzai.
example.ja: 何回も聞かないでよ、うざい。
example.english: Stop asking me over and over, it's so annoying.

items.notes: Short for uzattai. Much harsher than 'urusai' (shut up, noisy) and rude to anyone you're not close to.

items.english: are you an idiot?; don't be silly
items.use: Between close friends it's a laughing 'don't be ridiculous'; said coldly it's a real insult.

example.romaji: fuyu ni umi de oyogu? baka ja nai no.
example.ja: 冬に海で泳ぐ？バカじゃないの。
example.english: Swim in the sea in winter? Are you crazy?

items.notes: Tone decides whether it's affectionate or a fight; keep it for people you're close to.

items.english: how should I know!; who cares!
items.use: Snapped back in anger.

example.romaji: sonna no shiru ka yo!
example.ja: そんなの知るかよ！
example.english: How should I know that!

items.notes: Even plain shiranai can sound cold; wakaranai is the safe 'I don't know'.

items.english: don't mess with me; you've got to be kidding
items.use: Angry outburst at something unfair or insulting; hear it in films, don't use it.

example.romaji: fuzaken na, imasara muri da yo.
example.ja: ふざけんな、今さら無理だよ。
example.english: Are you kidding me? It's way too late now.

items.notes: From fuzakeru (to fool around); fuzakenaide (stop messing around) is milder.

blocks.label: Replying to kindness
blocks.rationale: Lets you accept or politely decline someone's fuss over you.
blocks.interference: enryo naku accepts, while okamai naku declines.

items.english: don't go to any trouble; you didn't have to
items.use: Said when someone fusses over you or brings a gift; it's polite modesty, so still accept with thanks.
items.politeJa: 気を使わないでください

example.romaji: sonna ni ki o tsukawanaide yo.
example.ja: そんなに気を使わないでよ。
example.english: Oh, you didn't need to go to all that trouble.

examplePolite.romaji: douzo ki o tsukawanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞ気を使わないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't go to any trouble.

items.notes: Formal set version: douzo okizukai naku. Ki o tsukau means to be considerate or fuss over someone.

items.english: without holding back; I'll gladly take it
items.use: Said when accepting an offer after the host insists, or to urge someone: enryo naku itte (just tell me).
items.politeJa: 遠慮なくいただきます

example.romaji: jaa, enryo naku moratte iku ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、遠慮なくもらっていくね。
example.english: Well then, I'll gladly take it.

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, enryo naku itadakimasu.
examplePolite.ja: では、遠慮なくいただきます。
examplePolite.english: Well then, I'll gladly accept.

items.english: please don't go to any trouble
items.use: A guest's polite line when the host offers tea or food.

example.romaji: a, douzo okamai naku. sugu kaerimasu kara.
example.ja: あ、どうぞおかまいなく。すぐ帰りますから。
example.english: Oh, please don't trouble yourself. I'm leaving soon.

items.notes: The host usually brings tea anyway; just thank them.

items.english: don't worry (about me); no need to worry
items.use: A polite way to turn down someone's concern or offer of help, often with people you don't know well.

example.romaji: hitori de kaeremasu kara, goshinpai naku.
example.ja: 一人で帰れますから、ご心配なく。
example.english: I can get home on my own, so don't worry.

items.notes: It can sound a bit cool, like I've got this; shinpai shinaide is warmer.

blocks.label: Thanks for everything
blocks.rationale: Lets you thank someone at the end of work, a stay or a stretch of time.
blocks.interference: otsukaresama deshita thanks effort and does not mean "you are tired".

items.english: good work today; thanks for your hard work
items.use: Said when work or an event ends, especially to someone leaving; the answer to osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.

example.romaji: kyou wa nagai ichinichi deshita ne. otsukaresama deshita.
example.ja: 今日は長い一日でしたね。お疲れ様でした。
example.english: Long day today. Good work.

items.notes: Casual: otsukare. Also said after a match, a show or a long trip.

items.use: Thanks for help over a stretch of time, often when someone leaves or a trip ends.
items.politeJa: いろいろありがとうございました

example.romaji: kono isshuukan, iroiro arigatou ne.
example.ja: この一週間、いろいろありがとうね。
example.english: Thanks for everything this week.

examplePolite.romaji: kono isshuukan, iroiro arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: この一週間、いろいろありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for everything this week.

items.english: thank you for all your help (at the end)
items.use: Said when a stay, job or course of care ends: to a host family, your old boss, hospital staff.

example.romaji: sannenkan, hontou ni osewa ni narimashita.
example.ja: 三年間、本当にお世話になりました。
example.english: Thank you so much for these three years.

items.notes: The ongoing form, osewa ni natte imasu, opens work emails and calls.

blocks.label: Leaving and coming home
blocks.rationale: Lets you use the set phrases at the door of a shared home.
blocks.interference: tadaima is said by the one arriving, okaeri by the one at home.

items.use: Called out as you walk in the door at home; whoever is in answers okaeri.

example.romaji: tadaima! aa, onaka suita.
example.ja: ただいま！あー、お腹すいた。
example.english: I'm home! Man, I'm starving.

examplePolite.romaji: tadaima modorimashita. nanika arimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: ただいま戻りました。何かありましたか？
examplePolite.english: I'm back. Did anything come up?

items.notes: At work, tadaima modorimashita when you return to the office. In announcements tadaima means 'right now'.

items.use: The answer to tadaima, said by whoever is home; also to a friend back from a trip.

example.romaji: okaeri! gohan dekiteru yo.
example.ja: おかえり！ご飯できてるよ。
example.english: Welcome home! Dinner's ready.

items.notes: Okaerinasai is the fuller, softer form.

items.english: I'm off; see you later (when leaving)
items.use: Said by the person leaving home, or the office for a while; the others answer itterasshai.

example.romaji: jaa, ittekimasu! yuugata ni wa kaeru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、行ってきます！夕方には帰るね。
example.english: Okay, I'm off! I'll be back by evening.

examplePolite.romaji: ginkou ni ittekimasu. sanjuppun de modorimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 銀行に行ってきます。三十分で戻ります。
examplePolite.english: I'm popping out to the bank. Back in thirty minutes.

items.notes: It stays in -masu even with family. Only when you're coming back; it means 'I'll go and come back'.

items.english: see you later; have a good day (to someone leaving)
items.use: The answer to ittekimasu, said by whoever stays behind; hotel staff say the -mase form to guests heading out.
items.politeJa: いってらっしゃいませ

example.romaji: itterasshai! ame furu kara kasa motte itte ne.
example.ja: いってらっしゃい！雨降るから傘持っていってね。
example.english: See you! It's going to rain, so take an umbrella.

examplePolite.romaji: itterasshaimase. oki o tsukete.
examplePolite.ja: いってらっしゃいませ。お気をつけて。
examplePolite.english: Have a good day. Take care.

items.notes: Not a general goodbye: only to someone who will come back.

items.use: Fuller, warmer form of okaeri; parents, partners, inn staff and coworkers say it to someone returning.

example.romaji: okaerinasai. tsukareta deshou, ofuro waiteru yo.
example.ja: おかえりなさい。疲れたでしょう、お風呂沸いてるよ。
example.english: Welcome home. You must be tired; the bath's ready.

examplePolite.romaji: okaerinasai. shutchou wa ikaga deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: おかえりなさい。出張はいかがでしたか？
examplePolite.english: Welcome back. How was the business trip?

blocks.label: Begging a favour
blocks.rationale: Lets you plead hard for help or forgiveness.
blocks.interference: tanomu kara and onegai dakara mean the same, and both are stronger than tanomu yo.

items.use: Emotional plea, usually before stop, listen or don't go.

example.romaji: onegai dakara, hanashi kiite.
example.ja: お願いだから、話聞いて。
example.english: Please, just listen to me.

examplePolite.romaji: onegai desu kara, yamete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: お願いですから、やめてください。
examplePolite.english: Please, I'm begging you, stop.

items.notes: Softer than tanomu kara and used by everyone.

items.use: Desperate or exasperated plea to a friend or family member to stop or do something.

example.romaji: tanomu kara, mou yamete.
example.ja: 頼むから、もうやめて。
example.english: Please, I'm begging you, just stop.

items.notes: Stronger than tanomu yo. Onegai dakara is the softer version anyone can use.

items.use: Pleading with someone close after hurting them, or a playful 'go easy on me'.

example.romaji: hontou ni gomen. onegai, yurushite.
example.ja: 本当にごめん。お願い、許して。
example.english: I'm really sorry. Please forgive me.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni sumimasen deshita. douka yurushite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 本当にすみませんでした。どうか許してください。
examplePolite.english: I'm truly sorry. Please forgive me.

items.notes: Heavy for everyday slips, where gomen is enough.

blocks.label: Polite apologies
blocks.rationale: Lets you apologise formally to someone outside your circle.
blocks.interference: doumo sumimasen can also mean thank you so much.

items.use: Light polite apology for a small slip: bumping someone, a wrong number, walking into the wrong room.

example.romaji: a, heya o machigaemashita. shitsurei shimashita.
example.ja: あ、部屋を間違えました。失礼しました。
example.english: Oh, wrong room. Excuse me.

items.notes: Shitsurei shimasu (present) is for entering, leaving or hanging up.

items.use: Apologizing for something already done, like a mistake at work or being rude.

example.romaji: kinou wa sumimasen deshita. chotto iisugimashita.
example.ja: 昨日はすみませんでした。ちょっと言いすぎました。
example.english: Sorry about yesterday. I said too much.

items.notes: Plain sumimasen also means excuse me and thanks; the -deshita form is only an apology.

items.english: I'm so sorry; thank you so much
items.use: A stronger sumimasen to staff, strangers or anyone you've put out: a real apology, or thanks that admits you caused trouble.

example.romaji: wazawaza todokete kudasatte, doumo sumimasen.
example.ja: わざわざ届けてくださって、どうもすみません。
example.english: Thank you so much for bringing it all this way.

items.notes: The situation tells you whether it's thanks or sorry; often it's both.

items.english: sorry I'm late; sorry for the slow reply
items.use: Said on arriving late, or at the start of a late reply to a message or email.
items.ja: 遅くなってすみません
items.kana: おそくなってすみません

example.romaji: osoku natte sumimasen, michi ga konde imashita.
example.ja: 遅くなってすみません、道が混んでいました。
example.english: Sorry I'm late, the roads were busy.

items.notes: With friends: osoku natte gomen. For a message: henji ga osoku natte sumimasen.

items.use: Plain-form apology, often from men or older people to friends, family or juniors.

example.romaji: isogashii no ni, moushiwake nai na.
example.ja: 忙しいのに、申し訳ないな。
example.english: Sorry to put you out when you're busy.

examplePolite.romaji: oisogashii no ni, moushiwake arimasen.
examplePolite.ja: お忙しいのに、申し訳ありません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy.

items.notes: Also 'I feel bad': kare ni moushiwake nai (I feel bad toward him).

blocks.label: Holiday greetings
blocks.rationale: Lets you greet friends at Christmas and New Year.
blocks.interference: yoi otoshi o is said before New Year, akemashite omedetou only after.

items.use: Said from January 1 into early January, the first time you see someone; never before New Year.
items.ja: あけましておめでとう
items.kana: あけましておめでとう
items.politeJa: あけましておめでとうございます

example.romaji: akemashite omedetou! kotoshi mo yoroshiku ne.
example.ja: あけましておめでとう！今年もよろしくね。
example.english: Happy New Year! Here's to another year.

examplePolite.romaji: akemashite omedetou gozaimasu. kotoshi mo yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: あけましておめでとうございます。今年もよろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Happy New Year. I look forward to another year with you.

items.notes: Friends shorten it to akeome.

items.use: Said among friends and couples; in Japan Christmas Eve is a date night, not a family holiday.

example.romaji: merii kurisumasu! kore, purezento da yo.
example.ja: メリークリスマス！これ、プレゼントだよ。
example.english: Merry Christmas! Here's your present.

examplePolite.romaji: merii kurisumasu. kore, purezento desu.
examplePolite.ja: メリークリスマス。これ、プレゼントです。
examplePolite.english: Merry Christmas. This is a present for you.

items.notes: Friends shorten it to merikuri.

items.use: Said in late December when parting from someone you won't see again before New Year.
items.politeJa: よいお年をお迎えください

example.romaji: ja, mata rainen. yoi otoshi o!
example.ja: じゃ、また来年。よいお年を！
example.english: See you next year. Have a good New Year!

examplePolite.romaji: dewa, mata rainen. yoi otoshi o omukae kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: では、また来年。よいお年をお迎えください。
examplePolite.english: See you next year, then. Have a happy New Year.

items.notes: From January 1 on, switch to akemashite omedetou.

items.english: I look forward to another year with you
items.use: New Year greeting said right after akemashite omedetou; answer with the same words, or kochira koso (same here).
items.ja: 今年もよろしくお願いします
items.kana: ことしもよろしくおねがいします

example.romaji: akeome! kotoshi mo yoroshiku ne.
example.ja: あけおめ！今年もよろしくね。
example.english: Happy New Year! Here's to another year.

examplePolite.romaji: kochira koso, kotoshi mo yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: こちらこそ、今年もよろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Same here, I look forward to another year with you.

items.notes: Friends shorten it to kotoshi mo yoroshiku (ne).

items.use: Year-end thanks to coworkers, neighbors, and friends, usually followed by yoi otoshi o.
items.ja: 今年もお世話になりました
items.kana: ことしもおせわになりました

example.romaji: kotoshi mo osewa ni narimashita. mata rainen ne!
example.ja: 今年もお世話になりました。また来年ね！
example.english: Thanks for everything this year. See you next year!

examplePolite.romaji: kotoshi mo osewa ni narimashita. rainen mo yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今年もお世話になりました。来年もよろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for everything this year. I look forward to next year.

items.notes: Close friends might just say kotoshi mo arigatou.

blocks.label: Asking and declining politely
blocks.rationale: Ask if something is okay, offer something, ask a favour or turn an offer down in any polite setting.
blocks.interference: Kekkou desu usually means no thanks rather than great, and yoroshii desu ka is just a politer ii desu ka.

items.use: Asks permission or checks something is fine; put the thing first (koko, ii desu ka?) or a -te mo verb (suwatte mo ii desu ka?).

example.romaji: sumimasen, koko suwatte mo ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、ここ座ってもいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, is it okay if I sit here?

items.notes: Casual is just ii? with a rising tone. Yes is hai, douzo; a no usually starts with chotto...

items.use: Firm, polite no to staff, salespeople or a host offering more; add iie or a reason to sound warmer.

example.romaji: iie, kekkou desu. mou juubun itadakimashita.
example.ja: いいえ、結構です。もう十分いただきました。
example.english: No, thank you. I've had plenty.

items.notes: Can sound cold to friends; use daijoubu instead. Kekkou also means quite: kekkou oishii (pretty tasty).

items.english: would you like some?; how about it?; how is it?
items.use: Polite offer or check-in from staff or a host (fukuro wa ikaga desu ka?); answer onegai shimasu or daijoubu desu.

example.romaji: koohii no okawari, ikaga desu ka?
example.ja: コーヒーのおかわり、いかがですか？
example.english: Would you like more coffee?

items.notes: Casual version: dou? Staff also say ikaga deshou ka, and ikaga deshita ka (how was it?).

items.english: could you do that for me?; could I ask for...?
items.use: Polite request to staff, colleagues or strangers, after naming the thing or task.

example.romaji: kore, kopii onegai dekimasu ka?
example.ja: これ、コピーお願いできますか？
example.english: Could you make a copy of this for me?

items.notes: Casual version: onegai dekiru?

items.english: would that be all right?; may I?
items.use: Very polite ii desu ka; you hear it from staff checking an order, and can use it with bosses and strangers.

example.romaji: kochira de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: こちらでよろしいですか？
example.english: Will this one be all right?

items.notes: Staff also say yoroshii deshou ka, softer still.

blocks.label: Eating out with friends
blocks.rationale: Get a meal or drinks with friends going, from the first beer to splitting the bill.
blocks.interference: Okawari (a refill) and okaikei (the bill) both start with o-ka and get swapped.

items.use: The classic first order at an izakaya so the group can toast quickly; food comes after.
items.politeJa: とりあえずビールお願いします

example.romaji: minna, toriaezu biiru de ii?
example.ja: みんな、とりあえずビールでいい？
example.english: Beer to start for everyone?

examplePolite.romaji: toriaezu biiru mittsu onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: とりあえずビール三つお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Three beers to start, please.

items.notes: Toriaezu alone means for now: toriaezu ikou (let's just go for now).

items.use: Asks for another bowl of rice or a refill, or offers one (okawari wa?).

example.romaji: okawari aru yo. iru?
example.ja: おかわりあるよ。いる？
example.english: There's seconds. Want some?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, gohan no okawari onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ご飯のおかわりお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could I get more rice?

items.notes: Okawari jiyuu means free refills. As a verb: okawari suru.

items.use: Asks restaurant or bar staff for the bill; at many places you then pay at the register (reji) by the exit.
items.kana: おかいけいおねがいします

example.romaji: sumimasen, okaikei onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、お会計お願いします。
example.english: Excuse me, could we get the bill?

items.notes: Okanjou onegai shimasu is also common at izakaya.

items.use: Asks to pay separately at the register; staff may ask goissho de yoroshii desu ka? (together?).
items.kana: べつべつでおねがいします

example.romaji: okaikei wa betsubetsu de onegai shimasu.
example.ja: お会計は別々でお願いします。
example.english: We'll pay separately, please.

items.notes: Splitting the total evenly among friends is warikan.

items.use: Calls staff over when you're ready to order; start with sumimasen!
items.kana: ちゅうもんいいですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, chuumon ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、注文いいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can we order?

items.notes: Many places have a call button on the table instead.

blocks.label: Ordering food
blocks.rationale: Pick dishes, ask what's good, get water and say you're done ordering.
blocks.interference: Ijou desu (that's all) is easy to mix with ii desu (no thanks).

items.use: The simplest way to buy or order: point at the thing at a counter, stall or menu.

example.romaji: kore to kore, kudasai.
example.ja: これとこれ、ください。
example.english: This and this, please.

items.notes: Add a count: kore futatsu kudasai (two of these).

items.english: I'll take this one; I'll have this
items.use: Tells staff your choice after looking or comparing; works for food orders too.

example.romaji: jaa, kore ni shimasu.
example.ja: じゃあ、これにします。
example.english: Okay, I'll go with this one.

items.notes: X ni suru means decide on X. Casual version: kore ni suru.

items.use: Ask staff at a restaurant or shop; casual version is osusume wa?
items.kana: おすすめはなんですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, osusume wa nan desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、おすすめは何ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, what do you recommend?

items.notes: Menus mark recommended dishes as osusume.

items.use: Asks staff for water; it's free, and some places have you pour it yourself (serufu saabisu).

example.romaji: sumimasen, omizu futatsu kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、お水二つください。
example.english: Excuse me, two waters, please.

items.use: Ends your order at a restaurant or counter; staff and speakers also use it to end a talk or report.

example.romaji: biiru futatsu to edamame, ijou desu.
example.ja: ビール二つと枝豆、以上です。
example.english: Two beers and edamame. That's all.

items.notes: Staff may check with ijou de yoroshii desu ka? (will that be all?).

blocks.label: Table or takeaway
blocks.rationale: Say how many you are, whether you're eating in or taking it away, and ask for a bigger portion.
blocks.interference: Tennai de (eat in) and mochikaeri de (take away) are easy to swap.

items.english: two people; a table for two
items.use: Answer at the restaurant door when staff ask nanmeisama desu ka? (how many?).

example.romaji: futari desu. kauntaa demo ii desu.
example.ja: 二人です。カウンターでもいいです。
example.english: Two of us. The counter's fine.

items.notes: One is hitori desu, three is sannin desu. Holding up fingers works too.

items.english: to eat in, please; for here
items.use: Answer at a cafe or fast-food counter when asked if you're eating here; the opposite is mochikaeri de.

example.romaji: tennai de, aisu koohii hitotsu.
example.ja: 店内で、アイスコーヒー一つ。
example.english: For here, one iced coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: tennai de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 店内でお願いします。
examplePolite.english: For here, please.

items.use: Answer at a cafe or fast-food counter when staff ask if you're eating in (tennai de omeshiagari desu ka?).
items.politeJa: 持ち帰りでお願いします

example.romaji: kore, mochikaeri de.
example.ja: これ、持ち帰りで。
example.english: This one to go.

examplePolite.romaji: mochikaeri de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 持ち帰りでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: To take away, please.

items.notes: Staff say omochikaeri; chains also use teikuauto.

items.use: Asks for an extra-large serving of rice or noodles, often for a small extra charge.
items.politeJa: 大盛りでお願いします

example.romaji: gyuudon hitotsu, oomori de.
example.ja: 牛丼一つ、大盛りで。
example.english: One beef bowl, large.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan wa oomori de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯は大盛りでお願いします。
examplePolite.english: A large serving of rice, please.

items.notes: Normal size is namimori; a smaller one is sukuname.

blocks.label: Paying at the till
blocks.rationale: Ask the price, check card and tax, and get a receipt when you pay.
blocks.interference: Ryoushuusho is the formal receipt for expenses, not the till slip reshiito.

items.use: Point at or name the item first: kore, ikura desu ka?

example.romaji: sumimasen, kore ikura desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、これいくらですか？
example.english: Excuse me, how much is this?

items.notes: Casual version: ikura? Prices come back as numbers plus en: sen en is 1,000 yen.

items.use: Ask before ordering or at the till; small places may be cash only.

example.romaji: sumimasen, kaado tsukaemasu ka?
example.ja: すみません、カード使えますか？
example.english: Excuse me, do you take cards?

items.notes: Genkin dake desu means cash only.

items.use: Answer at the till when staff ask how you'll pay (oshiharai wa?).
items.ja: カードでお願いします
items.kana: カードでおねがいします

example.romaji: a, kaado de onegai shimasu.
example.ja: あ、カードでお願いします。
example.english: Oh, by card, please.

items.notes: Cash is genkin de. If staff ask ikkai barai de yoroshii desu ka (one payment?), just say hai.

items.use: Checks a price tag or quote; prices are shown either with tax (zeikomi) or without (zeinuki).

example.romaji: kono nedan, zeikomi desu ka?
example.ja: この値段、税込みですか？
example.english: Does this price include tax?

items.use: Asks for a formal receipt for expenses at shops, restaurants and taxis; staff may then ask what name to write.
items.kana: りょうしゅうしょおねがいします

example.romaji: sumimasen, ryoushuusho onegai shimasu.
example.ja: すみません、領収書お願いします。
example.english: Excuse me, could I get a receipt?

items.notes: A reshiito is the printed till slip; a ryoushuusho is the formal one for claiming expenses.

blocks.label: Finding your way
blocks.rationale: Ask for the toilet or directions, say you're lost, and tell a driver or crowd where you're getting off.
blocks.interference: Koko doko (where am I?) sounds close to koko de ii desu (here is fine), and orimasu is also the humble word for 'to be' at work.

items.use: Ask staff in shops, restaurants and stations; casual is toire doko?

example.romaji: sumimasen, toire wa doko desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、トイレはどこですか？
example.english: Excuse me, where's the toilet?

items.notes: Otearai is a politer word for toilet. At someone's home: toire karite mo ii desu ka?

items.use: Ask a stranger or staff for directions after naming the place: X made dou ikeba ii desu ka?
items.ja: どう行けばいいですか
items.kana: どういけばいいですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, eki made dou ikeba ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、駅までどう行けばいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

items.notes: With friends: dou ikeba ii? Simpler still: eki wa doko desu ka? (where's the station?).

items.use: Tell a passer-by or a friend on the phone that you don't know where you are.

example.romaji: gomen, michi ni mayotta. chotto okureru.
example.ja: ごめん、道に迷った。ちょっと遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I got lost. I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, michi ni mayotte shimatte, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、道に迷ってしまって、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I got lost, so I'll be a little late.

items.notes: mayou alone also means 'can't decide': dotchi ni suru ka mayotteru.

items.english: where am I?; where is this?
items.use: Muttered on waking up somewhere strange or getting lost; ask strangers with the polite form.

example.romaji: are, koko doko? machigaeta kamo.
example.ja: あれ、ここどこ？間違えたかも。
example.english: Huh, where am I? I might've gone the wrong way.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, koko wa doko desu ka? chizu de oshiete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ここはどこですか？地図で教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, where is this? Could you show me on the map?

items.use: Tells a taxi driver to stop, or tells someone walking or driving you that they needn't go further.

example.romaji: a, koko de ii desu. arigatou gozaimasu.
example.ja: あ、ここでいいです。ありがとうございます。
example.english: Oh, here's fine. Thank you.

items.notes: Clearer to a taxi driver: koko de tomete kudasai (please stop here).

items.english: I'm getting off (on a crowded train or bus)
items.use: Said aloud to the people in your way as your stop comes, so they make room.

example.romaji: sumimasen, orimasu! chotto tooshite kudasai.
example.ja: すみません、降ります！ちょっと通してください。
example.english: Excuse me, getting off! Let me through, please.

items.notes: From oriru (get off). In a crowd, sumimasen alone also works.

blocks.label: Emergencies
blocks.rationale: Shout about an earthquake, say where it hurts and call for help or an ambulance.
blocks.interference: None.

items.use: Shouted when the shaking starts; announcements and teachers use jishin desu.

example.romaji: a, jishin da! hayaku tsukue no shita ni!
example.ja: あっ、地震だ！早く机の下に！
example.english: Whoa, earthquake! Quick, under the table!

examplePolite.romaji: jishin desu! tsukue no shita ni haitte kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: 地震です！机の下に入ってください！
examplePolite.english: Earthquake! Get under your desks!

items.notes: The early-warning alert on phones and TV says jishin desu, jishin desu.

items.use: Point and say it at a clinic or pharmacy; the doctor asks doko ga itai desu ka? (where does it hurt?).

example.romaji: kinou kara koko ga itai n da.
example.ja: 昨日からここが痛いんだ。
example.english: It's been hurting here since yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara koko ga itai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日からここが痛いんです。
examplePolite.english: It's been hurting here since yesterday.

items.notes: itai! alone is 'ouch!'; swap koko for a body part: atama ga itai (my head hurts).

items.use: Shout for help in danger; to a friend it can also be a jokey 'help me out'.

example.romaji: dareka tasukete! hito ga taoreta!
example.ja: 誰か助けて！人が倒れた！
example.english: Somebody help! Someone's collapsed!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tasukete kudasai! hito ga taoremashita!
examplePolite.ja: すみません、助けてください！人が倒れました！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please help! Someone's collapsed!

items.notes: For everyday help with a task, tetsudatte (give me a hand) is more natural.

items.use: Ask a bystander to call; the number in Japan is 119, which also reaches the fire service.
items.kana: きゅうきゅうしゃをよんで
items.politeJa: 救急車を呼んでください

example.romaji: hayaku kyuukyuusha o yonde! ishiki ga nai.
example.ja: 早く救急車を呼んで！意識がない。
example.english: Quick, call an ambulance! She's unconscious.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyuukyuusha o yonde kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: すみません、救急車を呼んでください！
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, please call an ambulance!

items.notes: Police is 110 (keisatsu); 119 is ambulance and fire.

blocks.label: Just browsing
blocks.rationale: Keep shop staff at bay, try things on and leave without buying.
blocks.interference: Chotto kangaemasu and ato de mata kimasu both usually mean no sale, not a real promise to come back.

items.use: Answer to a shop assistant who asks if you're looking for something.

example.romaji: a, daijoubu desu. miteru dake desu.
example.ja: あ、大丈夫です。見てるだけです。
example.english: Oh, I'm fine. Just looking.

items.notes: Also means I'm only watching when someone asks you to join in.

items.use: Polite way to leave without buying or to end a sales pitch; it usually means no.
items.kana: ちょっとかんがえます

example.romaji: sou desu ne... chotto kangaemasu.
example.ja: そうですね…ちょっと考えます。
example.english: Hmm... I'll think about it.

items.notes: Casual version: chotto kangaete miru.

items.use: Polite way to leave a shop or counter without buying now.

example.romaji: sumimasen, ato de mata kimasu.
example.ja: すみません、あとでまた来ます。
example.english: Sorry, I'll come back later.

items.notes: Casual version: mata kuru ne.

items.romaji: shichaku shite mo ii desu ka
items.use: Ask a clothes-shop assistant before taking things to the fitting room (shichakushitsu).
items.ja: 試着してもいいですか
items.kana: しちゃくしてもいいですか

example.romaji: sumimasen, kore shichaku shite mo ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、これ試着してもいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can I try this on?

items.notes: Staff usually answer douzo, kochira e (sure, this way).

blocks.label: Bags and wrapping
blocks.rationale: Accept or refuse a bag or receipt and say whether it needs gift wrapping.
blocks.interference: Daijoubu desu here means no thanks, so fukuro wa daijoubu desu turns the bag down.

items.use: Answer when the cashier asks if you want a bag; daijoubu here means no thanks.
items.kana: ふくろはだいじょうぶです

example.romaji: a, fukuro wa daijoubu desu.
example.ja: あ、袋は大丈夫です。
example.english: Oh, I don't need a bag.

items.notes: Bags cost a few yen, so you'll be asked at most tills.

items.use: Asks for a bag at the till; it usually costs a few yen.
items.kana: ふくろおねがいします

example.romaji: fukuro onegai shimasu. hitotsu de ii desu.
example.ja: 袋お願いします。一つでいいです。
example.english: A bag, please. Just one is fine.

items.use: Said when the cashier hands over or offers the receipt.
items.ja: レシートは大丈夫です
items.kana: レシートはだいじょうぶです

example.romaji: reshiito wa daijoubu desu. arigatou gozaimasu.
example.ja: レシートは大丈夫です。ありがとうございます。
example.english: I don't need the receipt. Thank you.

items.notes: A formal receipt for expenses is a ryoushuusho.

items.use: Tells staff you don't need a bag, wrapping or a box; also works for anything you'd leave unchanged.

example.romaji: sugu tsukau node, kono mama de ii desu.
example.ja: すぐ使うので、このままでいいです。
example.english: I'll use it right away, so it's fine as it is.

items.notes: Kono mama means like this, unchanged.

items.use: Tells staff the item is a present so they wrap it; they often ask gojitaku you desu ka? (is it for yourself?) first.

example.romaji: purezento you desu. tsutsunde moraemasu ka?
example.ja: プレゼント用です。包んでもらえますか？
example.english: It's a present. Could you wrap it?

items.notes: Here -you means for, not seems.

blocks.label: Around the office
blocks.rationale: Greet coworkers, head home before others and come back from going out.
blocks.interference: Gokurousama goes to juniors or workers, so saying it to a senior instead of otsukaresama is rude.

items.english: hello; thanks for your hard work (between coworkers)
items.use: The all-purpose work greeting: passing a coworker, starting a call or message, coming back to the office.

example.romaji: otsukaresama desu. kaigi, mou hajimatte imasu ka?
example.ja: お疲れ様です。会議、もう始まっていますか？
example.english: Hi. Has the meeting started yet?

items.notes: Friends say otsukare after a club, a shift or a long day.

items.english: I'll be leaving now, before you
items.use: Said to coworkers still working when you leave; they answer otsukaresama deshita.
items.kana: おさきにしつれいします

example.romaji: kyou wa kore de, osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.
example.ja: 今日はこれで、お先に失礼します。
example.english: That's it for me today. I'll head off before you.

items.notes: Also for leaving a party or meeting early.

items.use: Said on walking back into the office after going out; colleagues answer okaerinasai or otsukaresama desu.
items.kana: ただいまもどりました

example.romaji: tadaima modorimashita. nanika arimashita ka?
example.ja: ただいま戻りました。何かありましたか？
example.english: I'm back. Did anything come up?

items.notes: At home just say tadaima.

items.english: thanks for your trouble (to workers, juniors)
items.use: Said to delivery drivers, guards or juniors doing a job for you; not to your boss.

example.romaji: samui naka, gokurousama desu.
example.ja: 寒い中、ご苦労様です。
example.english: Thanks for coming out in the cold.

items.notes: Said upward it sounds bossy; to anyone above you, use otsukaresama desu.

items.english: thanks for your trouble; good job
items.use: Casual thanks from a boss or older person to someone below them; you'll mostly hear it.

example.romaji: kyou wa gokurousan. mou agatte ii yo.
example.ja: 今日はご苦労さん。もう上がっていいよ。
example.english: Thanks for today. You can head home now.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no naka, gokurousama desu.
examplePolite.ja: 雨の中、ご苦労様です。
examplePolite.english: Thanks for coming out in the rain.

items.notes: Only from higher to lower; never say it to your boss.

blocks.label: Staff making you wait
blocks.rationale: Understand staff saying certainly, one moment, coming, and here you are.
blocks.interference: Tadaima ukagaimasu (coming right away) is not tadaima, I'm home.

items.use: Staff's reply when they take your order or request; no answer needed.

example.romaji: kashikomarimashita. shoushou omachi kudasai.
example.ja: かしこまりました。少々お待ちください。
example.english: Certainly. One moment, please.

items.notes: At work you can say it to a boss or client; wakarimashita is the everyday version.

items.use: Staff say it before checking something or going to get it; just say hai and wait.
items.kana: しょうしょうおまちください

example.romaji: zaiko o kakunin shimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
example.ja: 在庫を確認しますので、少々お待ちください。
example.english: I'll check our stock, so one moment, please.

items.notes: The casual version is chotto matte. On the phone it means you're being put on hold.

items.english: sorry to keep you waiting; here you are
items.use: Staff say it when they bring your order or come back to you, even after a short wait.

example.romaji: omatase shimashita. raamen to gyouza desu.
example.ja: お待たせしました。ラーメンと餃子です。
example.english: Here you are. Ramen and gyoza.

items.notes: Say it yourself when you join someone who has been waiting; with friends just omatase.

items.english: I'll be right with you; coming right away
items.use: Staff call it back when you say sumimasen! and they're busy; just wait a moment.
items.kana: ただいまうかがいます

example.romaji: hai, tadaima ukagaimasu. shoushou omachi kudasai!
example.ja: はい、ただいま伺います。少々お待ちください！
example.english: Yes, I'll be right with you. One moment, please!

items.notes: Tadaima here means right now, not the I'm-home greeting. Ukagau is the humble verb for come or visit.

blocks.label: Staff greetings
blocks.rationale: Recognise the welcome, take your time and come again lines staff say as you arrive and leave.
blocks.interference: Omachi shite orimashita (we were expecting you) gets mixed with omatase shimashita (sorry to keep you waiting).

items.use: Called out by staff as you walk into a shop or restaurant; customers don't reply, a nod is enough.

example.romaji: irasshaimase! nanmeisama desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ！何名様ですか？
example.english: Welcome! How many in your party?

items.notes: At someone's home you'll hear irasshai (come on in).

items.english: enjoy your meal; enjoy your stay; take your time
items.use: Staff say it after serving food or showing you to a room; no reply needed, a nod or doumo is fine.

example.romaji: kochira koohii desu. goyukkuri douzo.
example.ja: こちらコーヒーです。ごゆっくりどうぞ。
example.english: Here's your coffee. Enjoy.

items.notes: Often shortened to just goyukkuri. A host says it to guests at home too.

items.use: Staff say it as you leave a shop or restaurant; no reply needed, or gochisousama deshita after a meal.

example.romaji: arigatou gozaimashita. mata okoshi kudasai.
example.ja: ありがとうございました。またお越しください。
example.english: Thank you very much. Please come again.

items.notes: Often heard as mata okoshi kudasaimase, even more polite.

items.use: Hotel or restaurant staff say it once they confirm your booking; a nod or yoroshiku onegai shimasu is fine.
items.ja: お待ちしておりました
items.kana: おまちしておりました

example.romaji: tanaka-sama desu ne. omachi shite orimashita.
example.ja: 田中様ですね。お待ちしておりました。
example.english: Mr. Tanaka? We've been expecting you.

items.notes: The casual equivalent between friends is matteta yo (I was waiting for you).

items.use: Staff and hosts use it about your coming: yoku okoshi kudasaimashita (thanks for coming), mata no okoshi o omachi shite orimasu (please come again).

example.romaji: mata no okoshi o omachi shite orimasu.
example.ja: またのお越しをお待ちしております。
example.english: We look forward to seeing you again.

items.notes: Never use it about yourself; for your own visit say ukagaimasu.

blocks.label: Getting seated
blocks.rationale: Answer the questions and directions staff give as they seat you.
blocks.interference: Kochira e douzo (this way) is easy to confuse with kochira no reji e douzo (this register).

items.english: how many people?; how many in your party?
items.use: The first thing restaurant staff ask; answer with the number, hitori desu or futari desu, and hold up fingers.

example.romaji: irasshaimase. nanmeisama desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか？
example.english: Welcome. How many people?

items.notes: Also heard as nanmeisama deshou ka. Watch the counting: hitori, futari, then sannin, yonin.

items.use: Staff say it while leading you to a seat or room; just follow them.

example.romaji: oseki e goannai shimasu. kochira e douzo.
example.ja: お席へご案内します。こちらへどうぞ。
example.english: I'll show you to your table. This way, please.

items.notes: You can say it too when guiding a guest. Kochira is the polite word for this way (casual kotchi).

items.use: Staff say it when there are free tables; just pick one.
items.kana: おすきなせきへどうぞ

example.romaji: ohitori desu ne. osuki na seki e douzo.
example.ja: お一人ですね。お好きな席へどうぞ。
example.english: Just one? Sit anywhere you like.

items.use: Asked at a restaurant door or hotel desk; answer hai, then your name + desu, or iie.
items.ja: ご予約はされていますか
items.kana: ごよやくはされていますか

example.romaji: irasshaimase. goyoyaku wa sarete imasu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。ご予約はされていますか？
example.english: Welcome. Do you have a reservation?

items.notes: Also heard as goyoyaku wa gozaimasu ka?

blocks.label: Staff taking your order
blocks.rationale: Follow the waiter asking if you're ready, what you'll drink, whether that's all and if they can clear plates.
blocks.interference: The two gochuumon questions differ only at the end: okimari (ready to order?) versus ijou de yoroshii (is that all?).

items.use: A waiter asks when they come to the table; answer hai, or mou sukoshi (a little more time).
items.ja: ご注文はお決まりですか
items.kana: ごちゅうもんはおきまりですか

example.romaji: shitsurei shimasu. gochuumon wa okimari desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼します。ご注文はお決まりですか？
example.english: Excuse me. Are you ready to order?

items.notes: In many places you call the waiter yourself with sumimasen! or a call button on the table.

items.english: what would you like to drink?; would you like a drink?
items.use: A waiter asks after you order food; answer X o onegai shimasu, or kekkou desu (no thanks).
items.ja: お飲み物はいかがなさいますか
items.kana: おのみものはいかがなさいますか

example.romaji: onomimono wa ikaga nasaimasu ka? hotto to aisu ga gozaimasu.
example.ja: お飲み物はいかがなさいますか？ホットとアイスがございます。
example.english: What would you like to drink? We have hot or iced.

items.notes: Ikaga nasaimasu ka (how would you like it?) also comes with other choices, like size or sauce.

items.romaji: gochuumon wa ijou de yoroshii desu ka
items.english: will that be all?; is that everything?
items.use: Staff check after you order; answer hai, or add something.
items.ja: ご注文は以上でよろしいですか
items.kana: ごちゅうもんはいじょうでよろしいですか

example.romaji: kashikomarimashita. gochuumon wa ijou de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: かしこまりました。ご注文は以上でよろしいですか？
example.english: Certainly. Will that be all?

items.notes: Often shortened to ijou de yoroshii desu ka? Ijou means that's all.

items.romaji: osage shite mo yoroshii desu ka
items.english: may I take your plate?; may I clear this?
items.use: A waiter asks before clearing dishes; answer hai, onegai shimasu, or mada desu (not yet).
items.ja: お下げしてもよろしいですか
items.kana: おさげしてもよろしいですか

example.romaji: kochira, osage shite mo yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: こちら、お下げしてもよろしいですか？
example.english: May I take this away?

items.notes: Sageru here means to clear away.

items.use: Staff's polite word for your order; for your own order you just say chuumon.

example.romaji: gochuumon wa okimari desu ka?
example.ja: ご注文はお決まりですか？
example.english: Are you ready to order?

items.notes: To ask for more time: mou sukoshi matte kudasai.

blocks.label: Convenience store questions
blocks.rationale: Answer the cashier's quick questions about heating, bags, chopsticks and points cards.
blocks.interference: Otsuke shimasu ka (shall I add one?) is easy to confuse with omochi desu ka (do you have one?).

items.use: Convenience-store staff ask about bento and other food; answer onegai shimasu, or daijoubu desu (no thanks).

example.romaji: kochira no obentou, atatamemasu ka?
example.ja: こちらのお弁当、温めますか？
example.english: Shall I heat up this bento?

items.notes: Also heard as oatatame shimasu ka? Daijoubu desu here means no thanks.

items.use: Cashiers ask because bags cost a few yen; answer onegai shimasu, or daijoubu desu (no thanks).
items.kana: ふくろはおつけしますか

example.romaji: fukuro wa otsuke shimasu ka? san en ni narimasu.
example.ja: 袋はお付けしますか？3円になります。
example.english: Do you need a bag? It's 3 yen.

items.notes: Also heard as fukuro wa goriyou desu ka? or fukuro irimasu ka?

items.use: Asked at convenience stores and takeout counters; answer onegai shimasu, or daijoubu desu (no thanks).
items.ja: お箸はお付けしますか
items.kana: おはしはおつけしますか

example.romaji: obentou futatsu desu ne. ohashi wa otsuke shimasu ka?
example.ja: お弁当二つですね。お箸はお付けしますか？
example.english: Two bentos, right? Do you need chopsticks?

items.notes: The same pattern comes for spoons: supuun wa otsuke shimasu ka?

items.romaji: pointo kaado wa omochi desu ka
items.english: do you have a points card?
items.use: Asked at almost every register; answer nai desu, or hand the card over.
items.ja: ポイントカードはお持ちですか
items.kana: ポイントカードはおもちですか

example.romaji: irasshaimase. pointo kaado wa omochi desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。ポイントカードはお持ちですか？
example.english: Hello. Do you have a points card?

items.notes: Omochi desu ka (do you have?) also comes up for tickets, coupons and receipts.

items.english: is a sticker okay? (instead of a bag)
items.use: When you buy one small item, the cashier offers to mark it paid with a sticker instead of bagging it; answer hai.

example.romaji: kochira, shiiru de ii desu ka?
example.ja: こちら、シールでいいですか？
example.english: Is a sticker okay for this?

items.notes: Also heard as teepu de yoroshii desu ka? (tape).

blocks.label: Staff taking payment
blocks.rationale: Follow the cashier through payment method, money handed over, change and one bill or one payment.
blocks.interference: Goissho (one bill for the group) and ikkatsu (one card payment, no instalments) both sound like 'all at once'.

items.english: how would you like to pay?
items.use: Asked at the register; answer kaado de, genkin de (cash), or an app name + de.
items.ja: お支払いはどうされますか
items.kana: おしはらいはどうされますか

example.romaji: zenbu de sanzen en desu. oshiharai wa dou saremasu ka?
example.ja: 全部で3000円です。お支払いはどうされますか？
example.english: That's 3,000 yen altogether. How would you like to pay?

items.notes: Also heard as oshiharai houhou wa? (payment method?).

items.english: out of (the amount you hand over); I'll take that for you
items.use: The cashier says it with the money you handed over: sen en oazukari shimasu means out of 1,000 yen.

example.romaji: ichiman en oazukari shimasu.
example.ja: 一万円お預かりします。
example.english: Out of 10,000 yen.

items.notes: Also said when staff take your coat, bag or card to hold for you.

items.use: The cashier says the amount first, then okaeshi desu, as they hand you the change.

example.romaji: sanbyaku nijuu en no okaeshi desu.
example.ja: 320円のお返しです。
example.english: Here's 320 yen in change.

items.notes: Okaeshi also means a return gift for a present you received.

items.english: all on one bill?; all together?
items.use: Asked at the register when a group pays; answer hai, or betsubetsu de (separately).
items.ja: ご一緒でよろしいですか
items.kana: ごいっしょでよろしいですか

example.romaji: okaikei wa goissho de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: お会計はご一緒でよろしいですか？
example.english: Will that be on one bill?

items.notes: In shops it can also mean all in one bag?

items.use: Asked when you pay by credit card, since installments are an option; answer hai.
items.ja: 一括でよろしいですか
items.kana: いっかつでよろしいですか

example.romaji: kaado de desu ne. ikkatsu de yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: カードでですね。一括でよろしいですか？
example.english: By card, then. In one payment?

items.notes: Bunkatsu means installments; you almost always want ikkatsu.

blocks.label: At the counter
blocks.rationale: Respond when you're called up to the counter and asked if it's for here or to go.
blocks.interference: Omeshiagari (eating, honorific) hides the plain tennai de you answer with.

items.english: for here?; are you eating in?
items.use: Asked at fast-food and café counters; answer hai, or mochikaeri de (to go).
items.ja: 店内でお召し上がりですか
items.kana: てんないでおめしあがりですか

example.romaji: tennai de omeshiagari desu ka, omochikaeri desu ka?
example.ja: 店内でお召し上がりですか、お持ち帰りですか？
example.english: For here or to go?

items.notes: Meshiagaru is the respectful verb for eat and drink.

items.use: Asked at fast-food, café and bento counters; answer hai, or tennai de (for here).

example.romaji: omochikaeri desu ka? fukuro ni oire shimasu ne.
example.ja: お持ち帰りですか？袋にお入れしますね。
example.english: To go? I'll put it in a bag.

items.notes: To ask for it yourself, say mochikaeri de onegai shimasu. Some places say teikuauto.

items.use: Called out at a counter, register or clinic when it's your turn; step forward.

example.romaji: omatase shimashita. tsugi no kata douzo.
example.ja: お待たせしました。次の方どうぞ。
example.english: Thanks for waiting. Next, please.

items.notes: Kata is the polite word for person, as in ano kata (that person).

items.english: this register, please; I can help you over here
items.use: A cashier opening another till calls the next customer over; go to that register.
items.ja: こちらのレジへどうぞ
items.kana: こちらのレジへどうぞ

example.romaji: otsugi no okyakusama, kochira no reji e douzo.
example.ja: お次のお客様、こちらのレジへどうぞ。
example.english: Next customer, over at this register, please.

items.notes: Reji means the cash register or checkout.

blocks.label: Shop staff approaching
blocks.rationale: Recognise staff offering help or inviting you to look, so you can answer with miteru dake desu.
blocks.interference: Nanika osagashi (looking for something?) and nanika goyou (need anything?) are near twins.

items.english: are you looking for something?; can I help you find anything?
items.use: Shop staff ask it while you browse; answer miteru dake desu (just looking) or name what you want.
items.kana: なにかおさがしですか

example.romaji: irasshaimase. nanika osagashi desu ka?
example.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何かお探しですか？
example.english: Hello. Are you looking for anything?

items.use: Shop staff, guides and presenters say it to point you at something; also common in announcements.

example.romaji: kochira no shashin o goran kudasai.
example.ja: こちらの写真をご覧ください。
example.english: Please take a look at this photo.

items.notes: The respectful form of mite kudasai. Douzo goran kudasai means feel free to look around.

items.english: can I help you?; what do you need?
items.use: Staff or a receptionist ask it when you walk up, or someone asks it at the door; say what you want.

example.romaji: sumimasen, nanika goyou desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、何かご用ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, can I help you?

items.notes: Goyou means your business or errand. From a stranger it can sound cool, like what do you want here?

items.english: thanks as always; hi there (shopkeeper's greeting)
items.use: Shopkeepers say maido arigatou gozaimasu to customers; in Osaka a bare maido! is a friendly hello.
items.politeJa: 毎度ありがとうございます

example.romaji: maido! kyou wa nani ni suru?
example.ja: 毎度！今日は何にする？
example.english: Hi there! What'll it be today?

examplePolite.romaji: maido arigatou gozaimasu. mata okoshi kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 毎度ありがとうございます。またお越しください。
examplePolite.english: Thank you as always. Please come again.

items.notes: Literally every time. Maido ari is the clipped market-stall version.

blocks.label: Formal replies at work
blocks.rationale: Answer a request or instruction at work with understood, I'll check, I'll consider it or you're right.
blocks.interference: Kentou shimasu often means a polite no, unlike kakunin shimasu, which promises a real check.

items.use: A polite yes to an instruction or request at work or from a customer.

example.romaji: shouchi shimashita. ashita made ni okurimasu.
example.ja: 承知しました。明日までに送ります。
example.english: Understood. I'll send it by tomorrow.

items.notes: Wakarimashita is fine with coworkers; kashikomarimashita is the shop-staff version.

items.use: Said when you need to look something up or ask someone before answering; staff say it a lot.

example.romaji: sumimasen, chotto kakunin shimasu ne.
example.ja: すみません、ちょっと確認しますね。
example.english: Sorry, let me just check.

items.notes: Casual: chotto mite miru. Staff often say kakunin itashimasu.

items.english: I'll think it over; we'll consider it
items.use: A business reply to a proposal or sales pitch; often a soft no.

example.romaji: sou desu ne, chotto kentou shimasu.
example.ja: そうですね、ちょっと検討します。
example.english: Hmm, let me think it over.

items.notes: Don't read it as a yes; a real yes sounds like zehi or onegai shimasu.

items.english: you're quite right; exactly as you say
items.use: Respectful agreement to a boss, client or customer, often before an apology or a fix.
items.ja: おっしゃるとおりです
items.kana: おっしゃるとおりです

example.romaji: ossharu toori desu. sugu ni naoshimasu.
example.ja: おっしゃるとおりです。すぐに直します。
example.english: You're quite right. I'll fix it right away.

items.notes: ossharu is the respectful form of iu (say). Among friends, sono toori is enough.

items.use: Humble way to talk about your own help, usually in oyaku ni tatete ureshii (glad I could help).

example.romaji: oyaku ni tatete yokatta. mata itsu demo itte ne.
example.ja: お役に立ててよかった。またいつでも言ってね。
example.english: Glad I could help. Ask me anytime.

examplePolite.romaji: oyaku ni tatete ureshii desu. mata itsu demo douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お役に立ててうれしいです。またいつでもどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm glad I could help. Feel free to ask anytime.

items.notes: Plain yaku ni tatsu means 'be useful': kono apuri, yaku ni tatsu yo.

blocks.label: Asking favours formally
blocks.rationale: Open and soften a request to someone senior or a stranger in a formal setting.
blocks.interference: Osoreirimasu works as both thanks and excuse me, much like sumimasen.

items.use: Humble version of onegai shimasu for requests at work, on the phone and from staff.

example.romaji: kochira no shorui, yoroshiku onegai itashimasu.
example.ja: こちらの書類、よろしくお願いいたします。
example.english: Please take care of these documents.

items.notes: Onegai shimasu is enough in daily life.

items.english: sorry to bother you when you're busy
items.use: Opens a request or question to a coworker, a clerk or a teacher.
items.ja: お忙しいところすみません
items.kana: おいそがしいところすみません

example.romaji: oisogashii tokoro sumimasen, chotto ii desu ka?
example.ja: お忙しいところすみません、ちょっといいですか？
example.english: Sorry to bother you, do you have a moment?

items.notes: A set opener; say it even if they don't look busy.

items.use: Polite lead-in before asking a client, staff member or stranger to do something; common in business emails, on forms and in announcements.

example.romaji: otesuu desu ga, kochira ni onamae o onegai shimasu.
example.ja: お手数ですが、こちらにお名前をお願いします。
example.english: Sorry to trouble you, but could you write your name here?

items.notes: Otesuu o okake shimasu means sorry for the trouble I'm causing. With friends say warui kedo instead.

items.use: Staff and business people use it for thanks or before asking a favour; you'll mostly hear it.

example.romaji: osoreirimasu ga, onamae o ukagatte mo yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: 恐れ入りますが、お名前を伺ってもよろしいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, may I ask your name?

items.notes: Osoreirimasu ga at the start works like a very polite sumimasen ga.

blocks.label: Formal apologies
blocks.rationale: Apologise seriously at work or to a customer for a mistake or trouble caused.
blocks.interference: Moushiwake arimasen and gozaimasen are the same apology; gozaimasen is the politer staff form.

items.use: A serious apology at work or to customers, for a mistake or an inconvenience.
items.kana: もうしわけありません

example.romaji: hontou ni moushiwake arimasen. sugu ni naoshimasu.
example.ja: 本当に申し訳ありません。すぐに直します。
example.english: I'm truly sorry. I'll fix it right away.

items.notes: Stronger than sumimasen; the right level for your own work mistakes.

items.english: sorry for the trouble I caused
items.use: Apology to coworkers or neighbours after you caused them trouble: a sick day, a mistake, noise.
items.ja: ご迷惑をおかけしました
items.kana: ごめいわくをおかけしました

example.romaji: kinou wa yasunde shimatte, gomeiwaku o okake shimashita.
example.ja: 昨日は休んでしまって、ご迷惑をおかけしました。
example.english: Sorry for the trouble my day off caused yesterday.

items.notes: Meiwaku is trouble or nuisance. Casual: meiwaku kakete gomen.

items.use: Staff to customers, and in official apologies and announcements.
items.kana: もうしわけございません

example.romaji: omatase shite, moushiwake gozaimasen.
example.ja: お待たせして、申し訳ございません。
example.english: We're very sorry to keep you waiting.

items.notes: You'll hear it far more than you say it; moushiwake arimasen is enough for you.

blocks.label: Business phone calls
blocks.rationale: Open a business call, ask who's calling and promise to call back.
blocks.interference: Orikaeshi (call back) sounds like okaeshi (your change).

items.use: Thanks for continuing help: staff to regular customers, or you to a coworker or delivery driver you see often.
items.ja: いつもありがとうございます
items.kana: いつもありがとうございます

example.romaji: itsumo arigatou gozaimasu. kyou wa nan ni shimasu ka?
example.ja: いつもありがとうございます。今日は何にしますか？
example.english: Thanks for coming again. What'll it be today?

items.notes: To family or friends: itsumo arigatou ne.

items.english: thanks for your continued support (business greeting)
items.use: Opens almost every work phone call or email to a client or partner; the other side answers kochira koso osewa ni natte orimasu.
items.ja: お世話になっております
items.kana: おせわになっております

example.romaji: itsumo osewa ni natte orimasu. tanaka desu.
example.ja: いつもお世話になっております。田中です。
example.english: Hello, it's Tanaka. Thanks as always for your support.

items.notes: The past form osewa ni narimashita thanks someone who looked after you, e.g. when you leave a host family or a job.

items.use: How shops and companies answer the phone, followed by their name; reply with your name and what you want.
items.ja: お電話ありがとうございます
items.kana: おでんわありがとうございます

example.romaji: odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. sakura shokudou desu.
example.ja: お電話ありがとうございます。さくら食堂です。
example.english: Thank you for calling. This is Sakura Diner.

items.notes: Not used on personal calls, where people answer with moshimoshi.

items.english: who is this?; may I ask who's calling?
items.use: Asked politely on the phone or at the door when the person is unknown; answer with your name + desu.

example.romaji: shitsurei desu ga, dochirasama desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼ですが、どちら様ですか？
example.english: Excuse me, but may I ask who's calling?

items.notes: The casual dare? sounds blunt to a stranger. Business calls often use dochirasama deshou ka.

items.english: I'll call you back; we'll return your call
items.use: Business phrase: staff say it when the person you want is out, and you can use it at work too.
items.ja: 折り返しお電話します
items.kana: おりかえしおでんわします

example.romaji: tantousha ga modorimashitara, orikaeshi odenwa shimasu.
example.ja: 担当者が戻りましたら、折り返しお電話します。
example.english: When the person in charge is back, we'll call you back.

items.notes: Casual: orikaesu ne. Orikaeshi denwa kudasai means please call me back.

blocks.label: At the clinic desk
blocks.rationale: Follow reception at a clinic or office asking what's wrong, your name and your insurance card.
blocks.interference: Okake kudasai (have a seat) is easy to mix with omachi kudasai (please wait).

items.english: what brings you in today?; what seems to be the problem?
items.use: The doctor's opening question; answer with your symptom, like nodo ga itai n desu (my throat hurts).
items.ja: 今日はどうされましたか
items.kana: きょうはどうされましたか

example.romaji: konnichiwa. kyou wa dou saremashita ka?
example.ja: こんにちは。今日はどうされましたか？
example.english: Hello. What brings you in today?

items.notes: Dou shita no? is what a friend would ask: what's wrong?

items.romaji: onamae o ukagatte mo yoroshii desu ka
items.use: Reception, phone staff or a booking desk asks it; answer with your family name + desu.
items.ja: お名前を伺ってもよろしいですか
items.kana: おなまえをうかがってもよろしいですか

example.romaji: kakunin shimasu node, onamae o ukagatte mo yoroshii desu ka?
example.ja: 確認しますので、お名前を伺ってもよろしいですか？
example.english: May I have your name so I can check?

items.notes: Ukagau here is the humble verb for ask; a friend would just say namae wa?

items.use: Clinic or pharmacy reception asks for it when you check in; hand over the card.
items.ja: 保険証をお願いします
items.kana: ほけんしょうをおねがいします

example.romaji: hajimete desu ka? hokenshou o onegai shimasu.
example.ja: 初めてですか？保険証をお願いします。
example.english: Is this your first visit? Your insurance card, please.

items.notes: Many clinics now take the My Number card instead: mainanbaa kaado.

items.use: Staff, hosts or interviewers invite you to sit; say shitsurei shimasu as you sit down.

example.romaji: douzo, kochira ni okake kudasai.
example.ja: どうぞ、こちらにおかけください。
example.english: Please, have a seat here.

items.notes: Casual: suwatte. In waiting rooms you'll hear okake ni natte omachi kudasai.
